Interview with Bill Challis
Cassette One
Interview by Ira Gitler

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S
To begin at the beginning, where were you born.
Wilkes Barre, Pennsylvania.
And what was the date?
That's my wife's birthday, July 8. Wilkes Barre, I used to go up to camp around Holmesdale and I know that area a little bit. That was coal mining area.
Very much so. It was the center of the coal mining industry, anthracite coal mining. The soft coal was out in Pittsburgh. Scranton you probably know.

I remember Scranton, because all the counselors used to talk about how they'd go to the whorehouses there. Scranton was famous, and we were just kids, you know, to hear these tales. That was Scranton's fame or infame in those days. This is the 1930's.
Yeah, well, even earlier than that.
I'm sure.
That was the home of the Scranton Sirens. And The Dorseys.
You are going to ask me the questions. Well, again, as I said, beginning at the beginning, was anyone in your family musical?

Well, let's see. Not particularly. My sister played the piano but I was interested in music -- I had a good ear, as far as I was concerned, I could tell it early, and I used to thump out on the piano, you know, without lessons. Harmony and things like that.

My uncle used to do the same thing. My grandfather told me one time that he was a tuba player. They came from England, Wales and we were all musically inclined. We liked music, but there's no one who was particular about seeing that I got to New England Conservatory.

But I did want to get an instrument early. I wanted to take lessons. First of all, they got me a fiddle, got me a violin. You know a violin, if you wanted to get any sounds out of it, it was going to take your three or four years before you could make the sounds, and it was nothing more -- except what Charlie Margulis used to say, mice. So I traded that in soon for a Wurlitzer, a C-melody saxophone. I'd watch the ads.
How old were you then?
I was, let's say, I would say 15, 14 or 15. [PAUSE]
You were with the C-melody.
The C-melody saxophone, well, you know, the Metronome. My sister used to get the Metronome and I'd look through it, and there was always a Wurlitzer ad in there
and tell you that the C-melody saxophone was coming along, you didn't have to transpose, it was all over, and it was no trouble reading, no trouble playing it in no time.

So after the violin this seemed like it would be a pretty good switch to me, so I got one nice shiny gold bell, and I wanted to take lessons this time and learn it right, so I went down to an old clarinet player, a Czechoslovakian. Bohemian he told me, came over and settled in the town and he had a son who played trumpet and another son who played oboe and his daughter would play the piano, and it was a musical family and he had a good musical background, so I went down and he gave me lessons.

Particularly how to blow it, long low tones and I got within a short time, I got a pretty good tone on it and I could -- it was very easy to finger, you know, it's not like the clarinet, where the octave is more than an octave -- this is an octave and it's an octave.

So it was really fairly easy to learn and I don't think I had it a month or more where I was blowing it, still taking lessons, but some of the local guys came around and wanted to know if I wanted to come around and play with them. So one of them came around and told me that they had a job and I'd come along and play. Get paid for it.
Had you been listening to the music of the day, what were --
Yes.
What were the things that you liked.

Well, at that time, there was Whiteman at that time, but there was a lot of -- the Original Dixieland Jazz Band. I listened to a lot of that. Joseph C. Smith. "There Are Smiles That Make You Happy." No saxophone, he just had strings in his orchestra and I think he played in the Waldorf.
I guess the Original Dixieland Jazz Band was 1917.
Yeah.
That's when they recorded.
Right. This was about roughly 1919. Let's see, late 1919 I suppose. I graduated from high school in '21 and I had this when I was about a junior.

And I listened to them and I used to like the band, of course. Who didn't. But the way they did things, they played things like "Margie" and "Strut Miss Lizzie." You know, they used to play -- they'd take a pop tune and put a tune like "Strut Miss Lizzie" or "Sweet Mama, Poppa's Getting Mad" in the middle of it and go back to the tunes they would play and I used to play along with them.
Play along with the records.
Right. Put the record on and play along with it, and they had -- well, they had two or three different saxophone players but the one who lasted with them
was Benny Gruger, if you remember and I used to try to play everything that he played.

I used to listen to the All Star Trio, Wheeler Wadsworth. Wheeler Wadsworth and one of the guys I used to play with later, he was a drummer and he played xylophones. When I worked later with Nat Shilkret and -- Green, Joe Green.
Was the drummer.

They didn't have a drummer, they just had a piano. I think it was maybe Frankie Bennett, somebody like that. Frankie Bennett and maybe Joe Green or one of the Greens. George Hamilton Green and Wheeler Wadsworth, and they used to play one that I copied, that is, no music. By ear. "Just Blue." It was a fantastic C-melody saxophone which the guy played, which Wadsworth played.
It was the blues.
Well, no --
A blues feeling.

That's right. It was "Just Blue" and it had a lot of the blue feeling, yes. But it got all over the instrument. He exploited the instrument from the low register to the high register and that interested me. I later played it as a solo in high school along with some other tune like "Ave Maria" or something like that.
So here you were studying with this Czechoslovakian and then starting to work jobs.

That's right. Non-union jobs. We played with a fiddle player. The usual band at that time was a fiddle, MR. GITLER: MR. CHALLIS: a saxophone, no bottom --^N accordinos, ?^N no accordions. Piano, banjo, and drums. Between the drums and the banjo that's where your rhythm came from but there was really no bottom in those bands. The Dixieland Jazz Band did the same thing.

Now, many of the early bands had tubas and occasionally a string bass, bowed. I played around -- well, first of all, I played a lot of these -- several of these non-union jobs and occasionally there was somebody in there that had played with the union guys and they liked what I was doing so they invited me around to take a job.
This is all in Wilkes Barre and the surrounding areas.

This is mostly in Wilkes Barre. Local, quite local. I was 15, 16 years old. I was really the kid among kids and I was at it all the time, and I mean I enjoyed it and if I weren't com-pahs thumping them with the record out there at the piano, where I got, I imagine a lot of my harmonies. There they were very plain. Plain chords the seventh seldom went beyond seventh, No or ninths elevenths or anything like that. That had to come later.
Did you start improvising on the C-Melody?
Oh, yes, it was all improvising. As a matter of fact, I couldn't read. I flunked my union test,

because I couldn't read. My teacher was on the board and he wouldn't do a thing for me, and then I played with a guy that came around that later played with the Scranton Sirens, a fellow by the name of Fred Smalls and he was a piano player and he had an orchestra and he was quite a piano player and he had drums, banjo, violin and occasionally bass, which I liked.

I liked that bottom. They had a man around there who could play em short. This is before the pizzicato. He was bowing. It was all bow then and some of them just bowed so long, it didn't make any difference to me whether they were there or not. But this one particular guy, he would shorten it up to where he gave a little beat to it, a little rhythm.

This piano player, he had trouble with his saxophone player and the saxophone player, I guess he didn't pay him. The saxophone player took him to the union, so I went down to the union for my second examination and it happened to be at the same time that he was being tried, so he asked the union 'If he's having problems -- he said he can't get a saxophone player,' how about if I used this kid?'
So they said okay. And that's how I got in the union.
Kind of start learning on the job.
Yes. I learned as I played.
Okay, so you're still in high school.
Still in high school. Then I got in

the high school orchestra and that was a -- there were several who played jobs. guys there, several musicians there, A drummer who played quite a bit around, a piano player who played around quite a bit and we had another saxophone player there, a trumpet player.

-- one or two of the fiddle players -- They played around and they were quite good and they you know, seemed to fall right into it and they took me along. Called up and said, "We're going to play a job here or there," and the jobs at that time ran from 8:00 to 11:00, sometimes 8:00 to 12:00. So this allowed me to -- although my studies suffered -- this allowed me to stay out and play, stay home, in town. No traveling around.
There was a time there and business was quite good. The dance business. There were dances all over the places, so I worked on the average of five nights a week for quite awhile.
What did you do in the summertime?

Well, that's what I did, played in the evening. We have a lake near us they here, that's called Harvey's Lake and there were several pavillions that bands used to come there and played and the local bands would play. It was busy almost every night. There was one outfit there that ran the dances in those days every night but Sunday. Sunday -- Pennsylvania was known for -- couldn't play on Sunday -- its blue laws but I played with a group there, played the whole summer and camped over at the lake with the drummer, So I was getting fairly good, I mean competent, but my reading was

not very good. Just hadn't developed. As a matter of fact, you didn't do much reading. With a The band in those days, well, you were the 2 front-line guys, and the fiddle player with a (inaudible) and both of you maybe would do most of the improvising.
Did you blow on Play the tunes of the day?
That's right. I would hear them on the records. I bought records, I'd hear them on the records and then I'd take them around and I could tell them what the harmony were, was.
You had that gift with the harmony.

That's right. C chord, C7, C4, C7, B-flat and the chords, so forth and the diminished, the augmented chorus, which was were The chords. very popular, very much used in those days. Augmented chorus. I was pretty well acquainted with them all, mostly from piano, and if I could play the melody over and they had an inkling of it once in awhile they'd bring along a commercial orchestration but the choruses you played and verses, lots of verses. Verse of everything. I can remember that.

And if there was a mistake the second time over, I'd get called to the banjo -- we had a good banjo player -- he and the piano player, had a good com-pah piano player, and between the two of them, they would play the right harmony and that, of course, pleased me. I liked that.
And then the improvising was -- you just go along and play pretty much what you heard the Dixieland Jazz Band
playing, the All Star Trio.
Did you hear the New Orleans Rhythm Kings playing.

No, I never did. Never bought their records. I remember -- well, you see there were race records in those days, and the colored records, once in awhile I'd go into a record shop and hear somebody like Johnny Dunn who played trumpet, --
The wah, wah style.

Yeah, and other than that I heard Henry Bussey who played with Whiteman and the trombone player and that was all 'waka waka do' a lot of that and the growl like -- I ran into Miff one day at NBC when we were doing some studio work and he come down from some rehearsal and looks at me with those big watery eyes through his glasses, and said, 'Well, I guess the growl is here to stay.' Typical Miff observation.
Well, there was a lot of that --
How about blues records?
Well, blues, in those days you know were very slow. Not the blues today, not the up-tempo blues.
There was the 'Downhearted Blues' and the 'Crazy Blues.'
Well, the 'Crazy Blues,' yes. From the Dixieland. They didn't play their blues slowly. They
played them the regular dance tempo.
I meant some of the singers like Mamie Smith and Bessie Smith and Trixie.
No.
You didn't hear them.

No, I didn't get into that. Not until months later. Ethel Waters was my favorite and I didn't get into that until later on when I was getting with into the Bix Goldke He band, Vince and I used to sit and listen to her records. But then they were beginning to be used more. When I was coming up in those days, let's say 1920, all the black records were race records.

You had to buy them under the race label and so consequently in the music stores where you'd go in and go into a booth, they wouldn't give you -- you'd have to ask for them, and many cases they didn't have them. Because they were interested in selling "Margie" and things like that that they had a lot of, "Whispering" and "Avalon" and all those things.
The jazz part that I liked was -- I liked Nick LaRocca, the way he played a melody, and I liked the sound of his melody and his cornet.

So that I would say if I ever got excited about playing a jazz chorus, it would be maybe along that line. Or I would be going up and down the -- well, not too much of that. get into I liked to listen to a little bit of rhythm. Most saxophone

players in those days were improvisers -- not like Trumbauer trombone are particularly. He was unique when he came along. Or Johnny Hodges or somebody that played a real meaningful saxophone glissandos, solo. Mostly it was lots of glissandos, noises, let's say. slap-tonguing
But what about the old slack tone idea?
I never did go for that, but there was an awful lot of that. An awful lot. I never did go much for that.
I guess that would come go in the category of noises.

Noises, that was noises. I could do it, almost any saxophone player could do it, but no, I went more for tone quality and I was encouraged to do it that way, play the melody, a lot of them would say "Play it straight, play a nice sounding melody, that's what we want to hear."

So in a band that way, it was I suppose more commercial, if you played some pop tune. Now, if we played the blues -- "St. Louis Blues was a big blues then and it was so slow, even W.C. Handy played it very slowly. But I had played a couple of black dances and you know, they used to almost wrap themselves up, dream around at the very slow pace. You never played them any one-steps. You never played them -- you played very few fox trots. You played blues, you played a lot of --
Slow drag.
Slow drag.
And it was -- I think the white man who got into the playing the blues who gave it an up tempo and dressed it up a little bit so it was a little bit more listenable.
Well, no, let's see.
So this is during your high school career.
This is during my high school.
What steps did you take next?
My next step was I went away to college at Bucknell University.
That's in Lewisburg.

Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and I played with an orchestra there and there was a chap there, a trombone player that I had played with the summer previous. He was from around Wilkes Barre and when I got there, and saw him, I heard he was there, I looked him up -- oh, he said, 'Come around and play with the band and join the fraternity and all that sort of thing.

But they worked every weekend. Friday and Saturday nights. The school had -- it was a coeducational school and they had lots of fraternities. The ladies had their fraternities, and the men they had theirs. So they would space out their dances and it was a small school. There weren't any more than 800 people at the time I got there -- so it's a lot bigger now.

They would space their dances out so that the boys could have the girlfriends and the girlfriends could have the boyfriends and they would go to a dance almost every week or weekend throughout the year, when they could get the band and this fellow, a fellow by the name of Diffendaffer. Diffy they called him. Diffy's orchestra, and we had two banjos. Banjo was rhythm, ukelele, very popular then and we had two banjos and then he had a saxophone player and I went down and played along-side of him.

But it wasn't very long before they had formed another orchestra. There was plenty of work around and we then had the two banjos, piano, drums and a trombone and a saxophone. And that was quite a combination, but everything then was melodic, play the popular tunes of the day, no blues, just -- there were no -- nothing more than that, play fox trots all the time and sometimes a fast one. The one-step was very popular then, if you could get it in.
Around the college they wanted pretty much a little beat and a little fox trot rhythm and waltzes.
No Charleston.

No, we had maybe one or two there that liked the Charleston or the Black Bottom, we would play it, but nobody seemed to be interested in that, you know, the way it came out and the way the records came out, everything was Charleston, every bar was Charleston. The whole thing, it got

monotonous and the band that we had, we played strictly for college crowd. We didn't go out -- very seldom would we go out to a dance hall. So that we had actually the cream of the listening crowd. The enthusiasm was great, when you play a fraternity dance and they all go and a lot of the same ones go to each one, throughout the year. I think they were allowed four in each one.
It doesn't take long for you to practically know everybody there and they come around to hear the music and to dance to it, if they like. We were popular there.

But other things that we used to play there too at the time were things like --- (SINGS) da, ded, ("Song of India" -- ed) Tommy made a record of that. I can't give it out. Well, (figure) to a Wild Rose, " for example, (inaudible) .
Light classical.
Right. " My Heart at Thy Sweet Voice."

Those were very popular with the band and they were well received by your dancing public, because what, it was nice smooth melody. You could get a nice, for a fox trot, you could wind up with a nice walk. And now we haven't mentioned trumpet, haven't got into the trumpet.
Well, the second year at Bucknell, I had the band, I had it the second, third and fourth year, and --
Did you have a special name for it.
Just Challis. (Challis Orchestra) So there was a trumpet

player and a trombone player came in with us and a saxophone player, so I had what, trumpet, trombone, first of all two saxophones and then there was a 4 and then piano, banjo and drums. That's seven instruments, and that was big, and this meant I had to pay another guy, another guy or two, so the prices go up and I used to get a few howls like that from the girls or from the other fraternities.

Well, you know, I was so interested and I wanted to develop this. I wanted to develop an orchestra because well, the bigger orchestras that I listened to, the Whiteman orchestra, the Ray Miller orchestra, they all had two saxophones. the Whiteman at that time had two saxophones and a fellow by the name of Byers, Hale Byers, you know, the guy who played everything.
Gallodoro.
Al Galadora.
Oh, yeah.
Oh, no, he wasn't anywhere around then.
I am going back before you, I can see that.
Well, he had Ross Gorman and PeeWee Byers, they called him.
Ross Gorman's name I'm familiar with.
Yeah, he had a band later too.
Right. PeeWee Byers I don't know.
The two of them. Alto and tenor. Then they had Henry Bussey and this was before Roy Maxey even, you know,

I knew -- you know how you know the names of the guys in the band, but they had -- Fende [Grofé] Freddie was the piano player and of course, Whiteman was still playing fiddle, standing up anyway, but let me see, whether they had McDonald or George Marshall I don't remember.
One or the other who played slide whistle was there.
This was one of your models.

Right, this was the model. Well, they were making most of the popular records. "Whispering," "Avalon," and those things were very popular, "Three O'Clock in the Morning," and you listened to the Whiteman band, because that is where I learned a lot of the tunes, and by this time I was reading a little better and I was writing on some of the parts, to add harmony to them.
What were you studying at Bucknell?

Just a simple arts course, liberal arts. Liberal arts, to get through. Oh, I took Latin, I had several languages. Latin, French. I don't know why I supposed they all helped. I was rubbing elbows. It was the popular thing to go to school in those days.
But you hadn't yet really started studying arranging.
Oh, no. This is all-- what was it Churchill said, "picking up a few things as I go along." Well, yeah, but where I got that was I still knew about my harmonies

and so forth and liking -- I liked harmony better than anything. And so I had four instruments that first year to deal with, so I would write out the two-part harmony and then the other two parts, the trumpet and the trombone, I would have to put them together to get an ensemble, and the way I would accomplish this was I would write out the parts, put a piece over here and then write out the other part and maybe look back to see what I did once in awhile and I would do it all by ear.

And of course, the piano and the guitar parts were the names of the chords. Now, at this time we still had no bottom in the band. The drummer I never bothered with him because he couldn't drum anyway. All he could do was keep a little time with us, most of them was some guy that had a set of drums. He'd have brushes and he would play a little bit on the drums. On the drums, he you better not play. It was mostly on the cymbals and a little bit wire brush.
Wood block.

Well, there were woodblocks there too, but not so much there as when I played around Wilkes Barre. That was a city. They had several theatres and they were more apt to pick up the legitimate. We had good legitimate drummers there. But in college, you know, you just pick up some guy that brings a set of drums or the one guy bought a set of drums just so he could play in the band.
We never paid too much attention to him, just so he
didn't get in the way and then occasionally he'd like to hit the cymbal once in awhile in an open spot, so that went along in the second year.

In the third year, I got another saxophone player. That's three saxophone players, trumpet and trombone and we got along nicely with that. Everything was beginning to sound a little bit better, fuller. Now all this time in the development of orchestras, particularly local orchestras and even back like the Whiteman, where they had two saxophones, that was like maybe my freshman year or something. The tendency was to expand the harmonies and even the recording companies liked that because they were delving into electronics in those days, They would give you the orthophonic and they would give -- I played with an orchestra my freshman year, I went down to Lafayette College to play with a friend of mine and they had a date to make a record at Edison.

So we went down there and if we didn't go into a little room and each one was on a different ladder and each one had a different horn to blow in, and I remember that experience. I never had that after and I -- but that was the experience of the records and when you bought that thick Edison record and they started everything off and "this is by so and so like it was coming out of a distant place, and this would start, the title would give and it's sung by the Edison record -- or made by or something like that," sung by so and so of the Edison

records," and that you could -- it was very pipey, but after that with the Whiteman, you're beginning to get other records that were pretty good, but they all sounded Mickey Mousish, you know, they were up in the upper stratus, there were no heavy basses in there.
Did you get a chance at that time to hear bands in person who you had heard on record and you could tell the difference.
Mostly the local bands, traveling bands.
You didn't get to hear any of the --

I got to hear Whiteman later on, I think. I heard him play a concert at the Masonic Hall in Wilkes Barre and went up with our former piano player, Diffy who lived up near there. We got together, we went in and we heard him do -- Morton Downey was even with him then, because that was later. They did the Rhapsody, we wanted to hear the Rhapsody. Ross Gorman, he played it and I still think he plays it -- he understands it. It was written, it's like it was written for him. And I think he does it better than a lot of the guys who do it today.

Simply because there probably may be better clarinet players, if you know what I mean. They have a better conception of things and the Rhapsody to them isn't anything. You know, as a title and as a song, as an era, it was great but it took
a band of that era to play it too.
Because that's where it came from.

Right. So we went up and heard that and by that time, Whiteman's got a full orchestra. He had a fellow by the name of Don Clark came in the band. I think they had three, maybe four saxophones, but they certainly had four brass, two trumpets and two trombones.

And to make my point, everything was getting fuller. And we come into the ortho-phononic stage a little later of the victrolas to where you could hear the bass, where you could hear the guts of the band, which was important and I found myself leaning towards that, so in my senior year, I had three saxophones and three brass and a bass, and the kids used to scream a little bit at the price but it was never -- we made about five or six bucks and I put in a couple of extra bucks for I was the leader.

So but that's all we did, but we came along and I think we had a pretty good band. Now, we got chances to listen to maybe the Mason Dixon orchestra which was a traveling band, The Waring Banjo Orchestra. Fred Waring.

Well Tom had it then. Fred was still at school while I was there. He was at Penn State which was 60 miles away. But he used to come down. My roommate was their booker, used to write the letters for them to get the jobs, which he did a little bit for us, having the advantage there.
Who was that?

A fellow by the name of Hack Gibson, Francis Gibson. I think his father put a little money in the band or helped him out someway, but anyway Fred would come down and he would come down with a banjo with one of those soft picks and he -- everybody played a banjo in those days, you know, it was all ukelele fingering.

So the Mason Dixon -- then I heard the Scranton Sirens and although I had heard about the Dorsey Brothers, because they were from I think Laneeford, not far away in the coal regions, but I had made up my mind, I had an offer from the Scranton Sirens.
What year was this?
Well, this was -- well, this was early.
Was it '22?

No, '20, '21 maybe. '20 or '21. I got out of high school in 1921. It was before I went to Bucknell and I turned it down. I didn't want to go, but then they had a trumpet player, a piano player that had the band, I can't get all of this straight -- I have to go back a little bit. This fellow Small, Freddie Small, had the band, the guy that got me in the union.
Right.
He later went, he was an excellent

piano player. He went with the Sirens and I saw him one day in Wilkes Barre and he said, "Why don't you come over to the Elks Hall tonight, we're playing. I want you to sit in, and I want these guys to hear you. Well, they didn't have a saxophone player. They had a fiddle, they had a trombone player who doubled on trumpet and a xylophone. And guitar and drums.

And let me see, I think they had a bass, I don't know, but they had a good solid sound and this is the first four-beat drummer I have ever heard. He wasn't a great drummer but the beat was four instead of one, two, one, two, that was wonderful, not what we were used to.

And I enjoyed playing that, it was easier to play. Well, anyway, he asked me to come over to the Elks and sit in, well, he said, "Bring your horn as if you're coming off a job." He rigged this all up, he was that kind of a guy. So he sees me when I'm coming in and I went for it. He sees me out there in the entrance and he tells the leader, Billy Lusdig, "I want to get this kid, I want to get him to sit in. He used to play for me."

So in those days, if you went around with a band, sitting in was something everybody did. So the end of the set was over and he called me over and I set up and played and they liked it. Lusdig liked it and they all liked it, so he wanted to know if I'd play a couple of dates and I said, "No, I got to go to school, my parents want me to go to school."

Well, he said, --he gave me a couple of jobs. He gave me a couple of weekend jobs, Friday and Saturday night, so I played a few of them and then he asked me again if I would go with the band. They were a great coal regions favorite and I turned it down again, and thanked him and all. I had to go to school.

So that was when I was a senior in high school. So I supposed I had that distinction. I was their first saxophone player, although Sid Trucker, I think they had him, but he played mostly clarinet. They didn't like his saxophone playing, his tone. They thought I had a pretty good tone.
So now we used to go around to hear that band, the Dorsey brothers got into that band and oh, eventually the Dorsey brothers got in it, Joe and Eddie got in it. Alphe Evans got in it.
I played with Alphe and I would occasionally get a job up in Scranton.
Joe and Eddie, you mean.
Yeah. Joe Moletti (phonetic) and Eddie Lang. Not while I played with them. This is what I used to go around and hear once in a while.
Is this while you're still at Bucknell.
While I'm still at Bucknell. Before that, or maybe it could have been during the summer I played a couple of jobs in Scranton.
I was going to say, what did you do in the summer during Bucknell. You played.
Yeah, I played all --
Did you keep your own band or did you play with other bands.
Played with other bands, the local bands.

Anyway, I played with a band in Scranton and I played with Alfie Evans and his father. His father was a trumpet player, and Alfie was a fiddle player. He came down and he -- you know, a fiddle was quite a thing in an orchestra in those days and Alfie could play very well. Played very well, and then the next time I run into Alfie he's playing saxophone with the Sirens, he and Jimmy.
We used to play some dances up at Penn State.
Proms.

Not a prom, but a fraternity dance$. House parties, and then we'd go around and hear the various bands. And also these bands would come to Bucknell and play the houseparties, and we'd get a chance to go around and hear them. I sat in with a few there. I sat in with the Warings. I Sat in with Dave Harman and which were all traveling bands.
Now, let's see. Well, the Waring band of course and he wanted me to play with that band and I told him that I couldn't leave school. So we had one time, we had Dave Harman

band which was a good band 30 miles up the river in Williamsport, that was their home base. Now, they came down and I sat in with them. They heard us play a couple of tunes like 'To a Wild Rose,' that type of tune, that type of arrangement or that type of selection is what they were looking for.

Now, they liked to have that in their orchestra, in their repertoire. So now let's see, in my senior year, things went along pretty well. I came out with about 500 bucks over that I had saved and that I was ahead, when I got out -- after paying my tuition.
Now then I didn't know what I was going to do. I got a call in --
You mean, you had more or less made up your mind by then you were going to be a professional musician.

No, I was going to go to law school. And I was a pre-legal student during my third and fourth years, I took up the things that would take me to -- well, you took pre-legal courses in college then. Then you come out and you spend three years, just like a doctor, you spend three, four years either at Harvard or Penn or one of the universities, so I still figured I would do it, but I had a terrific yen to play and to write.
You asked me what I was doing during the summer, if I can go back. During the -- one of these bands that came to
play a house party, I sat in and what's his name, the guy's in the movies now or was. He was a drummer. A real clown. He's a comedian and he used to do a lot of things, but he was in the band.
(Inaudible.)
MR. : McClure.
Fuzzy Knight. Remember Fuzzy Knight, he used to do some singing there. And later he went out in the movies and did a lot of hillbilly stuff. He was a hillbilly.

But this band, they had a job up in Syracuse in a Chinese-American restaurant. The guy came to me one time and he asked me if I'd like to take that job. He said, 'I think your band could do it well and you might like to do a job like that, the thing is you have to play two hours, and -- two hours from 6 to 8 and then you come back at 9 and play until 12. It's a lot of work, but you could get paid reasonably well.'

So I asked some of the guys and if they wanted to do that, and they said, 'We will stay together during the summer' and this was at the end of my junior year, so I'd still have to go back to Bucknell at the end of the summer.

So we took the job, and we went up there with the band and played and had a good time, got very well acquainted with the Chinese food and it was a lot of writing, you have to keep up with the tunes and the band got, you know, what it's got to get better, with all that playing. It got pretty good.
Well, one night there, who walks in but Vincent Lopez,

and he comes in with the manager or some such thing and listens to the band, likes the band and he says, 'They're going to open up a hotel here. Hotel Syracuse. How would you like the job?' He said, 'All we'll do is open it. I'll be there the first night,' and he said, 'You can have the job.' He said, 'You can go to school up here in Syracuse.'

Well, I guess we were loyal Bucknellians. To a man they wanted to go back home, I guess, and show the band off. So we turned that down, but it was a mark, you know, that a guy like Lopez would come along and liked the band. So we played -- that was one summer that we did stay in the business. And we came back to Bucknell and that was before I had a bass.

Then we had the bass and the band began to sound good and solid with a little bottom in it and we hated to give it up, but we had to do that. So I was out about a month, I didn't know what to do and I figured that --
You're back home in Wilkes Barre?
I'm back in Wilkes Barre and I figured that --
What did your family -- what did your father do?
Well, my father was interested in politics, local politics. He had a political job, superintendent of the streets of -- well, how would you call it? Superintendent of the streets was his title.
Improving the roads and keeping the roads --

That's correct. That sort of thing. The road was a road department, and they could have sent me away to school as far as that's concerned, but it was a kick to be able to pay my way. I didn't have to write home for money or anything like that. So now that I'm out, I really didn't know what to do. There was a guy that I had been playing with there, a fellow by the name of Guy Hall. He had an orchestra around there for years, and he wrote the "Johnson Rag," incidentally.

But in those days -- we played it, but in those days it was a different Johnson Rag then when Glenn Miller and Jimmy and Russ Morgan did, made records of it. They added a little bit in there to make it commercial and to -- I think they had some lyrics written to it.

Anyway, I didn't want to play with them. I didn't want to go away to school and come back and play with them, an orchestra I had been playing with. If I couldn't do it myself, why, and I didn't know where to look. I found out later I could have looked a lot of places. I was a stick in the mud guy I guess.
So I went up with a couple friends of mine, up to Delaware Water Gap and played and while I was up there, I think since I only played a couple of nights, I got a telegram from

this Dave Harman who was from Williamsport and he wanted to know if I'd join the band. There's a guy in there, an excellent saxophone player by the name of Joe Venuti and I had known him for sometime and liked him and he played C-melody like I did and he was giving it up, something about his family and he wanted to stay in Williamsport, which he did, so they wanted to know if I'd join them and I joined them. I played with the band and by that time, I was a pushover for taking a year off to save some money and then go back to school.

That would seem to be in my mind and it got there very easily, so I worked with him for several months and I gave -- that's the band that had heard my 'To a Wild Rose' arrangement earlier and liked it, and then of course they wanted me to do some writing. Any kind.
What year was this?

This is now 1925. I got out of school in 1925. So I worked with them for -- into the winter and we used to do some week stands at different places and there was one we did out in Toledo. And Toledo was 60 miles from Detroit, we got an electric car and went up to Detroit. Well, I had a brother there who was married and settled there-and I hadn't seen him for quite a long period. My oldest brother. I hadn't seen him in quite awhile. I thought I'd go see him but also the guys who were in the Scranton Sirens were working with Goldkette.
They had joined Goldkette.
That's right.

They had gone to the Sirens and now they were with Goldkette. There was Fuzzy Farrar the trumpet player whom I played with with one or two jobs with the Sirens and Itzy Riskin, the piano player who came from the south, and Russ and another guy by the name of Cooper. They were up there, and the Dorseys were up there, whom I hadn't met yet.
But you knew who they were.

I knew their work. They were in and out of the town and I was going to school. They were working with the Sirens, so unless I went around to see and hear the Sirens, I never got to meet them, but knew all about them.

Now then --oh, yes, I did hear them. They were with the Sirens at a house party at Penn.State. Maybe a year before or after, but didn't get a chance then to talk to them. Jimmy and Alfie were saxophone players.

Now, let me see, well, I went up one Sunday. We had Sunday off and they were working on Sunday in Detroit, it didn't make any difference. I think Monday was the night they had off, so I went down there and little old home week. Talking to Russ and Fuzzy and Itzy, they were in the band, and I met Jimmy then. So Russ took me down in the cellar, in the Greystone Ballroom, Charlie Horvath, the manager, his office was down in the cellar, way back in the back, so we went down there and he said, "I want you to meet this guy," and he went down talking
to -- we went down and talked to Charlie and Russ said, "Why don't you have this guy make some arrangements for you? He can write$."
This is Russ Morgan.

This is Russ, yes. He was from Nanticoke. I should mention that. And I had played with him at one or two jobs when the Sirens put on some extra men and he was playing, he and Fuzzy Farrar at the Armory, Scranton Armory, so and besides I knew him when he played a couple of jobs around Wilkes Barre, you know, admired his work, his trombone playing and all this (inaudible).

So I never played with him too much, but I knew him and I played with him a few times, but he was conducting the band then. He wasn't playing with the Goldkette band, they had Bill Rank and Spiegel (Newell Willcox -- ed.) and he said, "Why don't you have this guy make some arrangements for you?" he said to Charlie, and he said, "Okay, what do you want to do."

Well, they left me with something to do, I don't know what it was, to tell you the truth, I can't remember but I think it was one of those things like "Ave Maria," something. One of those standards, semi-classic things and anyway, I was going to do it after I got home and send it in. And so I find out that I did -- Tommy was playing down in the Book-Cadillac, Jean had a band in the Book-Cadillac Hotel under Owen Bartlett.
He was a contractor as well.
Jean?
: Yeah.

Oh, he had a lot of bands. He had jobs all around Detroit. But his main ones were the Greystone band is where the one band played and then the other one was the Book Cadillac band, and Owen Bartlett had that, and then he had other little hotels and he free-lanced, he had a job here and a job there and well, you wouldn't remember, but at that time there was a lot of work around, lot of dances, lot of things being done, but -- so I figured I had made a contact and I got home and I wrote out an arrangement. I still had a lot of time before I would go to --
(Recording interruption)
-- writing an arrangement and you were going to go to Penn law school.

I had that in mind in the fall. Now, this was some time during the winter that I was with the Harmán band. Something developed there, anyway, I left him and went back to my hometown, Wilkes Barre, and I played around with Guy Hall, with local bands, made some arrangements for them, just to -- you know, they were busy and I was making a little bit of money, but as I said, one of the reasons I wanted to go to law school, because I didn't want to sit around Wilkes Barre being a musician and I didn't know where to get to a bigger band, or to -- I thought, 'Well, this is not for me, the music business. I had better quit while I'm ahead and I am

prepared to go to law school," so now there must have been three, four months, maybe five months during that winter or spring and summer before I would decide to do this, to go away. At which time I went back to Wilkes Barre and I think, I made the arrangement of something -- I think it was something semi-classical. Anyway it was something that they didn't want as I know the Goldkette band now, so they sent it down to the Book, for the other band.
So I didn't pay too much attention. I didn't hear from them that they wanted more.
How much did you get paid for that?

I don't know. I think I got about 50 bucks. Maybe 25. I don't remember, but anyway I am busy around there and the idea of going to Penn was beginning to jell. I played around there during the summer and one time during -- towards the end of the summer, I am hearing that the Goldkette band is going to come through. I told a friend of mine who I played with, I said, "look, I made that arrangement for them. I don't know if they've played it." Let's see, in the meantime they had -- yes, I must have heard from them, because they had asked me to do another arrangement, an arrangement of "Baby Face."
So I had told them about these guys that I knew, he knew about the Scranton Sirens, there was a Cinderella Ballroom there and I said, "Let's go down and listen to the band."
Where was the Cinderella Ballroom?

In Wilkes Barre, right on the square. So, we went down and I knew, as I said, I knew Farrar and some of the guys in the band. I went up and talked to them and they played the arrangement. Who was in the band? There was Trumbauer in the band, there was Bix in the band. They now had five brass. Three trumpets, two trombones. Three saxophones. Jimmy had gone to New York and they got Trumbauer in there and Don Murray was a fine clarinet player, he played tenor, so actually it worked out well. Anyway, the band sounded great and I had given a trumpet part to Bix. I had given a trumpet part to play jazz and they had -- Given it to
You mentioned Bix. Was this the first time you saw Bix and Trumbauer?

No. When I was at school, I made a trip to New York one time. I never met them, but I went into to hear Ray Miller. I also, when I was at school I bought the records, the dance records, the phonograph records for the fraternity house that I was with and I used to like to listen to Trumbauer and then there was Miff was in the band, and it was very interesting to hear the choruses that they'd take and then they -- I went up one time to the Cinderella Ballroom and Bix is playing there with the Wolverines. I was told, 'Go in and hear this kid, he's good,' and I think he was about 16 then, so I went in and heard him and he was quite good. But I think he left after that from what I

can gather, he left the Wolverines because the Harman guys who told me about it, they played opposite the Wolverines in the Cinderella, and they told me that most of the time Jimmy McPartland had kind of taken his place for about five months or so, a six month engagement something like that.

So that's -- that was hearing, that was my experience hearing him, but here now it was a more mature Bix, and Trumbauer for that matter, and the band was -- it was good, they were on a road trip. The Goldkette band had been split up from out of the Greystone band that spring. They sent part of it which they called the waltz band and they played some job there and then they took the jazz group, took it down to a place called Hudson Lake and there was Bix and Murray and [Howdy] Quicksell (phonetic) and Bill Rank. And Trumbauer. They had a good jazz band there

Now, then, in August they brought them all together again because they were going to go back in to the Greystone. Whether the Greystone closed for the summer or what they did, that summer anyway, I don't know, but the band was taken out and split up. Now, they were putting them together so they booked them on a road trip and one of their stops was the Cinderella Ballroom in Wilkes Barre. So we went into hear them.

They sounded great. So I went up and I met Ray Ludwig (Phonetic) who seemed to be taking charge of the band. He had charge of the arrangements. He beat off, you know, started the band up. So he told me they liked that Baby Face"

arrangement. Great. I told him I was going to go back to school and he said, "How about making some more for us?" This was definite contact with the band, with the actual Greystone band, where before I had contacted the manager and they probably ran over something, they probably fluffed it off, you know, and "send it down to the Book," which could very well happen. Besides they didn't play that kind of music anyway.

I am pretty sure it was one of those semi-classic tunes. Anyway, I said okay. I had time and I made them an arrangement of "Blue Room." At that time, I dumped everything in it. At that time I had used before, what they call a buildup, chord, I hadn't heard anybody else use it. You know, this start on one note, and go through the whole scale. (Sings) and I stuck it in there and oh, boy, they took it. They liked it.

But anyway, I am getting ready to go and it can't be more than four or five days now that I get a telephone call and it's from Ludwig. They're up in a place in Massachusetts, Southboro, Massachusetts. He says, "I'm here with the Goldkette band, you remember me," and I said, "Oh, sure." He said, "Well, how would you like to join the band? Oh, boy. Well, I am going away to school. You would like me to make some arrangements?" and I said, "What will I do with my horn?" and he said "Bring it along."
I had then a baritone, a bass clarinet, if you look at any of those early pictures, everybody played those things.

As many as you could get, and "Bring it along." I guess this is the enticement, "Come on, bring them along, play them all," and so forth. Well, I had quite a problem getting up there with my bag and all my instruments and all I was loaded. And I had to change trains.

Anyway, I got up there and they had a rehearsal the next morning and they played the "Blue Room" for me and a couple of other things. You know, it was a thrill. Here are things, you write something down and the guys play it. Well, the improvised parts to it, these were the things I was interested in, and they played over things like that and beyond your expectations, you know, lift the whole thing right up. It was a kick.

So what to do. Then I got together and talked with Horvath and Sure, I'd like to join the band. I'd like to do this and do that, and they gave me for that time fairly good pay, and told me that they were on their way into New York to record. This is the way they did. They switched -- Henderson went out to the Greystone and they would come and sit in the Roseland Ballroom and of course, it was always about a day that they would overlap when they were both playing in each place.

"Well, we don't have our numbers picked out yet so just take it easy as much as you can and do whatever you want." It was about two weeks that we would get to the Roseland. So I got acquainted with the guys, that is, Trumbauer and Bix played
over his "In a Mist." It wasn't In a Mist then. Ludwig said, "Get him to play that thing for you, and it turned out to be In a Mist later."
He didn't have a title for it then.

Didn't have a title for it. Didn't have it finished. So I went out on the job to hear the band and all the time, I was knocked out. I wouldn't say knocked out, but I was highly impressed. I realized that these guys were way above me. I couldn't figure out what to do.
Were you playing with the band?

No. Well, when he called me into to talk to me, he said -- I asked him, if he wanted me to play -- Do you want Horvath, the manager, if he wanted me to play. What did he want me to do with my horns? "Don't worry about it," but he says, "I'll tell you, why don't you do this. Saxophone players are a dime a dozen. I can get them. I can't get any arrangers." And he said, "We only have seven arrangements." Well, seven arrangements, I guess what he meant by that was of the top tunes of the day, because they played all kinds of things. They played Singing the Blues, they played all those cuties that Trumbauer and Bix -- Trumbauer had a band previously to this in St. Louis and he had PeeWee Russell and he had Bix and he had several other guys there too -- I can't remember their names offhand, but I guess it was a pretty good band, and they worked out a lot of things and of course, when he joined the Goldkette band, he brought

those things along and a lot of them were memorized and a lot of them were put down like -- the Bix part would be written up, Trumbauer's part would be written up and then maybe some other part that they needed. The rhythm wouldn't be in there at all, so they had several of those things that they brought up and they played all -- a lot of Dixieland things that they later made records of with Trumbauer and with Bix, not with Goldkette.

The Goldkette band was a different thing. The only thing that they had and that they had set up was My Pretty Girl which is a fantastic thing anyway, and it had three trumpet, you know, Trumbauer played a great part in that, and the ensemble was good. They also had an arrangement of the --that Don Murray had made. The name doesn't come right now. But it was a fine arrangement. He was an excellent musician. Good arranger. But you couldn't get him to do anything, like a lot of guys.

I remember seeing a picture of him and he seemed like a very handsome guy, too, in fact, at the time that I saw the picture, you know, maybe 15 years ago or so, I drew a parallel with Stan Getz. He reminded me of Getz in this picture. I don't know what he looked like in real life.
I remember at the time -- what's that early tenor saxophone player Jack -- that used to play around New York.
Jack Pettis.
Jack Pettis.
He used to talk a lot about Jack Pettis.
Bud Freeman did too to me a lot.
Really?
Yeah, he mentioned Jack Pettis. He liked Jack Pettis.

MR. CHALLIS: So did Donald Murray. Well, so the band had those arrangements, but actually for nice tunes, pop tunes, they didn't have too many, and they were interested -- the band had always felt that it hadn't had any hits, recorded hits so they were sort of -- I was sort of lying back until they got the arrangements. They went down to New York and they were going to get the tunes to do and that would give me about a week or two weeks, ten days, something like that, to work on some of the tunes.

One of the first things, he says, he asked me, 'Do you score?' I thought, 'What the hell's he talking about? Asking me. Score, you get score paper, and you write it down,' and he explained it to me and I said, 'Oh, I just write out the parts and that's it.' So 'Well, we'll have to get you some score paper' and I didn't know too much and it's naive or stupid to say that. But at that time, I hadn't scored, I didn't know what scoring was all about. The only way to make an arrangement, I thought, was write out the parts and if you made a mistake, you could go back and look it over on the part. So anyway they had some

score paper around there and -- but there was nothing much that I could do except wait for him to come back with these tunes, which of course he never did. We got down into New York. I don't know what I did at that time but it really wasn't too much. But I did go out and listen to the band and got acquainted with the band and I must have done one or two things there, because we hadn't enough things to play, that is, we had a few things to play when we got into the Roseland. But we went in there, the first time we were in there, geez we really sort of knocked them cold. They didn't expect a band like that. Any band with Trumbauer and Bix in it is going to be Fantastic. And Murray and the other guys who were in it also.
But particularly those two.
Would you say essentially it was playing popular music but it had a jazz orientation.
Oh, yes.
Because of the players.
Now, see.
What about Goldkette himself?
Goldkette, he never appeared with the band.
Never.
He ran the business. They used to give a concert, I think once or twice a year. Once a year anyway in the Detroit Athletic Club which was his original

job. Detroit -- Jean was a fine guy, nice guy but he had had I think classical training in Europe, and to my way of thinking he was the kind of guy that played his jazz, his "Maple Leaf Rag" with his foot on the pedal and never let it off. You know, everything ran together. That type. He didn't fit in the band like that.
However, Charlie Horvath, who was the manager was the former drummer before they got Chauncey Morehouse. And from all reports that I heard, he was a fine drummer, very excellent drummer. So --
Who led the band, then, when you were there?
Nobody.
Did anybody get out front?

Well, Trumbauer started telling me about a deal he had to join that band and Horvath said that when he got to New York he could stand up in front of the band. However, the second trumpet player, Ray Ludwig was the guy who was beating off the tempos.
Right, as you said.

Now he started the band all that time, and when we got to New York -- I didn't get into this politics, you know, I didn't know what it was all about because it went back further than I knew anything about. Now, Trumbauer had his own band and I think he was ambitious to be a leader and

to come to New York and make records and to him, I mean, the Red Nichols saga was fantastic, because Red was making himself a pile of money. He only had five pieces to be concerned with and he was going around from this recording company to that recording company with the same arrangements, actually, you know, just play the thing. And he would get paid and I guess he had some sort of a deal where he was getting a percentage, but he was quite an angler and so was Trumbauer.

But he couldn't have turned a page with Red. Red had it made and he had been in New York for a long while and I think all the musicians had respect for Red because he had the business in his pocket as far as he was concerned.
Now, he used to tell me about working for Mike Markel or somebody like that and then we could do something here --
Is this Trumbauer?

Trumbauer. He wanted me to be his arranger, we could do this and do that and you know, and the possibilities were in New York. However, he was crazy about the band, no doubt about that. Now, then, he brought up his -- from St. Louis, as I think I said before, he had "Singing The Blues," he had some of those Dixieland things, like "Clarinet Marmalade Blues" and they had -- they were real flag waver arrangements, really. I know, I got them all together for the NEA,* I did them for the Goldkette thing, that was the concert thing
* National Endowment for the Arts

that I wanted to do, and I got them all there and the only thing is there is no Bix and there's no Trumbauer so I had those things written out in unison, actually for students. I had -- I went to great length to put three trumpets playing the part and with all the inflections and so forth, so when they read it, they would have come out like Bix, certainly not the fire but as close as possible. Written. Same way with Trumbauer.

In octaves or harmony. I didn't want any saxophone player who would try to make the record or try to make the concert to have the stigma of trying to play like Bix or trying to play like Trumbauer, because there is no such thing, as far as I'm concerned.

Well, anyway, so they had those arrangements and they played those. They played those flag waver things and they had a few nice waltzes that they'd play and the band had a good sound, used two megaphones in the trombones, with the baritone and it's a beautiful sound, full and rich, and even Fletcher was -- the guys in his band, they were -- it opened their eyes a little bit. They had a great band.
I don't know if you read Jazz Masters of the Thirties by Rex Stewart, but he had a whole chapter in there on the Goldkette band.
Yeah, I read that.
To show his appreciation.
Well, Don Redman was there, saxophone.
Let's see I think he was their lead and you know, the one and only clarinet player, I liked him, tall, thin fellow.
Buster Bailey.
Buster Bailey and there was the tenor sax, Hawkins. Oh, they had a great band. Really a fine band.
Were they there when you came to Roseland, like the overlapping.
The overlapping --
So you come to New York and that's the first thing you hear.

That's the first thing you hear and besides most of the guys that come up there to listen were musicians. They filled up Roseland and they gave them a lot of enthusiastic support too. And besides to hear both bands --
That would be the thing, if you know that both bands are going to be there on one night, the same night, you're going to go and hear it.

That's right, the place was loaded. And our band got along well. So I'm still waiting for arrangements to make the records and they come up with some dillies. Like 'I'M Looking Over a Four-Leaf Clover,' 'Idolizing' and a waltz thing called 'Hushabye' and oh, I don't know, they came up with several things like that, which in their own way are good tunes, but what they were trying to do was make the band popular. And besides, we had Eddie King there who was trying to suppress

the band. He didn't want any part of Bix. He didn't want any part of the jazz part of the band. He wanted it to be another Whiteman band, something which he was very successful with. and Eddie King, you know, he and Whiteman and Grofé were like that, all in one, and that was the (sings) which I'm a great favorite of, the oompha at that time, it's kept a good tempo, but that was Grofé's (phonetic) style and it was a style of the Whiteman band.

We had a more, aloofal style, and you couldn't make the one, ours go over into their type of thing, which had been very, very successful. So they come up, they're thinking the tunes can do it. They tried, but they didn't come up with anything. The first tune we got that was like anything like what we could do was "Sunday" and then they brought us a trio. They also picked out our singers, so we had Bix Murray, Frank Bessinger, guys like that although good in their own, they were successful, weren't good with us. And then they brought this trio in, a real fo-dodeo type of thing and -- but they did bring Joe and Eddie in, which they figured would -- "We won't use Bix but we'll use Joe and Eddie.

Now that's more improvising than you can get, but it's a different kind of improvising. Eddie King could probably go along with. It didn't hurt anything. So here we got Eddie right in front of the mike playing his guitar and we got a hell of a fine banjo player down there, Howdy Quicksell and

you don't even hear him. You know, they just ran roughshod over some of the things that we had that we could do. Later on we did 'My Pretty Girl' and it was liked by the musicians, which, I guess, that's what we were trying to satisfy and we were trying to make something that would impress the musicians.

The dance public in those days, anyway, it was a different dance public. It wasn't like the kind that would go into the Paramount and clap and scream like Benny Goodman had, which came along with swing. This was the old jazz and to try to impress them you had to things like the slide whistle and some of the tricks that Whiteman had, he had it made and besides they got all good tunes, and besides Shilkret got all the other good tunes. And Roger Kahn got the 'Blue Room' to do. We would have liked to have done Blue Room but Roger, you know, had a little club. He had his own club and he had a hell of a band.

Tommy Gott, Arnold Brilhant, Alfie Alphie Evans and Joe and Eddie. He had a real crackerjack band. We used to go over and listen to it. But these were angles that we couldn't seem to get by. So we went back to Detroit and let's say with out tail between our legs, but we were pretty sure -- waiting for the tunes to come out, nothing happened, but 'Sunday' gave us a little kick, but that was the only one.
So only with musicians did we cut any ice and they used to come up there quite a bit. But, of course, they came

up to listen to Bix and Trumbauer and Don Murray and Spiegel was in the band then. Spiegel used to have some kind of jug tone, and he played a megaphone and he'd play these melodic tunes and waltzes and he used to eat those things up. They liked that. He was the commercial part of our band.
You said they brought in Lang and Venuti.
For the recordings.
Just for the recordings.

Right, and then I would just leave out a part. They would bring in the singers and they would never call up and say, 'Look, they're going to sing this in such and such a key.' But they would just bring in the singer and I would have the arrangement made and they would say, 'We will cut here, play the verse and before you go into the chorus, Eddie, get us into the key you want and Joe, you and Eddie play the backup, in back of the voices.' You never could tell. We couldn't --unless I could get the part, the rhythm parts written out in harmony, you only heard it from Eddie. He was very predominate on the things, but they were a big help, these two guys, and so we didn't have too much trouble recording. We didn't have any rejected, or come back and make it again.
So as far as the recording was concerned, I would say that they didn't accomplish what they set out to accomplish.
They didn't have any hit tunes there. At least they didn't turn out to be hits.
So How long after they got back to Detroit did they come out.

Oh, shortly after. It wasn't too long. Another thing that was done, that seemed to bug some of the guys, the [disc-ers] discos today, is while we were there, and as I say, we were short on arrangements, at least they figured we were, I guess -- maybe it was Ludwig, it could have been Horvath but very often he wasn't around all the time, but Ludwig had charge of the library and that part of the band.
Oh, did I mention that when we got to the Roseland, Trumbauer was standing up in front of the band.
As he was promised.
As he was promised, and Ludwig is still beating off.
That didn't make for such a happy --

No, sir. That doesn't make sense anyway. Well, anyway, but Ludwig he really knew the tempo, he had been playing it for a long time. He had a lot to do with the band, and I'm just wondering what happened between him and Fletcher. They traded off a few new arrangements, so the first thing I know my Blue Room and a couple other things are being played by Fletcher, later, and we had a "Stampede," and

a couple of other things." Stampede" was supposed to have been recorded -- I just got a letter not long ago from Doc Reiker Ryker who has been bugged by some writer and he said, "You were there on the date, but ~~ and he said that you made Stampede, and I get credit for the arrangement. ^ Which You know, I didn't do ^ an's of course -- I am pretty sure I think it's Redmond's composition.

So I wrote back and told him, "Forget about things like that." The guy told him they had made it and I wasn't there at the recording so maybe they did n't make it; but some young kid tells me now that they made it but and it was rejected, so I don't know anything about it. But I think we had a couple other things too that were switched around between the bands.
That was They were a mutual admiration society. ^ We Got along very well with the Fletcher band.
Then they did "Singing the Blues" and I guess they did Bix's chorus.
Fletch?
Yeah.
Oh, yeah, I think I made that arrangement for them. Later on. I worked for Fletcher later on. I made arrangements for him and I made him a lot of things. I did some things of his.
How long were you in New York this first time?
I thought it was two weeks, but it
must have been a month.
This is your first stay in New York of any length, and what were some of the things that were happening that you absorbed there besides hearing Fletcher.

Well, I heard Fletcher and then one night, we went over to the Paracade to Par to hear Roger -- we had been invited over there and he had a very high faluting club, you know, there were fish in the tables and he had put the lights on them and where he had the band, and you could see the fish and then he'd put them out and the floor was lighted up and it was sort of a society place.

Anyway when we went in we had to go in the back way and we sat in the back of the band, off on the side where the waiters went back and forth in front of us. There was Trumbauer and Bix and I and I think a couple other guys. This was our first experience at hearing the band close. He didn't have that band too long, I think only a year or two.

But we were very happy to go to hear it, and then of course Jimmy came around. Murray took sick and Jimmy made a couple of records with us. Let's see I think it was the second time Danny Polo (phonetic) came and played. He made "My Pretty Girl" with us. So I didn't make a point of going around and hear too many bands, to tell you the truth. [They'd] go up to Harlem.
Do you think Redman had any effect
on you or Fletcher hearing those things. folks?
Oh --
Just appreciated them for what they were and you had your own --
I had never heard of Redmond Redman before until I met him there, and I don't think our arrangements are anything alike at all. But --
Sometimes you can get something from someone and you don't go over to their style but yet, you hear something and something seeps in.
You absorb it.
Yeah.

MR. CHALLIS: Well, I was sure taken by the Fletcher band. I liked it, and it was a rhythmical band, rhythmical big band, but all big black bands at the time, all black bands were big, you might say, where the white bands -- we had one of the few, what they call big bands. At that time there were very few bands that had three trumpets, three trumpets and two trombones. It was a big -- Whiteman of course had four of each. But then he was around doing theatres and was doing a lot of concerts, that sort of thing.

But the average band -- now, Fletcher had the band and well, I am pretty sure, he had three trumpets and trombone -- two trombones long before that. That was his usual combination, setup.

I can remember hearing Fletcher one time, went down to Nanticoke to hear him, he had King Oliver, Louis Armstrong and somebody else in there. There were three trumpets, those three and they had three saxophones then at least. They had a big band, filled up the whole stage and when they'd blast out at you, open horn. Gosh, it was something to hear because, as I say, a lot of the bands at that time were soft, muted and didn't have too much guts, too much body. They were all in the upper stratas.

An awful lot of them, later on they were called Mickey Mouse bands, but the -- but I usually tied this in with the electronic stage at that time was going beyond the orthophonic and they had said at Victor they were sorry when our band broke up, they were sorry to hear that the band had broken up, because it was only our band and Whiteman that had body to it, and if you'll remember any of those machines that used to come out -- you know, the playing machines. Victrolas. record players,

The next step was a zooming bass. Jess, Jesus, everything was boom, boom, boom. This they figured would sell the instrument. They used to push the bass in, but before that it was beginning to spread out, fill out, and fill a room when you listened to it. Later on they come to the stage today where they say it's like being in the room with the whole symphony. Wow, and all that. It's constantly been building up, and with me, and I am sure with almost every other arranger, you take advantage of that because

you could get the sound, you could get four saxophones, you could get five saxophones, and you could hear them. Before you had to have pretty much, you know, three saxophones or two saxophones and the same way with the brass. You got heavy brass and bands begin to have a larger sound, a larger scope, besides they would have flutes and they would also have the lower register of the saxophone, and the machines would take the recording.

I can remember recording up at Decca when you couldn't do that. I would have something like that in the arrangements. and they would suppress it. Tighten it up. Bring a vocalist in, all the time, that. I would ask one of the guys, "Can't you give me more body?" "No, all you want to hear is the vocal anyway, is what we want." the lead, Jack Kapp had a cigar store Indian out there, right there for the bands -- he can't hear -- he doesn't understand the jazz, give me the melody, and that's true. You probably have heard that.
Yeah, it's amazing.

It is. Well, they were interested in selling records. They had no idea, what arrangers, particularly arrangers were trying to do, trying to develop this and develop that and actually it was to satisfy themselves and maybe get the applause of the musicians who were playing it.
Who really understood.
That's right and as far as the people,

that was something else again. The bands never enjoyed that in those days, seldom, unless you played colleges. Those college kids, they'd be get right up front and listening and listen to the band and talking to the musicians. You'd they'd get a big kick out of that.

But you Id go to a ballroom and never get that. Seldom if ever. The only way you would really appreciate it would be if the crowd got excited and you could feel the pulse and they were in there dancing, but that was when dances got a little bit more active. In those days it was just strictly fox trot.
Cheek to cheek.
Fox trot.
So you're Back in Detroit, records come out, and then what happened?
Well, it was just a development.
Are Bix and Trumbauer still there?
Oh, yeah. And this was settling down now into the steady pace of playing at the Greystone and developing a few things.
Meanwhile, you're not playing your horn, you are just writing.
Yeah, just writing. They made an arranger out of me. So then they still --
Is this about 1927 or when?
Yeah, that was the fall of 1926 and

now this is 1927. This is the snow -- now, in January we came back again and made more records. I don't recall what some of them were, but we were a little more accepted, we had a little better tunes to do, but not much.

Now, the Goldkette organization, I don't want to take it down or anything like that, but it was not -- I have worked for different bands since, of course, and the band leader, he wants to know everything you put down and wants to know what it's all about and he comes around to rehearsal, and "I don't like that in there. Will you change it?" Nothing like that in the Goldkette band. I was there quite awhile before I met Jean over at the office.
Now, they didn't have the organization where there was someone to tell me, "Look, I'd like an arrangement of this, and I'd like an arrangement of that." There was nothing like that.
They just let you go.

Well, they let me go but who to follow, what to do. In other words, where am I going? What am I supposed to do? So I remember Bix and I got together one night and went over to the Goldkette school. Goldkette had a school there, a music school and he had rooms there and we were told that Russ Morgan taught over there a couple of times or taught some things over there; but they had nice grand pianos in there; and we went over there one night after the

job and Bix, you know, he had the interest, he said, 'What do you say we get together and do something?' Oh, fine, I'd love to do something. Well, he said, 'let's do Ostrich Walk,' go over there and sit down and he plays a little bit and I said, 'Okay, I don't even know the tune, how does it go.' So he sits down and plays it and he plays a little introduction, plays the thing over. So we got started on it, you know how it is, you get together and one thing leads to another. 'All right, put this down, let me get that down.' And he plays around some more and let me get this down, let me get that down, and then we get a melody down, so we got a chorus down and we got another chorus and we worked out a saxophone chorus and an ensemble and a couple of things and the first thing you know, we had an arrangement. We were there quite a bit. Took it over a couple of days, and they liked that. Now, this would have been a plan if we had gone on to more Dixieland, but there was just that spotty thing, 'let's do this, let's do that,' and then they come up with a couple other tunes that they had to have, like Jean came around one time and said, 'The Oldsmobile people want me to do -- we're going to play at a party out there and they want a couple of arrangements made, one in waltz and one in fox trot, In My Merry Oldsmobile.' Well, don't you know, I guess they said, 'They'll record it.' So we made it and I had nothing

to do with the vocal. I had made it all instrumental. Well, you know, the guys got together and made a quartet out of it and later on when they went there and they made a record of it, made a record both sides. One side fox trot and the other side waltz and you know, Bix takes off in one of those places. It's a collector's item, guys want to get a record of "My Merry Oldsmobile."
Was he music a lot of the time, you know, on and off the stand? Was he very much into his music as it has been written?

Oh, yeah, fine appreciation for music. Fine. Of course, I have sat with him at nights, nothing else would do, we would go over -- I had a suite in the hotel there and he had a little joint over in a place called the Billinghurst. They used to call them flea bags, and a lot of the musicians stayed there, but how long are musicians in their rooms? Very seldom.

But anyway I had a place, because I had to have a place to work, so we'd come over there and I think his favorite that he liked to listen to a lot was Afternoon of a Faun. We used to listen to that a lot and then the Firebird, of course, "La Mer." and Mamore. All the Debussy and --
How about Ravel?
Ravel.
Now, an American composer was always
mentioned too, who I'm not familiar with, Eastwood Lane.
Eastwood Lane. Absolutely. The Adirondacks -- he used to sit and play.
Were they very much in keeping with the impressionist schools or was it something parallel to that.

Let's see, I think that Eastwood Lane was a guy like Bix. There are several things in there that seem to me he got them from the effect of the Fawn, the orchestral effects. They both loved the orchestra, I'm sure. I didn't know Eastwood, but it's the harmonies that attracted Bix. He used to play -- he played a lot of his own harmony, the same type of thing. Only I think he developed them a little bit differently than Eastwood Lane. But are you familiar with the Land of the Loon.

No, that's what I said. There was just the name, which I have seen mentioned when musicians from that period we are talking about, their interests in the French impressionists, then Eastwood Lane's name would come up and I had never heard any of the things.

I think Eastwood Lane and Beiderbecke were strictly American, not New York American. You know, MacDowell, Adirondacks type of thing with MacDowell, Eastwood Lane, the harmonies, the type of harmonies, beautiful thing and the development of any thematic material. Well, you're familiar with Bix's things.
Yes.
The -- you know, the type of harmonies, the 6ths, the 9ths and the augmenteds how he used his augmenteds, was good, fine. Stuck them in.
The harmony seems like it just shade one into the other.
That's right. Now, he was very clever Bix Writing things like that. Well, we're not up to that stage yet.

But Eastwood Lane, I become more familiar with it, but I was made acquainted with it through Beiderbecke, I would say. He used to -- if we would go to a new job, if we got to a job and there was a piano there, or if after the job, there was a piano there and it's nice, he used to liked to sit down and play it. And he would do this, and he could play -- he was a fine pianist, but not any particular style. He was no Arthur Shutt or no Frankie Signorelli, anything like that.

All those good piano players, but yet he had his own, and sometimes, just a few little notes voiced. Voicing to him was very important and his chords were constructed correctly. I notated all his things and there aren't many, only five and I put them down exactly the way he played them. I made a point of that. They are unorthodox in some places.
His runs, but now he had the ear and the idea of the sound for all this. It was all orchestral and I think

Eastwood Lane is the same way. You can tell the way they put things in the left hand and fill out here, and it was not -- it was not instrumental in the sense that you find -- they didn't know anything about the fiddle, so they don't know any-things about the bowings, the fingerings and so forth of the fiddle, nor of the clarinet. It's put down harmonically.
Comes in the piano.
It's pianistic, and it's pianistic trying to be orchestral, if I'm making any kind of sense.
Yes. Well, what kind of effect do you think his cornet experience had on all this. It was a separate thing?

Now, when Bix wrote his piano things, he had one line melody, that was very few pianistic things in there, but that melody stuck out, and I would say that you could pick out some of these things, and there would be like he could play it on the cornet.

You know, it was in a certain range. Piano you can go all over the piano. You can play up here, it was down around here, you could go from down here up there, and from up there down here. But the cornet you have to stay in a certain range. Now, he does that on the piano. Now, he does that also with few exceptions, few flourishes. He sat down and dictated to me some choruses and that would be for Trumbauer. The chorus of 'Ostrich Walk,' for instance, (sings) , that was for
