saxophone. He had a very good idea, although I know he didn't play sax, he didn't know anything about it. I put it in the key, but he did have the idea of the way he wanted the saxophone to sound, and he used some saxophonistic curlicues or phrases that could be done nicely on a saxophone.

Now, on his trumpet, you know, there was more of a blare, we did a lot of three-part trumpet things together and all I did was harmonize though, like that thing on "Sunday." (sings). Now, that's typically trumpet there. I'd come under his fingers, but the other two guys when they got the other two parts, they followed right along.

That's all rhythmic and that's all cornet style of playing. So he had an excellent idea of that type of instrumentation, and in some of his things, he puts in a few things that could only come out right if you gave them to a horn and woodwinds, a lot.

What do you think about this has been advanced by somebody, I don't remember who about the effect of Bix on Hoagy Carmichael, that some of the songs that Hoagy wrote were really things he heard Bix play and he took those.
I think his Stardust is a little --
It's been said of that. Do you agree with that?
I agree with it to a certain extent, yes. He did a lot of that. Hoagy and I used to be very close.

He did -- I remember when he was doing that and before he got lyrics, he was crazy about (sings) , now that's Trumbauer's part, see. (sings) that's Bix's, see. Now, then Hoagy, he comes in "(Stardust)" you know, it sounds a lot --
It's something he heard.

It seems like he absorbed a little bit of Trumbauer and Bix to do something like that, although I think he's great. Hoagy, especially his early stuff. I did a lot of his early things with him. I mean arranging. I particularly liked the way he did "Washboard Blues." I think he's a real American composer; but he -- naturally he got commercial later on, but the way, our business, the way it is, you can't blame a guy for getting commercial. He's going to starve if he doesn't get commercial somehow or other.
Even some of his later hits like "Buttermilk Sky," it had a very good melody.
Well, he couldn't do anything bad. "Up A Lazy River." He wrote a lot of good tunes and there was one that never got around was "One Night in the band." Did you ever hear of that one?
Might have.
That was quite nice. [Paul] Mertz tells me it's recorded by somebody, but I don't know. I like Hoagy, I like his work.
But you would say he was generally
influenced by growing up and being part of that whole period.
Of course, but he added something to it on his own.
But he certainly liked Bix and he liked Trumbauer and he liked those choruses. I think they had somewhat of --
Everybody who listened to those -- of course, the famous story of Lester Young, told hearing "Singing the Blues" and that's --
Really?
In his style he was very influenced by Trumbauer, but I think everybody was influenced by Trumbauer, all the saxophone players.

Back in Detroit we settled down to an easy pace playing six nights a week, Mondays off. I remember one of those times we went out to Chicago on let's see, a Monday. I think they had Sunday night off, that is, they I am speaking of Ben Pollack. We were great admirers of the Ben Pollack orchestra which at the time had Glenn Miller and Jimmy McPartland and Benny Goodman, particularly.
Had you heard them on record?
Yes, we bought their records.
But you hadn't seen them in person.

I hadn't, but now we -- Trumbauer got this up. He said, 'We'll go sometime, let's go out to Chicago and hear Pollack, who was playing then at this place called the Southmore Hotel and I think he had made some records with the Williams Sisters and they were from Scranton, by the way, right outside of Scranton and I had worked with them. When I was home.

Anyway, so we decided to go. It was quite a trip. Trumbauer had a car, we got his wife and son and Bix and I and we had maybe Bill Rank. We had some guys in there and we decided to go out and listen to the band. Well, it was around dark when we got there, and Trumbauer seemed to know his way around. I hadn't been to Chicago, so they found the place, found the hotel when it was the proper time and we went up and
listened to the band. They played all of their goodies for us. There was Ben Pollack and Benny Goodman.
Did he play drums or did he front the band?

No, he played drums then. Fantastic drummer. "99 to the Bar," he used to tell us, but he was -- they had a feature that they used to do that knocked us out. They'd go along playing a tune you know, and play their choruses and this guy would play his chorus and that guy would play his chorus, and then they'd come to Benny's chorus and the rest of the band would drop out and it would be just drums and clarinet. My God, it was real -- it was great.
Of course, then Benny did it with Krupa later on in his own band.
He did? I never heard him do that.
Well, I mean, 'Sing, Sing, Sing,' the whole thing with the clarinet and the drums, that portion of Sing, Sing, Sing.

I'm not familiar with that. But they did it a couple of times and I remember later on when I was with the Whiteman band, they came to New York and played in a place called the Little Club and they did the same thing there, and you know, it went unappreciated. It was discouraging to see some things come along like that and not have somebody there to appreciate it, only a couple of musicians sitting around.

But they did that to perfection. You could tell all the harmony and Benny would come out with all the harmonies, you know, you listen to him, you knew what the harmonies were that he was playing, and you knew what the harmony of the tune was he was playing. And Pollack, he was a great drummer, he really was.

Well, we made that trip to Chicago and had a big kick -- got a big kick out of it and then we were hanging around the Greystone one night, about -- if the whole bunch of the Ben Pollack band didn't come in, they had come all the way from Chicago to listen to us, listen to the Greystone band. And that was well appreciated. But there they were, let's see, they had Jack Teagarden in the band then and I think Glenn Miller had given up the trombone and was just arranging.

Let's see, I don't know, McPartland -- there was another guy there too, beside McPartland, or after McPartland and he played very well. I forget what his name was. Jimmy told me one time what his name was, but I have forgotten.
But that's a band we really liked; they had a good beat.
They certainly had the soloists.

Yes, they had soloists and they had a good ensemble. We used to judge a band a lot by its ensemble. If it had a good swinging and good moving ensemble, why, that was a plus. Well, then there comes along more toward spring and the band goes on the road for a month.
Now this is the spring of '28?
This is the spring of '27. Still '27 and Cork O'Keefe comes to manage the band and I think he booked the band on the road trip and he had a desk in the office and he and I roomed together.
Where did he work out of? Detroit.

Well, he had been, I think, in Philadelphia; but he came out there and I think he told me later that Goldkette wanted him to come out there and do a lot of booking for the band. Anyway, the band went on a road trip which was to finish off in the month of August in Atlantic City. Well, I guess the road trip in some places, you know, theaters and a couple of places, was quite good, but it got to be a little bit disastrous and if you check back at that particular time the business was beginning to get disastrous for dance bands.

I think radio had been making a few strides towards coming -- towards becoming more prominent and more of a business and the people were beginning to lose interest in dancing, going out to places to dance. Now, so they went through that, and in the meantime I was asked in Detroit if I wouldn't work while the band's on the road, because they were doing one-nighters mostly. You couldn't get to them, couldn't rehearse anything, couldn't get anything, didn't need anything.
Also, another item is that back in those days a

tune could be a hit for about two years. They didn't have the means of communication that they have today. You put a tune out and the next week, you don't know what's going to happen to it. But at least a tune has to be out now four to six weeks anyway and it's heard, and you know, you hear about it.

But in those days, some of those tunes could go for a year, year and a half, two years without -- no problem whatever. Well, anyway, I didn't get out on the road at all with them and it seemed like there were no tunes required for the trip and I was asked to, by a guy in the office there if I wouldn't go down -- well, he went to Jean -- if I wouldn't go down on these boats, they had boats running down to a place called [Bob Lo] which is a little below Detroit. There was sort of a picnic ground down there and you go down the Detroit River to this thing. It's about an hour or so trip and they had a band there, and they'd play on the way down, and on the way back we'd rehearse.
So, okay, I went there and made a few trips down and made a few arrangements, made a few trips down and it happened to be the Casa Loma, which was not then the Casa Loma.
They came out of Canada. Originally.
Well, they were Detroit, all Detroit.
Well, they became the Casa Loma when they played at the Casa Loma, in Toronto.

At the Casa Loma outside of Toronto, right, so what the guy's name now, the head of it, the trumpet player. He had a desk in Goldkette's office and used to book these jobs and he'd keep these guys for as much as he could on the same job. So they got this job for the summer there, going down to [Bob Lo] and then in August, of course, the band went to Atlantic City where I was supposed to go.

I am trying to think of the guy's name, but I can't now, but he had the band. He was the trumpet player who had running this thing up in the band and he got the job as I understand it, at Toronto for this Casa Loma, later on, and he went up there and I guess his band was successful and they stayed up there and they took the name of the place, which was Casa Loma, and became the Casa Loma band about a year or so later.
Where did Glen Gray come in?
Well, he was the saxophone player, but he was --
He wasn't the leader then.

That was much later on. It became a cooperative band. The name is on the tip of my tongue, but they got him out and he had the band and they had all -- they had Tony Brilia (brass) they had a lot of guys that didn't stay after it became cooperative, the bass player, the piano player --
Kenny Sargent.
No.
He hadn't come yet.
He didn't come till later. He's very good. These were guys that were playing jobs around Detroit. There was another guy that played there, he wasn't in that band, but I wouldn't be at all surprised.

Also, I think they called them the Orange Blossoms at that time and they played also, opposite the band, the relief band in the Grays tone. That was one of their jobs and Bob Chester was also -- he's from Detroit, he had a band later on.
I remember.

Well, he was a tenor saxophone player out of Detroit. He played around -- Jean had quite a business working up there. And it was evidently failing, that is, not only from Jean, all of them. It was undergoing a change.
Then when radio got big, radio was a boost to the bands, because you would hear them all over the country.
Right, when they began to use it that way. But at the beginning people wanted to buy radios, I guess, to be entertained.
Stay home.
Right.
So anyway, we got down to Atlantic City in August, the Goldkette band, and I did very few arrange-

ments down there, because I think I started to say before the Goldkette band wasn't very well organized and -- from the administrative standpoint. There was no one there that was -- to say 'We are going in this direction, I want to make six arrangements and we'll go out and try to record them,' anything like that. We're going to lay on a job like in Atlantic City, and there was no incentive, nothing to say, 'Bill, do this or do that, or do whatever you want,' or something like that.

You would have to go around, hang around and wait to find out through different ways what should be done here. But yet they wanted you around. They wanted you to be around for any kind of recording that had to be done, and that used to irk me a little bit, because you feel as if you're not doing anything, not contributing.

So anyway, we were playing at the Pier down there -- this was the -- was it the Steel or the Million Dollar Pier, that's often confused, said Steel Pier, but I think it's the Million Dollar Pier. The band is doing very well, as far as that's concerned, but no tremendous crowds down there. So one night we're around there and who walks in but Jimmy. Now, Jimmy had made several of our recording dates and all the guys knew him anyway and liked him, but he comes in this one night and he's bringing Paul Whiteman, and he's bringing Henry Busse and he's got Bing and the other Rhythm Boys, Barris and Rinker and let's see, he's got Matty Malneck was there. Well, he
had quite a bit and he had talked them all into driving down. I guess he had talked Paul into driving them down --
From New York.

From Philadelphia. They were appearing in Philadelphia at a theatre and I guess after the last show they came down, had enough time. We were very happy to see them, of course, and it was an event. So we got talking between sets and Bix and I went over to Paul and said, 'Why don't you come up on the stand, and conduct the band?' 'I don't know any of the arrangements,' he said. 'You don't have to know the arrangements, beat lead off and the band plays, that's all.' Okay.

He comes up on the stand and he goes off, in the way -- Lawrence Welk all over, a-one and a-two, you know, I think that's where Welk got it. But he used to clown around a lot and he starts that off, 'What will we play?' so they start off with something, I forget, I think it was a thing called 'Sorry,' where the band starts off like a shotgun. Chauncey used to start it off with a revolver, bang, on a rimshot and it was one of Quicksell's tunes.

Well, they get started on that, he's up there and as soon as he's there, it seemed like we had a hell of a crowd. They came from all over and they gather around the stand, which pointed out that this is what our band needed all the time, somebody to stand up.
An identity, personality.

Right, somebody to make the announcements, somebody to sing, somebody to do something. We had guys to sing, and Frankie was in front of the band, but it wasn't the same thing. You could tell when he was up there, he was just standing up, where with Whiteman there's so much presence there that these are my boys, that sort of thing. You don't get that with the other guys. But anyway, the people gather around then he turns around and talks to them. "What do you want to hear?" Well, I can almost tell in his mind what the next tune is going to be, "St. Louis Blues" or one of those things. He didn't care what they said they wanted to hear, he was going to play St. Louis Blues and this is what he did, he turned around and said "Okay," and whatever the guys said out there, or one of them, he'd pick one out and turn around and then they started and the guys right away, if there was any tune they hated to play it was "St. Louis Blues" and you know how you get requests for "St. Louis Blues," in those days at least.

And they started off playing it in such a corny way, (Sings), they started going like that until they realized there's Paul up there and let's not make a fool out of him because actually it was his decision. He made "St. Louis Blues" and this is something we never played. Then they played it and you know, it was faked mostly, and they played it very well. Beautifully, in fact, and at the end of it, of course, this "St. Louis Blues," the applause we got it was tremendous. The
band never got applause like that. What else happened, I suppose, I don't know whether I should say this, but who's standing down at the door just came in, was Jean.
And he wasn't usually around.

He came in and he saw this, even wanted to know who did that. He was upset, but at least he could see for him we didn't mean any harm. We were just trying to make Paul feel good. So the guys, I guess, they went all around Atlantic City, and then Paul came up in the musician's room which was upstairs and we got talking. What are you guys going to do? -- actually what they heard was that the band was going to break up.

See, they couldn't get -- Jean couldn't book the band; O'Keefe couldn't book the band. Horvath couldn't book the band; and they wound up trying to book it in New York, at a place called the New York Club. So Paul had told the guys, he said, 'Well, I'd turn down that job. I don't think it will last ten days.' Anyway, what the guys were going to do they didn't know. They were mulling it over, trying to figure out what they should do and he said, 'Well, any of you guys could come with me, whenever you want.'

Now, Paul had a contract for 44 weeks a year for four or five years, but it was in theatres and then he had a European trip scheduled and then he had his recordings, and let's see, there was something else, recordings and then he

had whatever he could fill in with dance tours and concerts, so here's a guy's not worrying. The Goldkette organization is worried because they can't book the band. It's not any particular guy's fault. It's just that there were very few bands being booked anywhere. The business was bad for them. So what happened with the Goldkette band they had nothing to look forward to but to break up. They didn't know where they were going after Atlantic City.

However, Jean comes down and he has the Roseland booked for two weeks, at which time they want to make some records again. But that was the only thing they had to look forward to. Well, I jumped at the opportunity -- I said, 'I'd like to go.' 'Well, that's okay, you can come along on the 20th of September. Just be at the Paramount and we'll -- we go out from there. We go to Boston, and go to Boston with them.

I was elated and for an arranger, a guy who had just been arranging for a year, here was a band with strings yet. Four, only four of them, but that's they way they used them then. Then he had four trumpets, four trombones. He had eight saxophones, and he was playing theatres and he was playing 1812 Overture and all that junk but all these guys had jobs. Oh, the picture, he had a movie picture in mind. They were going to make a moving picture.
That's the one that came out in 1930.
The King of Jazz, so this to me

looked very solid and besides there was a guy, Ferdie Grofé, who -- I had never met him, but I was always a great admirer of his music ability, his arranging, and then there was Jimmy. He said, "You ought to come with us," and Tommy was in the band then and Red Nichols had left, had been in the band and left and there was some talk of Miff, but I understand that Miff never got to the band. At that time.

And they had, what, here's a guy with a sub-tone, Chester Hazlett and they had so many things that you could use and good musical surroundings, Malneck, and they had a saxophone player, Max Farley and then they had the Rhythm Boys, which didn't particularly appeal to me. You know, I didn't know them -- they also had another trio that they used to use quite a bit. They had six singers, so as far as I was concerned, I was looking forward to September and the end of the job.

So I stayed with the band until the end of that engagement. Then another weekend, down comes Rollini, Adrian, and he said that he wanted to know the same thing, "What are you guys going to do?" And he wants to take all the guys but he won't have Steve Brown. Steve Brown was a big feature in our band, because he plays bass himself, but the bass fiddle is out.
So now he wants Bix and I think he wanted Farrar, it seems Farrar was in that; but Farrar was going to work with Shilkret anyway, and Shulkret (phonetic) was in doing -- what they
call transcriptions and he was big wheel and power down at the Victor and he had four or five radio shows, so he was -- you know, he would be the guy for a guy like Farrar to go with. And he did.

So what's his name took -- he didn't take Itzy Itzy Riscoll -- he didn't know what Itzy was going to do. Let's see, who else -- Chauncey, well he could have used Chauncey too. He went with the New Yorkers, and then he wanted me to go with the New Yorkers and play, back on the saxophone.
Had you played at all in these years?
No.
Not even just to fool around.

Oh, once in awhile, I'd practice and blow a couple of tunes. I filled in one night when Trumbauer had the mole taken off under his eye. He used to have a mole there and he had it taken off. I played, but it was only one night.

So he wanted me to play and arrange, but the difference of playing with that band, the guys would be great, but the difference of playing with them. He was going -- he got the New Yorker job, the Goldkette band didn't get it and Whiteman didn't want it. So this is what these guys had to look forward to, and he also said he could get them a lot of recordings, that he did a lot of recording himself.
So to me there was no choice. I thought it would

be an advancement for me to go with the Whiteman band. There were more instruments, arrangements, a lot more possibilities in the band and as far as Trumbauer and Bix were concerned, it would be logical for them to go with Rollini, but I tried to get them to go with Paul, and no, they didn't want to go there.

So that was my next move, anyway. But the band, in the meantime, as I understand it, they left here and went to Roseland and that's where they made "Clementine," at that particular time. I contributed another arrangement that I did for them. That was strictly a head arrangement. If anybody should have should be Doc Ryker, credit for it, it was Doc Reiker, who used to take the band is conduct and where they were going and what they were going to do very seriously. He was afraid it would break up. He was afraid the band wouldn't go on. He had been in it since its beginning and he didn't want to see anything happen to it if it could be avoided.

So he would be around and he would, I guess he took the orchestration and told Trumbauer to get his saxophone thing, work out a saxophone chorus and then it would give -- well, Bix didn't have -- tell them to woodshed, we had a term then go over in your corner and woodshed these parts and then we'd come back and put the whole thing together.
Now, I think that Doc deserves a lot of the credit for doing that. He told me that he was afraid that they wouldn't get anything done on the date. I think it was down

in Camden that that was made.
Anyway, it turned out fine. Bix played one of his best choruses, and the saxophone chorus was terrific. So I went around to the Paramount and got in touch with Whiteman and he said, 'Okay, we go up to Boston and so be there and go up with us,' so he said, 'Don't worry about doing any arrangements; just get acquainted with the guys in the band and what we do.'
So I joined the band and went out on the road with them. Went to Boston and I think Charlie Margulis joined us soon and Jimmy and Tommy were there, Charlie and let's see --
Charlie?

MR. CHALLIS: Charlie Margose. Shulvret Farrar went with Shulper so I got acquainted with the guys, you know, and kidded around and Jimmy and I became, we were roommates. We went out and Jimmy, you know, was very fine for me to have him in my corner. I -- he's the guy I think that got me in the band and when we roomed together, why we went around to these different towns and he knew everybody there, he had been around and played all around, and he took me around, you know, to some of these places, meet a lot of guys and then on the road, with the Whiteman band, I took some of the old Goldkette arrangements that I had made like Sugar and Sometimes I'm Happy, Just like a Butterfly and a few more things and made them out for the Whiteman band.
Using that instrumentation.

Yes, enlarging it which I always liked to do, so I filled them all out. My God, I used the eight saxophones with a little bass in there. It was brutal, it was just like making a hog of myself with all these instruments. I was pigging it. So we spent about ten weeks that way, there were ten weeks before we come into Chicago and at that time we were going to have a recording date there, going to do some recording, so the time was not yet right to get tunes or anything. So, Jimmy had his car on the road and Curt Dieterle one of the fiddle players, he drove Whiteman's car and Jimmy had to have his car which was a former Whiteman car and he and I would take -- would start about the last day the band would be in and we'd drive to the next town, and boy, I saw a lot of the country that I don't see however I would otherwise see it.

And we went through a lot of college towns and it was in the fall, beautiful. And in the meantime, I didn't hear much from the guys in the band and I just figured they went their separate ways and that the most of them had gone with the New Yorkers with Adrian Rollini.

Let's see, we got to Chicago and -- oh, we got to Indianapolis, and there we ran into Hoagy. In the Whiteman band, they had a little hand organ and Whiteman had the manager, the guy who handled all the instruments, the baggage man besides -- he wasn't exactly a baggage man, but that was his job on the
road, he took care of the music, he took care of everything. He would bring it up to my room in the hotel, and I would have something to work on.
Now, to get to Indianapolis --
Was that a little pump organ.
Yeah, you pumped it with your feet and I didn't like using it much, but I was the kind of the guy that had to -- I had to hear what I was doing. A lot of guys -- see, I'm not studying or anything.
I know. You're still learning on the road.
I'm still lapping things up. So what was important to me was to hear what I had done and to hear the chords and I got a lot of instruments to fill in the chorus, to fill in the parts.

So I am sure I am not doing it in a very orthodox way. I am just taking this section and making that sound and this section and making that sound and I am doing a lot of it on paper but at the same time I still had it here.

We come down to Indianapolis, maybe some time in October. There's a knock on my door about 2 o'clock one morning and in comes three guys, Jimmy, Paul and Hoagy and you know, they had been drinking, enjoying each other's company; but they weren't stewed or anything like that. They came in, you could tell they were having a good time, and Paul says, 'this guy's got a number and I want you to hear it. I want him to play it

for you. I want you to hear it and make it up for us. So get out the organ, " you know, so we get out the organ and Hoagy sits down and plays "Washboard Blues," and he sings most of it, you know, the way he sings --
That nasal --

Not only that, he tries to sing a little bit out of tune and then come back on key, so he went over the whole thing. I liked it very much and said, "I could do that." And they stayed there a little while. I didn't have anything more to drink for them, so Hoagy said he was going to come along with the band for a little while and we could work together, and I said, "Good." There really wasn't much that he could do, because he sang so much of it.

But I had to figure out something to put behind and the [fiddles,] what to do with, so he comes along two or three times and in the meantime some of the guys in the band go over with him, he had come around and Jimmy and Tommy would come over, and they made this "One Night in HANAMA the Band," I think, over there for Gennett. Jenette.
Indiana.

A little outside of the place, so anyway I worked with Hoag and he sits down and sings it over three times and then I figure I got to get a combination on it, to put behind it. I didn't want to put the whole band in it, so I got something down there, you know, no cello or

anything, I got the bass clarinet, and all the clarinets and strings and Matty doubled on the viola, he had a viola he liked to play, so Hoagy plays the thing over and sings it and I put down the accompaniment pretty much the way he plays it, fills it out a little bit.

And then there's Jimmy and Tommy and Bix and Steve. Oh, by this time I had talked to Paul, "How about Steve? I think he'd be good in the band." Steve wasn't the best reader in the world and for all the faking he did, who knows what you're going to do if he played the tune often enough, he's got the part pretty well figured out. But to bow, things like that, which maybe that required, Mike Trafficante was playing the fiddle then, switched over to tuba and that would allow -- Steve also played tuba so the two of them played, things like "1812 Overture" and then Steve played the fiddle. But see, there's all these things to play and I think there are only about four numbers that they played. There was "Chloë" that was a record that sold well, I guess.
And there was "Sundown" -- do you remember that tune?
: At Sundown?

Yes, Jack Fulton sang that and Skin Young sang the "Chloë" and let's see I think there was another number that we did in the beginning, two numbers. One of them I had made an arrangement of. They used two of them, but they were nondescript numbers. They were nice, but nothing had been
done with them. There had been no records made or anything like that. He used them because he liked them.

The rest was stage stuff, you know, you come on with "Rhapsody in Blue," and then I think they did part of something of -- I think they did the Rhapsody in Blue, a piece of cut, you know, and they did that, and then the -- Willie Hall had a spot and the Rhythm Boys had a spot, 20 minutes or so, and then they did "Chloe" and then at the end it was "1812 Overture".

Now, you can get awfully sick, if you're in the band, you got to play that stuff, especially when you got some guys that love to improvise, like Jimmy and Tommy and Steve and well, let's see, at that time Trumbauer and Bix had joined, they joined in Indianapolis.
They finally came with Paul.
Yeah, they came in because they weren't doing -- the band wasn't doing so hot, they had a lot of time on their hands. So they joined the band in Indianapolis, Steve had joined it before that.

So I just figured I'd get a little jazz band in there somewhere on the record, so I had Jimmy, Tommy and I didn't have a piano -- Jimmy, Tommy and Steve and Bix and they played the part. They just played just a chorus or so and then we went back to Hoagy's singing, and geez, it worked out well.
That was our record, and then they gave me a tune by the name of "Changes," a Walter Donaldson tune, awfully nice.

It turned out well. I used all the voices in there. I went to Paul and asked him, I said, 'What do I use or what don't I use?' 'Use whatever you want.' So boy I did. I had everybody and I had the 'sweet' trio, 'sweet' in quotes and that is Johnny Fulton, Skin Young and Charlie Gaylord and then I put let's see, I put Rinker in with them because he could sing a falsetto and I had Bing sing -- he sang the patter. That worked out great, and Steve, of course, spanked his bass on the Beiderbecke part of it, and the vocalists I used in back of Bix and that was like a first, you know.

It turned out good and so did the other record, the Washboard and that and I was off to a good start, so in the meantime I'm working out a couple arrangements with like Tommy and Jimmy, trying to get them set in what they like to do. One night out in Chicago, we played three different theatres in Chicago and one night uptown, or downtown, I don't know what it was. It was near the outside of the city, Tommy comes down and says, 'I'm going to quit.' 'What? Gee, we're just getting started. What are you going to do?'
He didn't want to stay in the band. I didn't know whether he had an argument with anybody or what, but --
Were he and Jimmy fighting with each other then?
Oh, no.
That didn't come till later.

No more than usual. They didn't room together. I was rooming with Jimmy, but Jimmy came around and said, 'The brother's going to quit.' That's the way they talked about each other. Tommy called Jimmy 'lad.' 'Hey, lad,' and he was younger.
Tommy was younger?
Yeah.
For some reason, I remember growing up and not knowing their ages, I always thought Tommy was the older brother.
He was the younger brother. Jimmy was older.
But it appeared that way.

It's just like the band. He had the band, and he knew what he was going to do with it, he made it, he dumped the -- wholesale dumping out of his band, when he wanted to change it. When a guy on the payroll got too big, this is Tommy -- this is the way a band should be operated, you might say. This guy knows where he's going and knows what he's going to do.

So and the same thing with their lives, Jimmy was an easygoing guy. So he said to me, one time, 'The brother's going to quit and I can't talk him out of it.' 'Well, what are you going to do?' So then I got a call from Whiteman, says Tommy wants to quit. He's going to quit. He said, 'Who do you
think I can get in his place? " I don't know. We had a good trombone player in the Goldkette band, Bill Rank, fine, Good, can you get him? " Oh, I think so .

Anyway it was from Chicago I came back to New York and I went up to the Strand where Bill Rank was playing with Shilkret Childrick (phonetic) and I went in and talked to him and he was tickled to death. Oh, yeah, he'd go. So he joined the band then, someplace on the road. Tommy played for a couple of places after that and Tommy was great. He had a little E-flat -- I think E-flat or C-trumpet about that big, that he used to go around playing all kinds of Louis's choruses. He had every one of them memorized, and he would play them all, besides playing his records, backstage, he'd get this little thing out and play it.
The guys used to like to hear him.
I guess he recorded some on trumpet, in those days, he recorded some dates.
He could have done that, I think, had he stayed in the band a little while --
He would have started to play his trumpet.

I think we would have worked -- what I wanted to bring up, is here we had all this talent in the band and yet I blame myself for this, at least for not mentioning it, I could have gone to Paul and said, 'Look,' especially

after the record of Washboard Blues, he was using the Rhythm Boys, he was using Willie Hall out there, of course, they were standard acts. We could have had a good jazz band out of this group. A real ODJB, that would have been great. With The Bix, Trumbauer, Tommy and Jimmy and -- but we never used it. We never got around to doing it.
Yet, Whiteman had the title, the King of Jazz.

Well, I think he was the King of Jazz all right. That was the Jazz Era with Benny, you know, he was King of Swing. Anyway, let's see, we come back and we made a few records, Old Man River and something -- another thing I must say, first, Ferde he was wonderful to me, he took me in. After all I was a real know-nothing, you might say, and there's a guy that had symphony experience and music. He knew what he was doing and for years, he knew what he was doing; but he was awfully nice to me, and he gave me nice tunes to work on.

Very often, I was in the -- I did some work in the show business actually, for theatres and you get four or five arrangers, and also I did it around the studios, I had the experience, of the guys wanting to pick out tunes. They're around with the leader and they want to grab this tune and grab that tune. It was dog eat dog sort of thing, and with Ferdie, he comes up with Old Man River and he comes up with several other tunes, and they were all nice, but I never had this

experience, with Goldkette, and here I run across a guy who is awfully nice about this. The tunes are given to him and he picks a nice one out to give to you. So from the very beginning we got along famously.

Well, anyway, we had the other recordings then in the fall and after that, they're going back on the road again and of course, Bix and Trumbauer had been making their records, you know, in between, whenever they could get to it.
Like those things that came out later, Bix and His Gang and all those kind of things.
Right, whatever came out --
"Goosepimples" and those things.

But this is the fall of -- I think it's 27. -- No, '28. And we have a guy, Jack Robbins, who was a great publisher, I think, and he was in business with Paul. They had a thing called Whiteman Publications and he was hanging around the band quite a bit and he wanted -- like he got Malnyck and Signorelli together to do "Stairway to the Stars," or something like that, whatever they could do, write it down, I'll publish it, and of course, he's figuring Whiteman will play it.

Which is all logical, but it's a step in the right direction, to have a guy like Robbins, he put these things out very nicely. He had a great publishing company to do it. So I got -- he stopped in some place to see me or I stopped in

with him and he said, "You know that thing of Bix's, well, he had a guy up in the office there, that got together with Bix and Bix, of course, along with some of his drinking and a couple of other things, didn't always get together with the guy and he had some problems, he couldn't get it down.

So he said, "I tell you what I'd like you to do," he said, "I'd like you to get that thing of Bix's down on paper." Well, I said, "that's all right with me if it's all right with Bix." "Oh, that would be all right," so Bix was of course -- he thought I should have done it in the first place, but you know a guy with his own team up there, he knew what they wanted to do, so anyway, it didn't work out.

So Bix and I, we got together and we got together first in Philadelphia, it was a matter of being a little diplomatic about getting him -- if he wanted to do a little drinking, get him aside and put it down. He was enthusiastic about getting it down, but boy that "IN" a Mist," that thing came along and it was rough. Sometimes we'd just get together and get a couple of bars and then the band was on the road all the time. I wasn't.

But I'll bet it took us about six months to get that thing down. First of all in about the middle of it, we had finished the part that he had done, most of the part that he had made a record an arrangement of. He does those little things of his that are rhythmical and he plays his piano and then at

the end it ran to about two minutes 2, 15 or something like that, so he sits down there and he improvises and plays it, you know the way he goes, he just went over the thing and just faked along for about a half hour, until he got the three minutes, and that was it. That's the record.

So anyway we got it down and Jack comes along one day and says, 'Look, this is fine,' but he says, 'You know how the Rhapsody in Blue is?' He says, 'You get a lot of those fireworks and so forth, and in the middle you get that theme? Da, da (sings) I'd like him to write a slow theme, a major theme and we add it to this and that will be it.'

Well, that hit Bix fine, in no time at all, he came up with the theme that he wanted. But here again, he didn't do anything like cross-hand piano to get it -- (sings) he didn't it down in the other register. He still sticks in this same register and that's what I say is the same thing with Eastwood Lane, pretty much. They play like they're playing a single line instrument, and they're playing it on a certain part of the piano. And that part they didn't develop. They didn't have the orchestral education; they had the feeling.

So -- and Bix had a couple of nice little things and have, nice little things that can be orchestrated, but he still had this one thing -- he really knew he had to use a trumpet, and saxophone, or an oboe, something in that register, and you would have to orchestrate it so that like when I did this, you
will find it's all like in the one -- in the staff or maybe a little bit above, all the way through the melody. I don't know if I'm making myself clear -- I'm doing a good job of clouding this up.

No. Now, at the same time you were writing different things for Whiteman, I am familiar with a couple of things that have been reissued, which feature Bix and Bix and Trumbauer. I know the one thing, Lonely Melody." Lovely thing.
Yeah, now --
When was that, was that right around that time or was that a little later?

This came -- we did that at Victor, and see, it was not too long after this maybe a year that we changed -- Whiteman changed his affiliation from the Victor over to the Columbia. Now, this was still in the Victor contract. We were still making recordings, arrangements, now mostly over at Lederkrautz. This is where we were doing most of the recording. And then we'd come around and we were working pretty much out of New York, but they're going on the road and in the beginning of this season, I think -- I don't know when we got the Old Gold -- I think that was later, that was later.
But anyway, there's Old Man River, Lonely Melody." We got down to Camden and made a few down there.
Are those the ones with Crosby that Bix and Trumbauer kind of chase choruses on 'You Took Advantage of Me.' Did you do that arrangement?
No, no. Tommy Satterfield, he was in the band then. Very fine arranger, but he didn't stay too long, but then after he left they got Lenny Hayden.
Lenny Hayden.
Yeah, but now that I guess that is a whole year in there, that comes in. Anyway I had any number of things that worked out with Bix, but Bix being away I did some of these three-trumpet things.
He went in and out of the band.
No, no, he was in the band, but the band was in and out of New York.
Oh, in and out of New York, I see.
I stayed in New York, Ferde was over in Jersey, and let's see, we went along about a whole year like that before we changed over to the Columbia. I think -- a little mixed up --
Did you go out to the coast with the band for the movie?
No. Now, --
When did Venuti come into the band?
I think he went out to the coast.
I know he did. He's in the movie,
Yeah, he and Eddie.
Were they there for awhile in the band?
Before the movie.

Yes, I think they became members of the band by then. The band went out and didn't do anything at one particular time, but as far as the recordings now, I want to get back to -- we went along with Victor for quite awhile and we made a bunch of records over at Leiderkrautz and then they -- let's see, at one of the rehearsals over there, Ravel came and visited and we were in the control room and he wanted to know what's that sound. It was Chester's subtone. He hadn't heard anything like that before. They wanted him to evaluate Ferde's compositions. Ferde was making the Grand Canyon Suite and it was another one, another suite that he did before that. The one that Bix played in, the only one he played in as a matter of fact. He wrote a part out for Bix and I remember Bix coming to the rehearsal and going over and over it, rehearsing it and rehearsing it, and he had the reputation of not being able to read so well.

He was no great reader, but he could read, as long as he had guys like Trumbauer and the other guys alongside of him, he knew where he was. Well, let's see, so there was something else I wanted to get said there.
Talking about the recordings.

Leiderkrantz -- we finished up there and then it was shortly after that, it seemed to me, we made a few there, but maybe quite some time before we went over to Columbia, and made all the records at Columbia, and I think -- then we began to get into the Old Gold Show -- oh, going out to the coast, like the first time, I was working here in the city and I got a call one day from Fletcher, you know, he wanted to know if I'd like to do some arrangements for Vincent Youmans. Well, he said, his band was playing at --- Well, yeah, sure, this was "Great Day." It didn't last very long.
But the music did.
Oh, the music was beautiful. I'm a great admirer of Youmans' music anyway, but they were doing it in Columbus Circle, there was a Columbus Circle Theatre.
Circle Theatre.
Yeah, is that still there?
No.
I thought so.
That's where the Coliseum is, where they have the shows, the trade boat shows and all that sort of thing. That's where that was. I remember the theatre. I used to go there.
But it was a jinxed theatre. They had a lot of things there, particularly at that time.
I guess that's the original -- that's
the site where Riesenweber's was, where the Original -- so.
I think it was.
That's the same place, where the Original Dixieland Jazz Band played.

Right. Anyway, so they said, he come on down to the theatre now, because he's here and I talked to him, and he said, 'You can talk to him.' I don't know what had happened, but he evidently couldn't get anybody to do something he wanted, so I went down to the theatre and stayed around awhile and listened --
(Recording interruption)
You say you went down to Youman's rehearsal and nothing ever happened --

Nothing was happened then and he said, 'I got a tune,' he says, and he says, 'I want to have somebody do it and I want you to come over to my office,' and he said, 'There's a girl over there, Marian Harris. She's going to sing in the show and I want you to hear her sing. And make an arrangement,' and fine. I went over there, it was on the 24th floor of some building I used to know, but I don't know it now, and she was in the office there lying down on the couch, she had just come in town and she was tired. He made all the explanations and so forth, and he sat down at the piano and played.
He used to play, he had very full piano and then he'd whistle the melody, and he played it over, whistled the melody,
and so forth and gave me a copy of the first verse, and then he had her sing it.

She sang it beautifully. The verse and the chorus and then he had her do it again and do it again and he was a very understanding man, musician, music-wise anyway and he knew what arrangers -- you know, we got to get the idea. Of course, he wanted you to orchestrate pretty much what he had on the piano, the way he did it. So this was fine. So I took it home and week or so, whenever he wanted it, I had it done. He played it over and she sang -- I thought, 'Oh, God, he doesn't like it. I hope I did the right things,' I was having qualms about it. The phone rang and he gets on the phone and he says, 'Beautiful. Nice, kid, very good, very nice.' So I had done just pretty much what he wanted.

Fletcher liked it, and Hawkins, you know, he comes around later and he says, 'How come you didn't put a chorus in there for me? I wish I had.' Imagine, a real slow ballad -- well, anyway, that was good.

I had to get Whiteman's permission to do that which I got while he was out on the coast. And so you know, I figured it's another connection. It was good, nice experience and it was nice to work with somebody that likes your work. That sort of thing. Ideal conditions.
Well, the band had gone out on the coast and they had been out there for a long time. I had made -- I was so

taken with the tunes that he had: Without a Song, Great Day, "Happy Because I'm In Love and there's another one. Anyway I made them all, sent them out, and they recorded-- Bing recorded More Than You Know." Bing recorded Without a Song and they didn't record Happy Because I'm in Love, but "Great Day," at that time Bix wasn't in the band. He had been sick and he didn't play the chorus on "Great Day." I mention this for a reason. He didn't play it. I didn't like what Andy did.

Andy Secrist played it, and Bix, I know what Bix would have done. It would have been tasty, whatever it was. Andy, I think, smeared all over the thing, but Bing did a great job on it, "Without A Song" (Mildred Bailey -- ed.) Mildred had just come into the band. Bing had brought around Mildred who was Rinker's sister and she had just come into the band. I guess she didn't have anything to do, any songs arranged for her.

So this was her -- she did More Than You Know, and from what I hear -- I never heard it done, they didn't record it -- from what I hear, she did it very well and Paul was crazy about it. But anyway later on after "Great Day" came out, I had told Vince that I was going to send it to Paul and when he heard Great Day he thought Ferde did it. I don't know why. Ferde would have done a fine job, but he said to me, that arrangement that Ferde did -- Ferde hadn't done it

at all, and I guess maybe he was trying to spare my feelings. He said, 'that stinks. That's lousy,' and he said, 'I am going to get it recalled.' You know, he went up to the Columbia office and tried to get them to bring that back if anything is possible to -- you know, not to put it out. And to recall it.

He made a big fuss over it for awhile. I could see his point to a certain extent. Andy has done better choruses, but it's just the way things happened, so it was left in but at that time the band come back and the boys had all been out there and they told me what a wonderful time they had. And the -- but one of the guys got killed. I think Joe was riding with him. Mario Perry. They all had cars, they all had houses and they all got paid, all the time they didn't make the picture.

And you know, all I could hear was, 'You should have been along.' We met so and so and they all had young starlets and things. They must have had a real ball. But the band came back and then they went out again later on to make the picture. When something was straightened out, the book was straightened out and a couple of things, and at that time Paul said, 'You better come out with us this time,' and I said, 'I got a car here and I got an apartment here and I don't know what to do with all that.'
He said, 'Can't you sublet them or something like that, something like that, he said. Anyway he says, 'Okay, if you don't

want to go it's all right." He said, "I have to have somebody here to talk with Phil [Kornhiser] and a couple of the guys that the -- the publishers and get tunes from them and you can do that, and we'll go out.

So they went out and then they made the picture so I had nothing to do with it. I wasn't in it. I wasn't around when it was done, and they were doing, now, they're doing the Old Gold Show, doing them all from the road, and at the same time business is getting worse and worse and we have had the Wall Street crash.
The Depression.

The Depression has set in. It had set in and went on for a years, you see, before it bothered us. In other words, there were the theatres that they could do, there were the records, but the records were falling off and we had gone over to Columbia. The Victor records, and then the European trip had been cancelled and the picture was a sort of a bust.
(Telephone interruption)
Was I talking about the band went out.
Yeah, you said the picture was a bust.
Well, anyway, the band came back and they played down here at Valley Stream, played a few dates and
waiting for the picture, the release of the picture.
The picture was released in 1930,

That's the date I received. 1930, in June. It came to the Roxy and at that time Paul had been complaining about the band, that the band business was lousy and the only thing that he was depending on mostly was the Old Gold Show and well, anyway, they brought the picture into the Roxy, it could have been May, but anyway at that particular time, they brought it into the Roxy, and Gershwin appeared with them and the Rhythm Boys had not come back with them now, which probably doesn't make any difference, as far as this is the Whiteman thing, but the -- I remember going to the show, the band was there a week and Gershwin had appeared -- they put the show on for a whole week and they didn't draw anybody. It flopped. The whole thing flopped, and they made up their minds by the end of the week that they would continue without the band and just Gershwin would be there to play the "Rhapsody," and they were showing the picture.
So I remember going there one day and I went upstairs and he says, "You're fired."
Just like that?
Yeah, well, you know, then he says, "I'm sorry, but I'm going to have to cut the band down, the way things are going now, he says we can't keep the big band.
So I am going to cut it down to 16 pieces, so I went out in good company. Lenny and I and Joe and Eddie and let's see, there were eight of us altogether.
What about Bix and Trumbauer? Had they gone already, or were they still there.
No, I think -- Trumbauer I think was still there.
Bix had gotten sick.
Yeah, and they never got him back in the band, which is another item that's questionable with all this. There are some guys, particularly the book says that Paul offered him a job.
You mean, Sudhalter's (phonetic) book.

Yeah. Said that Whiteman offered him a job. Well, I'm positive that Whiteman didn't. I wouldn't go out on a limb and say that, but actually I can't say it because I wasn't there, but they didn't get him in there. Bix was the kind of a guy that could, as I say, if Charlie were there and he had good guys surrounding him that could read, he could read. No problem.

But to take a part and mark it, segue down to here, cut here and move down to here, that's studio expertise and Charlie had that and a lot of the other guys in the band had that, but not Bix. Bix wants to know on his part, where do I

come in? What do I do to play? And you write a few things out for him, he'll play anything, as far as that's concerned, but to do that studio stuff, it was not for Bix. I would say. They always say that he wasn't really happy in that situation.

Well, at this time, you know, there's another thing. We're not making many records, we're doing a radio show and this is 18 to 20 numbers patterned after the Lucky Strike, B. A. Rolfe thing, this is 16, 18, 20 numbers an hour and you had to have the cuts, you had everything marked and at your rehearsal, which Roy was now in front of the band --
Roy Barbey? Bargy?

Roy Barbey had the band. Whiteman is in the studio, and -- in the control room -- and it's not a good situation for the band, as it as, when we were all happy. We're not making many records. Particularly because they're not selling. Nobody's records are selling at this time.

This was a new low in record sales and it was not a good situation, so when this comes, I could see it. Everybody else could see it and it was -- the Whiteman band had been lucky for the previous two years to have had these -- to have had that moving picture contract, the Old Gold contract and the contract for the theatres. The theatre contract.
So which was Paramount Republics. Now this -- So the only thing to do is cut down the band. I'm surprised

he even did this. But he cut down the band, he had a job up or someplace up there, in Pelham Heath, or up in the Pelham Parkway for the summer, so he cut the band down to 16 pieces and it was not long after that even Grote got out of there. I think Grote -- it was maybe around that time, I don't know. I don't remember.

But I know eight of us got out at the time and the Rhythm Boys had not come back with the band, so that they only had the other trio and it was getting down with whatever bands were around, big bands, were around at that time, so that he was entering a new phase with his band.

Now, he had to look forward to the radio business. The dance business had gone by and in this radio thing, you know, we weren't -- Ferde and I both, we were not used to that either. We were not you know, "Get this out by 8 o'clock." We were not used to that sort of thing. Barby and Lenny, they were doing five, six arrangements a week. Take a print, cut and paste, take it and throw it together and you take a chorus, I'll take a chorus," that was not the kind of thing that we were used to doing.

Ferde was used to trying to make his stuff, I was used to trying to do mine, and we hadn't for quite some time now, we hadn't been doing things like that, but these guys were now doing a radio type of show which the idea was to make enough arrangements. Paul was paying them 50 bucks for every arrangement, besides their salary and they were making -- in

those days, 300 bucks easily every week, over their salary and the other things that they would do. They were busy enough but they could take that, both of them. They were great at it. Ferde and I were still plodding along on our two a week.
So that's the way it ended, with the Whiteman. Went up to hear the band when we were up in Pelham a couple of times. That was the end.
That was it?
Yeah.
All right, so what did you do after that and let's synopsize this.

Well, I got out of the Whiteman band and I called up Nat or Nat called me up, heard about it and he wanted to know if I'd do some work in the radio and I had been in touch -- I ran into Willard Robinson Rose and he asked me if I would do some things for him and his Deep River orchestra. Bill had still been working with us in the Whiteman band on the radio show, so I don't know what he did, I think he went out to the coast, or he did something else.

Anyway, Willard asked me to do some work for him and I did, so I was sort of free-lancing around, at different places. I did a couple of things, and I also did some work for Don Vorhees and none of this jelled for me because it didn't jell for any of these guys except Nat. And Nat was working you know, he had about five radio -- radio was his bag. So I went to work for
Nat and I worked for him about three years. And the Casa Loma.
And then it became --
They were working one-nighters.
Then it became Glen Gray's -- later.
Not for a long while -- the Casa Loma they were out and they had their problems. You know, some of them wanted to quit. Business was bad. I think --
For everybody.

For everybody, but I had -- I was making arrangements for them, and I also made arrangements for Fletcher. He was up in Connie's Inn in Harlem and this is a nightclub job, a steady job and he was doing a couple extra -- making some recordings now and then so --
You used to go up to Connie's Inn to hear the band actually after you wrote the arrangements.
I also went up to hear them, not only that, I went up there to rehearse them. I went up there --
Who was in the band then, because I know the personnel had -- was Hawkins still there.
Hawkins was there. A fellow by the name of Boone, saxophone player.
Lester Boone?
(Harvey Boone -- ed.)
No, no. Boone, he was the alto player, he copied from a lot of Fletcher's arrangements. Boone and Buster. Well, Boone took Don Redman's place. That was it.
And then I don't Rex Stewart was there then. They got a little guy there --
Dick Vance, was he there?

No. This is a nice-looking little stark fellow and he played pretty good. Can't think -- Harrison was on trombone and then I think the guy from -- that used to be with the -- McKinney's Cotton Pickers, what's his name. With the toupee, played trombone. Clyde something.
Claude Jones.
Claude Jones. And I don't think Kayser Marshall was there.
What arrangements did you do for Fletcher, do you remember?

I did 'My Gal Sal,' I did a 'Stardust' for him. I had them all -- I think I might still have them downstairs. I did quite a number of them, but he got -- after he got out of there, he was having his problems. Everybody's beginning to have problems.
Now, this is what year, about 30 what.
'32, '33 around in there somewhere.
At the height of the Depression.
Right. Then, of course, with radio, Nat had about five shows.
So you were busy with that.
So I became busy with that. I worked for him for about three years.
How did the resurgence of the bands, in the Swing Era, affect you.
This Goodman, about 35, 36 --
I'm an old man for them by this time. I'm in the studio. And they don't particularly want any part of me, I imagine.
You stayed in the studio until '39, right.

I would say so, yeah. At different places and different times. I worked here and there, and the work was getting spotty, although there was a time around there that Glenn Miller, I think, was coming up. He wanted me to do a couple of arrangements.
Did he ask you to do some specific things?
Yeah.
Then he didn't use them?
No, He never used them, but I think they come out somehow or other.
What was the remark you heard later, he made, that came back to you.
I asked him, I said, hey, I called him, you know, 'How about those arrangements?' I wanted to get

some more to do. His band was coming along good, so he said, "We're going to record, why don't you come down?" I went down and he played the thing over and it didn't sound too bad to me, but it wasn't a Glenn Miller type arrangement, evidently.

So anyway, it wasn't that that bothered him. He played the arrangement over and he says, "This is built a lot on Bix's stuff, isn't it, Bix type," you know, so I -- what could I say, "Yeah," and he said, what the hell -- it wasn't any more Bix than I was, but if he wanted to figure it that way, let him figure it.

So anyway, well, he said, "These kids never even heard of him. They don't know anything about Bix." So okay, and you know, I didn't want to force myself on anybody. I know what it was, the first year of my marriage, I wanted to get some work.
You had just gotten married.

I was married that year, because I remember calling. I lived up in 57th Street. I called -- I think that could have been the reason why I called -- I called him to get a check. Anyway it didn't make that much difference. I mean if I was going to do some work I wanted to do it on my own and there was plenty around in the studios.
So I don't know, but there was a lot of this stuff well, it was free-lancing, it was hit or miss, do it there or here. Half of it I don't remember. Then actually -- and then

the Casa Loma they came along and they wanted to pay me off on standby money when they come in and play at the Paramount and they played there quite a bit. They had a Camel show, the 'Camel Caravan' and --
I remember as a kid my mother taking me to see them and I remember Pee Wee Hunt doing 'The Music Goes Round and Round.' That was about 1935 or '6.
In the Paramount.
Yeah, I remember it like it was yesterday. In fact, I just wrote something about that recently in another article.
The dates in there, the time in there,
That song, of course, was the craze at that time. And they had, I guess, one of the -- they must have recorded it, he was doing it as a feature on the stage show.

I don't really recall. I wasn't working with them. As I say, they wanted to pay me off. I was getting at that time 75 bucks everytime I would make an arrangement for them, and I would go out and rehearse them. I did a lot of things with that band but it was good. I was busy with other things, and so I didn't go around for any arrangements, but they wanted to give me 50 bucks and they were getting it from the -- either the Paramount or the Union or somebody and the union was giving me up. That's the way it
works. You get paid off in standby money. 50 percent goes to the union, 50 percent goes to whoever you want to hire, and they wanted to pay me off.
Oh, I worked for Dick Himber, I did a lot of things for Dick Himber on that little group he had called Studebaker Champion. Artie Shaw, was -- he played the subtone clarinet.
I don't remember this.
You don't?
I remember Richard Himber.
Richard Himber, there was Jack Sadey, Sleninsky, the guy that traveled around with the Boston Symphony with Bazhinsky (all phonetics) Freddie Fradkin and somebody else. They had four fiddles.
And Shaw was playing the clarinet.
Shaw was playing the subtone. He only played a chorus. Berley Middles, Arnold Brillhart's wife, played the harp and then we used whatever saxophones or whatever clarinets in the band.
I guess you knew Shaw from around New York anyway.
Oh, yeah, had him -- got Nat to use him, as a side man. He played our -- he was our first saxophone player. This is when he was -- we used to go out and listen to bands together.
Well, anyway, he gets his band together and he's

out. Tommy's got his band out first, you know, and he comes in occasionally with Eli Oversinger was down at Victor and he comes in with, he told me, "The way I do it, I come back in with about 30 arrangements and make them in maybe one or two settings."
: Because the band has already been playing them.

The band has already been playing them out on the road. And I knew a lot of the guys in the band. But I knew Tommy better, you know. I didn't do any work for him, which was all right with me, I didn't look for any work. I was busy in the studios. I was content.
So let's see --
: Then Shaw made his big hit and then he went to Mexico, right, and when he came back --
When he came back, there was --
: What year was that.
It would have to be around the forties, somewhere around there.
: He contacted you.

He was putting together a new band. His lawyer called me up. What was his name? Andy Weinberg. He called up and he said, "Artie's getting this band together, and he would like you to give him a call." So we got together, we went down and made a record before we got the band together, we went down and made a record with Lena Horne.
: Who was that for?
For Victor. I think it came out. At least I got it on tape up there. They guy -- had to get it from some guy. Vince Giordano, I think, gave it to me.
Well, let's see that didn't last too long because he went in the Army -- he went in the Navy.
: But you did some things that Lips Page sang on, with Artie.

With Artie. "Blues in the Night," Take Your Shoes Off, Baby. Several other things. Johnny Guarnieri was in the band then. Georgie Auld. Les Robinson. Fine lead player. Jack Jenney, and his wife sang. She sang This Time The Dream's On Me-" That was recorded.
: I don't know her. If you say the name, I'd probably know it. Who was he married to then?
Bonnie --
(Bonnie Lake -- ed.)
: All right, so Shaw goes in the Navy.
Bonnie -- she wrote -- the Dorsey Brothers when they had a band, she wrote the Dorsey Brothers theme, very talented girl. She's Ann Southern's sister.
: But she sang with Artie Shaw.
She made this record with him. She sang -- she went out on the road and sang, I remember. Jack was you know, and Ray Coniff was in the band. Ray and I were
good friends. I got him to do a lot of work with us. So then let's see, I ran into O'Keefe on the street, and he asked me if I would --
That's when it became Glen Gray's --

By this time it was Glen Gray. They had Dissolved the corporation. All the guys had gone out and they bought them out and only the two of them, and now it's Glen Gray and they went down to Florida one time, in the fall, and they asked me to go down with them there, they said, 'It's a good vacation, you can get with the band, so I went down to Florida, for six or eight weeks.

This was right when the Air Corps was down there. They ran that school down there for the Air Corps -- Clark Gable was down there. I knew a guy who was pretty high up and he wanted me to enlist. I went down and tried to enlist and they wouldn't take me. Later on -- I did the 'Kate Smith Show' too, while that was going on. I did that for three years, and then when I ran into O'Keefe, 'What are you doing,' and so forth, well, the 'Kate Smith Show' was thinking about going off the air and the way things were going, I don't know. It was --
You wouldn't be able to on that show you'd be off during the summer. Get the summer replacements.
So this was a steady job and they were booked up so he said, so I went with the band. I said okay. I went with the band, they treated me well, and that lasted almost
five years.
Till when?
I don't remember.
When did it start.
It was after the Shaw thing. It was in the early 1940's, maybe 1946.
That you ended?
Yeah.
So then what happened. The war is over. The war ends that year.

I was living in Forestville. I bought a house out here, this place, that was 35 years ago? 1944. Well, then things -- there wasn't too much to be done then. I did a few things, what free lanced Himber, Bernie Green and radio and television and then I'm gradually getting out of the picture.
Still we have the 50's and 60's. What were you doing in the 50's and 60's.

I didn't do too much, that I can sometimes think of now. There wasn't much around for me to do. Oh, then there was a time I took a job, an office job for a little by this time over a year. My mind's a blank. I didn't -- I did a little -- I can't think offhand.
What you're saying is that after World War II ended, you really started -- scaling down.
That's right, scaling down. I scaled down after that.
How did you support yourself in the 50's and 60's? Didn't do any freelance writing.
Well, as I said, I did a little, yeah, I did a few things here and there. Not much.
It wasn't until the 70's then when some of these projects were undertaken.
That's right.
How did that come about? Who sought you out.
George Wein had called up one time --
This was before the Wein thing, wasn't it. This Beiderbecke thing.
Oh, Bill Borden -- oh, you mean this. Oh, yeah, well, that's only about two or three years ago.
But I think it was before the Wein and Goldkette thing.
Yes, I guess it was. Yeah, that's right.
This was recorded in '74. So that's five years ago.
That's right. Well, see, I went over to -- I was going over to Jersey and this Platter Club over
there, Hot Platter Club.
Kind of an offshoot of the New Jersey Jazz Society.

Right. They asked me -- oh, Bill Borden is a member of it, and they mentioned in New Jersey Jazz who their guests are and I went over there with my brother and Bill saw us and so he came up and he says, "I just come up to see you. I wondered what happened to you." Well, nothing much. He said, "You got anything around that you would like to record?" and I guess he thought I was a real hot jazz man.
"Anything of Beiderbecke's?" Well, I said, "I have the piano pieces," but that's recorded in 1904, that took me a little while to do --
You mean 1974.

1974, I'd say at least 1973 that was working, because I'm not had another guitar player, and had to work that out, and I couldn't get in touch with -- I couldn't (Bucky Pizzarelli -- ed.) get Bucky because he's busy so I had to piece a couple of things here, piece a couple of things here and work on it, gradually, over and over and over and I finally got the things together, and let's see, the Wein thing came up about that time, I think.
Yeah, right after that.
You were telling me, it didn't go through because
Right.
-- you wanted to do it.
In the meantime I had been working on these things, because I wanted to do them.
The Goldkette thing.

And he called me when I had a lot of them finished. I had tried to get these and put them all together, so that would have been before the guitar. Because I wanted to try to interest somebody in making it for a band. That stuff is hard to get out.
I had to get the records and take them off the record, which is very tedious.
So what did you do for the National Endowment?
Well, I did that.
And it was recorded.
No. They were waiting for me to record it.
Did you do a concert?
I didn't do a concert.
You just did the --
I just did the material and applied for it. My brother got me to apply for that. He dug up the
books and dug up the NEA material and application form for it and so forth.
So where does it stand now.
They want to do it down in Walt Disney place down in Florida.
Disneyworld.

Yes. I don't want to do it that way. You get down there and they give you about four days rehearsal. Similar to Wein's and you know, all you need is a substitute, and you can throw the whole thing right off. I don't want -- especially out of town, although a guy like Joe has been very nice. He wanted me to go to Europe and do it.
Joe.

Venuti. He had traveled all over Europe and he told me that he could get anything he wanted over there in the way of musicians and Sudhalter even wanted me to go to England and do it. 'You could get good musicians over there' and he did some concerts over there and called me up from England and wanted me to come over there, but he didn't want to pay enough. Didn't want to pay the expense.
I don't know how he made out, he must have made out all right. He went up to Williams, and got all the material out of Williams College. He copied it off and took it over there and gave concerts.
What was it doing at Williams College?
That's where the Whiteman collection is.
I see.

All the arrangements, from the 30's Fende's and all Lenny's and Roy's, the whole works, the whole Whiteman library is up in Williams College and I have been up there and it's a -- it's nice. They got a cue, cross-cue, it's beautifully done, and well, what's his name, went up there and copied it all off, had them xeroxed and took them over to England and gave concerts, and they were mostly my arrangements, so --
You didn't get anything from it.
I didn't get anything from it.

Now, recently Time-Life has -- they're going to do a Beiderbecke thing and they hired Sudhalter (Phonetic) and they hired some other guy from the United Nations and he came up here. Then they got a lot of material -- the last time Sudhalter called up and he wanted to know about Bud Livingston. I said well, look, I gave him all the information I had, and I said, 'Hey, you're working for a big outfit -- at that time I would have loved to have something like that -- I said, 'Don't they pay anything for some of this information?' He said, 'No, that's the way they are.' I'll bet he's getting paid.
The guy who was out here, he sent my sister a

beautiful thing there. One of those books.
Let's see how. I had my interest in something --
Well, it must have been something but there were few and far
between, I'll tell you that. And nothing that meant anything.
Uninteresting stuff.
So you went to work in an office.

An office of a cement company.
I was a dispatcher there.
When was this? In the 60's.

The late 60's. There were -- something
happened (inaudible).
So that was about a year, you said.

That was over a year. About a year
and two months. I did a couple of things while I was there.
I did some thing for Bernie Green. Do you know Bernie Green?

I know his name very well, from back
in radio days.

He got some nice things to do on
television.
When did you do this?

Well, I think I did the Ethel Merman
and what's her name, the girl from Texas, Mary Martin, and
the Ethel Merman show. That was special.

When was that, that was in the
early seventies. Was it in the late sixties. It was in the
sixties. Yes, it was in the sixties.
Let's see. I can't pull them out.

Let's go back and talk about some of the personalities that you were associated with, some of your impressions and reminiscences. For instance, we talked about Venuti and he had this reputation for being this wild prankster and even with a mean streak in him and ready to fight at the drop of a hat --

I didn't hear that until late. I never got that. I always got very nice treatment from Joe but actually I put him into some good spots. I mean Goldkette thing, everything we did, I had Joe and Eddie in there.
I was responsible for putting them in, the way I did put them in and it went smoothly, easily and we had no problem.

Now, I worked with Eddie after on several shows around the studios. I worked with Joe on one or two of them. But Joe, I never had that problem. It's always been laughs. Now I hear later he got to be a tough guy to get along with. But as I say I didn't find that.
They were both master musicians.

Fine. Very good musicians. I would like to have used Joe in something that I had done rather -- I had an opportunity to do some things for him because O'Keefe was his manager for awhile, and booked him when he had a band. I went around with O'Keefe to listen to him.
He had a big band for awhile.
Oh, yeah. And I remember a time when I had rejoined the Casa Loma, that it, it was then called the Glen Gray Orchestra, down in Miami.
I went down there with them and we were about to leave and the next guy following us in for his stint was Venuti, so Spike -- you know, he used to be with Goldkette band years ago.
When you say Spike, do you mean Glen Gray?
Yes.
How did he get that nickname because I have seen it.
We have always called him Spike. His name is Glen Gray Knoblauch, and we always called him Spike.
I know I have seen that in the Encyclopedia but I have never seen him referred to as Spike in any of his -- publicly he was Glen Gray.
Anyway you said Spike had been with Goldkette.

No, Joe had been with the Goldkette band. Way back. We're talking about now way back before I got there. So Spike, I guess, maybe could have known him. There was another Spike out there that played violin, Spike Hamilton. He's George Hamilton's father.
I didn't know that, but I knew when
you said Spike then you meant Glen Gray, because I had seen it in the Encyclopedia.
Well, Spike said, he said, "Hey, what do you say we go over to the place, the joint and see Joe and get some laughs?"

So we went over there, the dances ran there. There was this service place, the Air Force place, where all the guys, the enlisted men were there, and draftees and they'd come dancing in this place, and it started at 8 o'clock and finished off at 12:00. No real late stuff there.

So we went over, we got over there a little early while they were setting up. quarter of eight maybe, and we talked to Joe and during those times, everybody was having trouble with your musicians, they are all 4-F's.
Right, everybody was being drafted.

He was having his troubles and we are having ours. And I had charge of hiring them, you see, I couldn't fire them, but I could hire them. And boy I got to try hard not to make a mistake, because there was some real kooks that you'd pick up that they got out of some other band and they were only around because they were 4-F. They would get out and you would try to get the dope on them. "Oh, they play good, but -- and you never knew what the but was so you got them in the band.
And then they'd wind up with tea, smoking tea or
something like that, to excess.

Anyway we went over and there's Joe, we talked to Joe, he had a couple guys there that we knew, and we gabbed and talked about the business and how it was and he was having his problems. He says he's now without two saxophones players.
"What are you going to do?"

He said, "I called up the union this afternoon and asked them to send me two saxophone players to come to the job by 8 o'clock." Well, they hadn't shown up. So they're all tuning up, getting straightened out, getting set up and looked down the door, and in come a couple with saxophones under their arm with -- the way I used to carry mine, with felt, the green felt. They got them under their arms and they come in, and it's a couple of girls.

They come down, hiya, and so forth, and so on, and Joe says, "Sit here, sit here, take this book, take that book." Fine, all right to them. So there's hardly anybody there so they ran over a couple of numbers and he said, "Take one," and the girl takes one and it wasn't bad. I mean, it wasn't good, awful. So Joe's laughing, "Great, great, take another." And he went on like that, and Spike and I had a fit, but we could tell with Joe, he could put up with something like that. It could be rotten, lousy and he'd put up with it and make a joke out of it.
I don't know what the rest of them thought, but it

was really something, and he had the other one do the same thing. We got out of there very shortly, after we said hello and listened to a couple of numbers.
