But to see these girls come in and have them set and happened right off, give them a chorus, to take, He wanted to hear everything they could do and it was pretty bad. "Take another."
What about Bing? What are you reminiscences of Bing?
In what way? Oh Bing was great.
Being around him with the Whiteman band.

Bing's a fine guy. He was ambitious but not -- I don't think he wanted to stay in the band too long. Rinker and I was pretty close friends. Well, Bing and I were too and Al describes the two of them as singers of fast songs.

I said, "What did you do before you got with Paul?" "We were singers of fast songs." Vaudeville jobs, up and down the coast. They said they played all the circuits out there and then Paul picked them up and I guess they were a bust until he brought [Harry] Barris in and then they were a hit right off.
Barris, I guess, of course, wrote some great songs.
Yeah, well, Bing helped him with his lyrics, I think, but Bing was -- he was a great performer.

Particularly in recording. I remember 'Taint So, Honey,' one of Willard Robison's things. I wanted to -- I don't know why, I wanted to start it off with a vocal, just a prank sort of, without any introduction, so I just gave him the note he starts on. He knew the song, got to know the song (sings), that's the verse and I wanted him to sing the verse. Well, I just gave him the note and I think Paul beat off, or I did, well, anyway, he came right in and sang it. No problems like that, or anything.

And no problems with changes of key. He was a very musical guy, had a wonderful ear and then he was a lot of fun, a lot of laughs, makes with the big words, liked to do that. I think he must have written a lot of the script or helped those guys, because when I'd hear him on the air, he was that way around -- very, very normal and natural. Doing what came naturally.
You would say he was influenced by the jazz music of that period in his singing.

Oh, yeah, he knew a good band when he heard one. Good musicians, he understood -- he was a good jazz man, that's all there was to it. Good singer. What, he was a former drummer had a good sense of rhythm. In my opinion -- shouldn't be opinionated -- I think if you listen to Bing, I think you will find he got a lot of his stuff but modernized it at his age, from Jolson.
You think musicians like Louis and
Bix influenced him too, would you say.
Bix and Louis, oh, yeah.
Because they influenced everybody, I guess.

That's right. They were right up in the top and they were standards to go by. I remember in this Old Miss Hannah, he had to do a vocal in Old Miss Hannah, and the way he got into it, he was just supposed to start on Old Miss Hannah, (sings) he goes into something like that and it just worked out beautifully. He had excellent taste.
That's the way I say about these guys, they had excellent taste. Bix, fine, fine taste and Bing the same way. And Trumbauer.
I read some place, I don't know where, but Trumbauer was part Indian.
Yes, that's what he told me. I am pretty sure he is or was. Part Indian.
Did he have any of that so-called Indian stoicism, you know --
No, but his color, he was very swarthy and liked outdoors, very much.
What kind of a guy was he, was he kind of quiet.
Oh, yeah, Frankie was a nice guy, real nice guy. I don't think -- he was an angler, I think he

wanted to comehere and do -- make a lot of money. That was his -- he sure didn't make his mark when it came to making money, although he was well paid, but I mean making big money. He wanted a band, he wanted to make big money. Wanted to be a big shot. Wanted to stand in front of the band and be somebody.
But when he stood in front of the band, he didn't get to lead it.
That's right.
I remember seeing a picture of him as a pilot.
Right, he was very interested in that and the Whiteman era, we were down in Valley Stream at a place called Pavlon Royal and it was right near -- not the Roosevelt Field -- the other field.
Mitchell Field.
No, no.
Floyd Bennett. No, that's in Brooklyn.
No, there's another one. It's right near there. We can see it from Valley Stream.
Well, anyway.
Oh, boy, don't ever get old. Anyway, he used to come all the time and as a matter of fact, I think when he left all the bands and went out, he was a pilot instructor.
Wasn't he with the Civilian Aeronautics Board or something. I remember seeing his picture.
Right. Well, he was doing that in the band here. Another guy was Roger Kahn, he wound up over here at Grumman's.
Roger Wolfe Kahn.
Roger Wolfe, he was a test pilot there.
His father was Otto Kahn, the banker.
Right. He was a nice guy.

Speaking of Trumbauer. You spoke about the C-melody earlier when you talked about its functions, its use when you first took it up. Why do you think it just suddenly phased out? The tenor seemed to take over and in the alto.
They were the ones it was written for. All your orchestrations --
Why didn't anyone write for the C-melody anymore?

Well, I don't know. Not everybody was a soloist. You came up and you played either first, second alto in the band. The parts were there for you. If you played print orchestrations, you -- there were first and second alto parts, and the parts were written that way, otherwise you would have to take -- I used to play them on the C-melody.

Well, we were talking about your career, and you made the point that with Goldkette and with Liz Galleat and Lynn Whiteman, you were an arranger, and later at a certain point you were an orchestrator, not an arranger. Would you elaborate on that a little bit?

Yes. During the '20s I was -- I was an arranger to set up something, maybe some sort of a style, to contribute any way I could. They were willing to accept that, and I did my work as I thought best. In other words, they gave me a tune to arrange. When the business -- when it came to 19 -- in the 1930s, middle 1930s anyway -- I was told what to do. I was told -- I was -- the radio business had developed to such an extent where your first number was almost bound to be cut. You didn't make an arrangement for it. You made an orchestration for it, and if you weren't aware of the fact that it was going to be cut, if there were -- if there was any time -- if they needed a minute, if they needed a minute and a half, it usually would go off the first number, the entrance number.
So get it over fast, make it full, get it over fast and -- and it would usually run about -- if you made it three minutes, that would give them at least a minute or so to cut.
So you were told to do these things. Or, if you weren't told, you found it out, because that's usually what

happened on a radio show.

And that's what happened when I was with the Whiteman band the second time. It happened on the Kate Smith show. It happened on most any show, on all the Shirket Shooret shows. You'd sit down and make an arrangement, what you thought -- you're just given the tune, nice tune, and you would make an arrangement that you thought, 'Well, this is going to sound pretty good, with these guys and those guys and this effect and that effect with a large orchestra, which they usually were.

You wanted to listen to it. You -- it was usually a sparkling number. So you would enter the way -- the way it -- you would start the arrangement out and make it nice and full for the first chorus, and then usually they would wave the thing down, and somebody would make an announcement about the product.

So I had that happen over some of the best arrangements that I'd thought I'd made, and then, whenever the announcement was over, they would bring it up. You didn't know where it would happen. But so long as it was enough of the orchestration there; then they would cut it or segue seg-way to the end. And they would really brutalize your arrangmeent.

If you put any time in it and wanted to make it so that it had some kind of style of sound or something like an arrangement -- so that all these things was a little expertise in radio business. This was not like going out in on the dance

hall and having them beat their feet as, you know, to the -- to the rhythm of the thing and get the good, giving some guys some good solos, some good backgrounds and that sort of thing. It was entirely different.
I guess -- yeah, and I guess this carried over, you said -- you know, the orchestrator as opposed to the arranger when you did work for TV for Bernie Green.

Oh, Bernie particularly. He was very sharp on his -- he would get together with the talent and with the director of the show, and he was a very capable musician, orchestrator as well as composer, at least TV composer.

And he would sit down and write these things out, put them all together, and call you up and give them to you. He didn't have time to orchestrate the whole show. So he'd call you and want this, want that, and they're going to do this here and this there. And you'd spend a half hour or so with him. You'd take it home and make the orchestration.
You worked, you said, on the Mary Martin-Ethel Merman special with him, with Bernie.
With -- yeah. I also worked with -- yeah?
When was that? Must have been in the late '60s or early '70s, I guess, you know -- I'd say within the last ten years?
Oh, possibly. Bernie's been gone for
some time. Well, I don't know, but that was one of the specials that I enjoyed doing with somebody who I had worked with as an arranger, and who knew what the business was all about.
Right, and the music was -- you know, the material was good.
That's right. Now, back further there was -- the guy that used to have the Lucky Strike. He used to like my work too. Not his brother --
Mark Warnow?
Mark Warno. I worked with Mark Warno.

Well, I remember working hard on an arrangement. You know, these are guys that call up and say, 'Where's the arrangement?' You know, 'I have a problem. I have to meet the schedule, a certain schedule.' 'Okay, I'll get it in to you.' So I would come up with something that I thought was pretty good, like Lucky Strike one time. You know, there was a real formula. You did about four bars of the theme, and then you get down to all strings where they get soften it for the announcement, telling how good the tune was and what place it had.
Yeah, I remember that very well.

And up we'll come, and you had to bring the brass in. I had to bring everybody. It was an ensemble, and you had to work out some sort of an ensemble, which was acceptable to the agency, to the director who put on this, and he had his -- he had his innings with George Washington Hill,
so that he knew what George Washington Hill wanted, and this is what it was.

So I remember one time going in there, and I got this -- pretty much the same effect, at least Mark Martin Warno liked it, in strings. It was a beautiful tune, I forget the name of it now, but so many of them were in those days.

And I played along the whole thing. I didn't have a brass figure in the whole first chorus, but it sounded full, because I had the strings in the proper register, and everything was full. I had the saxophones and the strings and all, and it sounded -- in the control room it sounded like the brass was playing, as far as that was concerned. It was filled up strata-wise, up here, here, down here.

So the guys give me the violin bow treatment, you know, on the stand after it was over, and Mark Martin Warno said, 'that's fine.' Just then the director walks in from -- he's coming into the rehearsal. And he said, 'Did you hear that?' He said, 'Yes.' Do you think I can play that first chorus without the brass? He just shook his head. He didn't say no, but, yes or no.

Now, this is a case where I didn't have exact instructions, but I think what they figured is I should have known better, because I'd worked on the Lucky Strike before. I had another experience with a guy who used -- who used to do a beer program out in Detroit. He used to go out there and do
this show with the Detroit Symphony, and it was a nice -- it was a nice job.

They paid well for the arrangements, you know, and the band was big. That was the way you'd tell if it's a good job or not. If the band was big, you got paid so much a page and for so many instruments.
Right.

And so I made an arrangement one time, and I had a couple of little things in there that I had done and that I carried over, let's say, from the dance business, which I was doing all the time, because that was my -- that was my bag.

So I did it, did it with strings, and I thought, 'Well, a little unusual to do this.' And he called me in one time after it, and he says, 'You know, that's nice,' he says. 'Strings are nice when you divide them and get a lot of harmony out of them, but,' he said, 'we're not trying to educate them.'
(Laughter)

He didn't want me to do that anymore. So he gave me a couple of Phil Walls arrangements to look over. And, you know, Phil was a piano player on Kostelanetz' show and on this guy's show, and he used to make -- I heard one time that he had made 18 arrangements in one week.
Wow!
Let's say at 50 bucks in those days --

he'd probably get paid by the page, but an average fee of 50 bucks, that's a lot of money. Somebody told me that he never spent any of his arranging money. He only spent what he had to live on playing the job.

Well, I looked at it, you know. There isn't a nicer effect than all the strings playing in unison, you know, particularly in the low register, and I thought, My God, a guy could do this going home in the subway after he got the assignment.
But I couldn't bring myself around to that. So actually with few exceptions I was an unsuccessful radio orchestrator. I knew my business --
But it wasn't what you were --
-- but -- as far as orchestration was concerned -- but as far as making money was concerned, I just couldn't get around to that, you know, force it out.

The same thing would happen on the Kate Smith Show, which I did for three years. I remember one time changing what they wanted -- you know, what they wanted was Kate Smith sings the first chorus, and then for 16 bars you've got to bring the orchestra in, and they had four trumpets, four trombones. They had five saxophones, and they wanted them all, whether it was in -- whether it was all harmonized out, and they had guys like Charlie Margolis and -- and the guy that used to play -- play out in Detroit with us occasionally, a
good friend of Bix's Vic, Nat Natoli. And they had Russ Case and Andy Secress.
So they figured they're paying for all those instruments, they want to hear them.
"I want to hear" One each -- one by one --
(Laughter)
They would count every part. Now then, we had trombones under there with Jack Jenny and Buddy Morrow and several other guys that could really belt it out, and those guys stood up.
We used to do this in a theater down on 46th Street, and they used to stand up and just blow it out. And you had to do that for 16 bars.
Then she'd come back in on the bridge, huh?
Then she'd come back in. And that -- that was the whole arrangement.

I remember Jack gave me -- Jack Miller, who had the band -- he gave me five of those things to do one week, and, you know, it could have meant demand a little money. I couldn't get -- maybe -- I think I got three, maybe four or five, squeezing, you know.
But this was the -- now, with Shilkret Shoret it was a little different. Shoret was more of a musician, and he was a little bit more of that style of the '20s. That's when he came up also.

And besides, he recorded so many bands that he had a great appreciation of what each band was like, and he was never like King down there. He never -- he always tried to help. If he could put in a little part, put a celeste part in, which he did for us one time, he would do things like that, never cut you down.

So I worked for him for three years after the Whiteman, after I got out of the Whiteman bands and he was excellent. We had a little style, and there was a little style to the band. We had a fine band, you know. Then we had both Dorseys and Artie Shaw. And guys like that we had in the band.
But I think the show come on about Saturday evening when it was -- what do they call that -- that's --
Prime time?
Yeah, but that is not prime time. That's in the -- that's the worst time you can get in radio, is Saturday evening.
Because people are all going out.
That's right. But we used to sound pretty good. We used to have mostly musicians would listen, but the show lasted, I think, one season, and then it -- they changed it, too, changed it around.
But now, you said when you went back with Casa Loma the last time, you were hired -- you were more
Now, what happened here, from the time I got out of the Whiteman band, and I did -- I did arrange-ments for Casa Loma. I did some for Fletcher. I even did one or two for Duke Ellington.
Really?
That's right.
Do you remember what they were?
Yeah, one of them was a start-up, "Stardust," which Duke come around and wanted to know what else I was going to do, and Irving, the publisher --
Mills.

-- Irving Mills -- he says, 'I expected something a lot more spectacular.' So I didn't do any more. You know, he made it -- he played it so well, and I only heard it at rehearsal. Usually with those Black orchestras, they -- their rehearsals, they never bothered too much to play the part. They were just getting familiar with what you had done. And if you heard them about two weeks later play an arrangement of yours, you'd be very happy about it. They -- because everyone knew what he was supposed to do and would blend his part in, and he would be -- he would do the part a lot of justice.
And the arrangement would sound good after that.
You said you made two. What was
the other one? Do you remember?
I can't remember offhand.
Was it a standard? Like "Stardust," you know?
Well, it could have been.
Or a pop tune of the day or --

I went up to the Cotton Club, rehearsed -- Mills was there. He had given me the two tunes to do. And I really didn't know Ellington. It was the first I had met him. But we got along very -- right away, you know, we got along very well. I think he mentions it in someplace, in an album that came out. I think the album -- it's on the cover of the album that came out that I did with Bobby Hackett for Decca. He mentions something about, you know, mentions my name.
Who does?
Ellington.
Oh, he's quoted on the album?
No, he's not quoted.
(Interruption)
This was Bobby Hackett, an album you did with Bobby Hackett on Decca?
Yeah. Now, that was when Bobby was with the Casa Loma, which -- that's the second time I was with him. They were called down, the Glen Gray orchestra.
And how did Ellington come to make a
Well, now, that was made for Decca, but it was put out by that company, which was not defunct, but it wasn't -- Brunswick. Brunswick put out a sort of a --
Oh, was it a, like a 78 album, about three 78s in it or four 78s, whatever?
Well, no, ours had, I think, six of them.
Six?
Yeah. So we did it in two sessions. I had some wonderful guys there.
What year was this?
It was when I was with the Glen Gray band.
With the Glen Gray orchestra,
This was the second time now.
Yeah, so what year was that? That was in the '40s?
In the '40s sometime, yeah, around the early '40s.
And Hackett was featured?

Well, yeah, you know. Red Nichols was in the band for a while. This was after the war. And Red comes out of a factory. He'd been working in a factory, and during the war he had done that kind of work, you know, for
his draft service or something like that, and he'd gone out of the business for a couple of years.
So O'Keefe, the manager, he's come to me, and he said -- we both knew that we -- all three of us lived in the same building during the '20s.
You're talking about O'Keefe now.
I'm talking now about O'Keefe and --
Nichols.

And Nichols. We lived up -- up at the end of the drive there at the time I was with Whiteman, and Nichols was doing the show with Don Voorhees, Don Voorhees or Roger Kahn. I think he had written a show then. But anyway, let me see now.

See, well, the three of us were well acquainted with each other. So O'Keefe comes to me one day as the manager, and he was also one of the members of the corporation, and by this time the corporation had -- had been pretty much dissolved, and he and Glen Gray owned the band as a partnership.

Now, he came to me one time because, you know, we had to dig around for 4-F -- through 4-Fs, and this was my job. You know, I go from one band -- what band had he played with? What -- where did this guy come from that I was supposed to hire. And he would either -- he would tell me all the time, I've been with Benny Goodman; I was with this band and that

band.'"

So I would have to dig around, see who he was, and usually I found out so many guys we got in the band, and you'd have to let them go, because they were either dopes or -- some reason why they're 4-Fs. Some of them we had were excellent.

Anyway, we were always looking for trumpet players. So he came to me one day, and he said, "Nichols is coming up. He'd like to join the band. What do you think?" Frankly, I was against it. I thought, "We got enough headaches," and here's Nichols coming in the band --
Out of the war plant.

-- out of the war plant or -- I didn't worry about his playing because I know he's -- he's an expert. You know, he knows what to do with something. He's great in the studio, and he was great recording. But it's just a matter of he was also a fantastic angler, you know. Miff -- I think he could have given Miff a better deal, Miff Mol and his Moilers. And there was always Red and Miff together. They made all those records. But Red's the guy that came out on top.

Anyway, I told him that. But then he overruled me. He said, "Well, the first thing I know, we're going out to Chicago, and there's Red. So, you know, so I said, "If this is the way it is, this is the way it is.""

So what Red told me, what he wanted to do, he wanted to play fourth trumpet. He says, 'I want to get my lip in shape, and give me the fourth trumpet part. That's enough.' We had four trumpets and -- four trumpets, four trombones -- big bands in those days.

So Red starts in the band, and we were playing at the Sherman, and I'd go over sometimes. I was staying at the Sherman. And I'd go downstairs. I'd hear Red down in the musicians' room. He was practicing his long, low tones, getting his embouchure back, you know, and he would sit in the band, and play his part.
And he had it all planned. And this was fine; however, after about three, four weeks or maybe six weeks or so, his lip is in pretty good shape. Now he wants the third parts.

Now, trumpet players in those days, you -- you know that these kids during the war, they got to be -- before the war they got to be fantastic. They had guys like Louis Armstrong to look back on. Now they were fluffing him off, and Harry James, those guys were getting passé. These kids were coming along and they could play twice as high and probably twice as fast, and they had fantastic commands of their instruments, and the only thing that they worried about, most of them being 4-Fs, is the fact that they'd be pulled in the Army, got out of the band. So they wanted to show off as
much as they could.

Now, you take a part, even a fourth part, away from some kid because usually you gave him a solo now and then, and he'd get up and blow his brains out for that 16 or 32 bars because he, you know, "this is my chance."

So Red's coming in. He's creeping in. Then he creeps up into the third part. Then he wanted to get to the second part, and, you know, he couldn't play the high ones. So he would be satisfied with the second part, but he wanted some lead.

And by this time I could give him, as far as an arranger, I could give him a few things to do, to utilize his talents. But he was -- you know, he wanted it done more quickly. Well, how -- how long does it take to make an arrangement for -- put him in a spot -- when you got 14 or 13 other guys that you have to --
(Simultaneous remarks)
Where does Hackett come into this?

Oh, I'm getting to it. Well, anyway, I guess I'm a little too detailed, but I want to lay that thing for -- anyway, it got to the point where he -- he wanted some solos to do. He was in the band about six months, and by the time we got around to it, I had made him a chorus, and put a nice background in for him on a record. I don't think you'd be familiar with it. I don't know what the name -- da-da-dee-dee-
dee-da-da-da-dee-da-dee-dee. Remember that tune?
Yeah.
Da-da-da-dee-dee-daa-da?
'Don't Take Your Love from Me.'

"Don't Take Your Love from Me." I think that's one of the best solos he ever played. Now, he came into the studio, and he played it over, and we had the arrangement about two weeks before, and by the time he finished it, polished it off to play, it was -- he was the old Red Nichols.

He had made a nice chorus, and I was never a great admirer of what he played, but he did an awfully nice job. And he wanted more. Finally he quit, you know. Then he wanted to front the band, and he did. Glen Gray took sick, and I think he later died from the -- got cancer. He went to the clinic up in Boston. And Red took over. This was the, over at the old Pennsylvania Hotel.

Well, after that, I guess, the way things turned out, he figured he's well enough and good enough to go on his own. So he leaves the band and he tells your old magazine, I think -- Down Beat -- I don't think he could remember -- that he didn't get any kind of good treatment there in the Glen Gray band, that they were trying to stifle him, hold him down, something like that. I don't know who would have written that article.
But it did come out.
They're always looking for some
controversy.

Yes, that's right. Well, anyway, it came out. So we didn't pay too much attention to it. But he went out, and he got a band, and he started his second time around, and he got a fine band. I heard him out in Los Angeles.

Now then, when he gets out of the band, he left us with a spot to fill because no one else played like Red Nichols either. So we're looking around and looking around, and I'm walking over 52nd Street one day, and I run into Bobby Hackett. And Bobby, he was stewed.
(Laughter)

"What's going with you," you know? I hadn't seen him in quite a while. But, you know, it was arm around each other and gabbing around like that. So I guess he was trying to get a job somewhere. So I said, "It gives me an idea. How would you like to come with the Casa Loma or with Glen Gray?"
Well, he didn't want any part of a band like that. It didn't impress him at all. But he needed a job. His -- he had come out of the --
: Glenn Miller --
Glenn Miller outfit, you know, where Glenn Miller, being an arranger, knew how to use him. He doubled him back, just let him play choruses, I think, and had him play his guitar.
: Guitar, yeah.

So anyway, he thought it might be a good idea. He said he'd be interested. So O'Keefe was on the Coast. I wired him, and he sent back. I said, 'How about Bobby Hackett?' So he sent a wire back -- 'If he behaves himself he'd be fine.'
So I talked to Bobby, and he was going to behave himself. I talked to his wife. He didn't have any money. He was in bad shape. He didn't have a horn. His horn was in hock.

So we straightened that all out, and I took -- the band was playing in Chicago for six weeks. I took him out there and set him up in the band. We were doing a show for the Navy every Saturday. Anyway, we got him out there, when he took over Nichols' book, played a lot of nice solos, and he played them -- but I thought I had got him in the band all right, and then Glen called me. I got a call from him, and he says, 'This has got to stop.'
He says, 'This guy falls down on the stand, and nothing comes out of his horn.' So when I got out -- out there --
: He wasn't playing any guitar at all at this time?
No, no.
: Just trumpet.
That's right. And besides, he was playing a lot of spots that Red had left, which we didn't necessarily record, but he had a lot of them there.
So -- but he couldn't give up the drinking. And I heard him on a Navy broadcast one time, and --
(Side B.)
All right, so you said you heard Hackett on this Navy broadcast.

Yeah, and it really wasn't good. And so I -- you know, just to check up. This had been after I brought -- after I'd get him into -- set him in the band. And this was when we were going to leave there. Well, we're going to still do a couple weeks at the Stevens Hotel.

So I took him out to dinner. I said, 'Hey,' -- now, this -- a couple of days passed, because I took him out to dinner. We went down, and I said, 'How about a glass of wine?' and he said, 'Not touching it.'

So I said, 'Look, Bob. Touch it if you want to. I'm not going to stop you.' I said, 'I'm not trying to make you over or anything.' 'No,' he says. 'I've given it up.' And I looked at him, and I almost had to laugh, smile anyway, smirk.

So anyway, he takes out a couple of pamphlets out of his pocket, and he shows them to me. He says, 'Did you ever hear of the AAA?' I said, 'Yeah.' I said, 'I know about it.' 'Well,' he said -- 'Not much,' I said. He said, 'Well, I've been to a

meeting. I've been going to a couple, but, he says, I went to one, and he told me about a trumpet player. I forget what his name is, whether it's Wingy Manone or somebody like that. And he told me about Raleigh Hamsley, the --
The catcher?
-- the catcher, and several other guys. And he says, Jesus, they've given it up. He said, there's one thing you find out. If you don't take the first drink, you have no problem.
(Laughter)
But you have to resist the first one. That's what they -- he says, I'm impressed with that.
And, by God, I don't think he's had a drink of hard liquor, you know, since -- before he died. Some of the guys told me --
He used to drink beer. I know that.

Some guys told me that he used to take a glass of beer, but I know -- and then he came back. He stayed in the band, and there was one time he had a nervous breakdown. He got out of the band. They had to take him up to Providence. He lived up there.

But he was exemplary. And his playing improved, and then we made that album while he was in the band, and he -- it turned out very well, and he was in the band about 12, about a year or 14 months after that, did very well. And he was --

he was fine, cooperative, everything else and played well, and I guess he finally got a job -- he wanted to be in the city -- he got a job at the broadcasting company. I think it was WJZ at that time. Wait, it was either that or had been turned over to WABC. One or the other, but he had a program there, and it was his program. He did it, I think, for about 13 weeks.

And then he went along, and he got out of that, and he started doing, you know, his combo, all this -- trios and quartets. He did that for some time, and I guess he made an excellent living out of it, and he was always good to hear.
But anyway, you did the album with him, and Ellington had some comment on the cover about your writing?
No, he just had a comment that -- I had made some arrangement for him or something like that.
Oh, I see.

It wasn't anything that I should -- I'm very happy to mention it because it happened. But now, to get to another guy that I had experience with that you might like to hear was Willard Robeson. Did you ever hear of Willard?
Well, I know about him, you know, something about him. I know some of this music.
Yeah. Well now, Willard was quite a

character and also an excellent talent. He had a -- what he called a Deep River Orchestra. And he used to delve into these spiritual books, and he dug out any number of them. I don't know where he got them, but they were always -- they had blues in, and they had a lot of colored -- Black people's works in them, you know.
Well anyway, I ran into Willard. He called me, wanted to get together on something. I think we were doing a show together with Shilkret. And --
But you had known him long before this?
Well, I knew him --
From Whiteman's --
Well, I didn't know him when he was in the Whiteman band.
Uh-huh.
But I had heard about him. But we came in contact with each other, and he wanted to do some things together, with his Deep River Orchestra.
Now, Billy Still, William Grant Still, he was one of the arrangers in the Whiteman band. He, Ferde and I were three, you know, we were the arranging staff at one time.
I guess he was one of the leading Black composers of that period.
Well, I guess he was. I had heard of
him through the Deep River Orchestra. They had done a lot of wonderful stuff there.

Now, I used to listen to that over WOR when they first -- when the station first started out to play the -- they used to do a lot of work there. And most of that was Bill Still's work. And I guess he -- I know we needed help on the Old Gold Show, and Whiteman got him to help out. He did his two a week like Ferde and I.
So I didn't see him after that. I have an idea he must have gone to the Coast when the situation turned up. Maybe, you know, when Whiteman cut the band down, I think he got out at that time.

Anyway, I got in touch with Willard. He was working with Shilkret on different things. Shilkret at that time had five radio accounts, and at that time a man like Shilkret would have the whole thing. He hired the singers. He hired the talent. He hired the musicians. It was what they call, I think, a package show.

So Willard was one of the -- one of the talents. We got together, and at that time he had a house up in Tuckahoe, up here in Westchester. And he wanted me to come up there, and, you know, it was always interesting to me, his music, and I would like very much to have gotten in with him.
So I went up there in Tuckahoe, and he trotted out a lot of these things like -- one of them got to Mildred Bailey.

She was with the Whiteman band also. She was beginning to do things on her own. And one of them got there to the Red Norvo thing, and it came out as a record with Mildred doing it. I think Eddie Sauter gets credit for it, but it was mine, I did it with Willard -- (inaudible) the tune called --
Uh-huh. But Eddie Sauter got -- was given credit for it?
Well, I think his name was on the -- he was the -- he was the arranger for Red.
Yeah, Red --
And he got credit for that one, not that it makes any difference. It's just that -- it's just that it was a Willie Robeson arrangement, and I have worked together with Willard.
On this particular --
That's right, on this one. And then we did one on St. Louis Blues.
For Mildred and Red?
No, no, no, I didn't do any work for them. This was strictly Willard and his Deep River Orchestra.
I see.
But having done the vocal, Mildred and Willard were very close. You know, they were mutual admirers. And I did that and Joe Turner Blues. We -- all these things out of the book.

And the other day I spent an awful lot of time trying to remember them. But they came so fast, and I would go up there with Willard and do this work with him. And, you know, his rehearsals were always nice. He had good studio musicians, bass clarinets, mostly clarinets, (inaudible) mostly saxophone and strings and viola. He had some fine musicians in there and some nice rehearsals and some nice sounds.

But Willard wasn't much of a businessman. He eventually lost his home. We started off one fall with the Maxwell House broadcast, and they catered to him. You know, they liked his music, and they wanted to do a lot. That's when we did a lot of this less work. I was quite busy, I remember.
About what year was this?

Oh, this was -- this had to be around the early '30s, after I'd gotten out of the Whiteman band. When I was working with Shilkret Shooret -- I was doing a lot of freelancing then. And if these guys would go off the air, you had a lot of free time, and sometimes they'd go off -- and Willard would work during the summer.
He'd be the replacement shows.

Well, he could have been. I know he did a lot of the work that Nat had, and Nat had these shows, and there was one there that they passed on that Bix got onto. That was a guy who -- who later went out to the Coast. He's in all the books, but I -- it was the Camel Pleasure -- it was
the Camel show, and it was a great big band.
This was after Bix had been sick and gone back to Davenport, and then he came back to New York?
Right, and couldn't get back in the Whiteman band. We had all been out of the Whiteman band now for about a year or so. And, you know, there was -- radio work was beginning to come on.

As a matter of fact, I worked in radio for about 12 to 15 years, this was where I spent a lot of my time. But the first part of it I worked with these guys who had been in the dance business and were transferring over from the dance business and getting their -- getting their licks in in the radio business.
So Bix got into this band?

Well, Bix got into this. Now, you'd know -- you'd know the guy, I'm pretty sure. He's in nearly all the books. Anyway, Nat had fixed it up, and they got Bix in this band. You know, we had Del Staigers, Charlie Margolis was playing second trumpet. That was a sort of a mix-up you'd run into over at NBC in that big studio they had up on the 12th or 13 floor.

Anyway, we -- Lenny was out of the band then. He was playing and Arthur Shutt. They were the two piano players -- two pianos, lots of strings, couple of horns, three and three brass and trombones, big bands, tympanis, and they
played all kinds of music. That was the type of thing like light opera plus pop tunes.
Anyway -- I forget what the tune was too -- me and my forgetfulness. I got a good forgetter.
(Laughter.)

Anyway, At Bix -- I picked a the chorus for Bix, a nice background on some -- some pop tune of the day. And it went along, and he got up, and then he blew a chorus for 16 -- he blew for 16 bars. It was really beautiful to me at the time. And -- you know, I'm pausing to try and remember this guy's name. He later went out to the Coast and did a lot of work in the studio.
I'm sure I know it, but I just don't --

Yeah, I don't either. But anyway, here he is. He's taken back, you know. He thinks, 'Oh, this is great.' He says, 'This is just what I've been looking for,' you know, But, you know, they go over it the second time, and here he is in front of Bix like this directing him. Can you imagine anything like this?

This is -- these guys, you know -- this is actually what they wanted, but they should just let the band go, you know. So Bix was off that show. He wasn't on it long. I wasn't on it long. But I had other work to do. As far as Bix was concerned, he needed the work. He was broke, and we
were then at that time, we were pretty much working on piano things after --
Where was he living then, in the hotel or --

Well, he must have been. As I understand it, he -- I don't know where he lived, but all that time it seems to me that -- I always hear that he'd been living at the 44th Street Hotel. That seems to -- I've seen bills there. Guys have dug up bills, and he'd always been there, at the 44th Street Hotel.
Someone talked about an apartment over in Astoria.
Well, that was later on. That was at the --
Near the end.

-- near the end, yeah. They had-- there's a friend of mine that has that pretty well documented, even with pictures. But there's an awful lot he doesn't know. He was supposed to have found a girlfriend who was straightening him out.
Right.

And then there was -- he had a friend who still has his piano somewhere. Oh, all that sort of thing which -- which I didn't get into. I didn't know much about when it was happening. I had moved up to Greenwich,

Connecticut, and once or twice we got together to finish off and polish off a few of his piano numbers, which we got off, and then I ran into one of the Whiteman guys one time. He told me, "Did you know that Bix had died?" That's the only way I --
You hadn't even -- you hadn't even known it.

Well, he didn't, like, call me up or I call him every so often. A month could go by, and then the first thing you know, he knew where I could get him, but I didn't know where I could get him. So he would call up and say, "I got another number, or something like that, "I'd like to put down anytime you're ready."

So, well, Bix got off this show, but they have something. They have -- the books, you know, Man and Legend, they have this documented. They dug into the circumstances, and they have it put in the book.

But there again was -- I think I mentioned before -- his lack of expertise, studio expertise, you know, like cuing in this, cuing in -- all that sort of thing, which you had to have if you're in the studio because a guy could go in the control room and take a look at the script and come out and say, "We've got to cut -- we've got to cut 30 seconds off this."
So he would tell that to the orchestra leader, and the orchestra leader would say, "Segua from here to here."
(Simultaneous remarks)
Right. You didn't know what that would cut out. Well, Willard, we did a lot of work with Willard. Let's say, I don't know if I finished with him or not.

I wanted to ask you something a propos of Bix's -- in listening, you know, to the whole set of pieces, you know, not so much Davenport Blues but, you know, "Flashes," "Candlelight," "In the Dark" and -- there is -- there are certain similarities from piece to piece and certain things were -- makes them sound very much, almost of one.
Yeah, out of the same mold.
Yeah.
Yeah, well, this is what -- this is what -- well, I think he could have gotten over it. Now, "Davenport Blues" was done way back.
Right.
I had to get that. I was given a record to take it off, and then I had to put in the introduction and the ending and make it like it would conform to what Bix was doing.
Yeah.
So he was putting on his introduction, and he was putting on his endings; you know, he'd always have that slow part, beautiful part. He'd go out with some nice
chords and so forth. So I did that on Davenport." Now, that's over with. That was done after his death.
Yeah, I realize that.

They were trying to get as much material as possible. Now, he used to do one -- he did one that he called For No Reason at All in C." And they gave me that to do too. But if you listen to it, it's just a hodge-podge of improvisation. In other words, there's little or no thematic material that you could, you know, make the second eight bars similar to the first and the middle eight bars and then the next, last eight bars, or however it was constructed.

But it was constructed on I'd Climb the Highest Mountain. We used to play it in the Goldkette band. You know, it was a beautiful tune. And they used to improvise on it. So this is with the Goldkette band. And every time you'd hear it, it would be different. You didn't know what they were playing unless you could follow the harmonic sequence in I'd Climb the Highest Mountain." Now, I -- so I told him, I said, 'I don't think it's a wise thing to do that.' Besides, I said, 'it's beyond me. I don't know how to do it. I can't put that together to where it will sound.' Now, then we did the other five. Now, In a Mist

he had played for me when I first joined the Gold Kette band. Now, there was no name on it then. So he had played that for me, and all the guys in the band knew it plus any other musicians that were hanging around. There were a lot of them.
But after he was a year or so in the Whiteman band, Jack Robbins came around, the publisher.
Yeah, I think you told me that once.

Yeah. And he said -- Will you put this down on paper? And he says, 'I'd like to get it.' So we went to work on that, and it was quite a job. At first, it sounded like it might be easy, but even on 'In a Mist' --
Oh, I wouldn't think so, just from hearing --
Yeah, digging it out here and digging it out there and digging him out there, and besides, the last half a minute on the record was, again, just complete improvisation.

So anyway, when we got it down and went back and forth with each other, I was telling him, 'Bix, you'll have to play this sometime, somewhere, and you'll have to play it just like we've got it down. You can't just go up and improvise on it and play a few of those little noodles that you put in there.'
So he knew it, and we did that. We completed it,

took it into Robbins, and Robbins said he wanted the broad theme, which we worked on. When we got that, which, you know, he fell right into it, and it was a very short time where we had that together.

Now then, after that -- well, he had been sick in the band. Then he gets sick again and goes out to Davenport. And he works on the next one. Robbins, one of them -- this is one good thing about Robbins. Jesus, 'do more, do more. What else have you got?'

So he went out, and he worked on the thing called 'Candelights,' and he made that much more musical, much more orchestratable, and it was -- it was nice. He was going along very fine. And he also put in his slow themes, and --
But as we said, they are very much of a piece.

Well, that -- he had got away from 'In a Mist.' He had a little development there. Now, then, he needed money, and he always needed money at that time, and he wanted to -- he'd call and say, 'Look, I got another one.'
Okay, let's get together. We'd get together and put it down, and it was just a little theme, very nicely done, but it was very similar in overall sound.
In concept, too.
In concept, yeah. In other words, he had this formula, and he did -- he did those two, although he
had new things, but the formula was the same, and he did it pretty much the same way, as "Flashes" and "In the Dark." Of course, after that he died.
Well, what do you think he would have developed into, had he --
I think he would have gone on, you know.
Yeah, and what-- I mean, can you conjecture at all? What do you think he would have done?

I think, you know, coupled with his playing -- Jesus, the way things were at that time, there was nothing. He couldn't drop anything and go play somewhere; that is, play his trumpet, which was what he was known for. But I think he would have developed his piano things. You know, in my estimation, a guy has a piece of work in his mind. He has some things in his mind. He sits down, and then in order to get the next one out, he may -- you know, he may get excited and get a little bit more or have an idea, and then he goes back, and especially if he's plagued by, "Jesus, I need the money. I want to get it out." He stays on the same plateau.

And I think that that's why I thought, if he had gone back in the Whiteman band, he would have had the money; even if he drank, he would have had the money. He could have thought a little bit more, and I know he would have come up and
say, 'I got another one. Wait until you hear this.' And he would have -- he would have begun to rise a little bit more and develop a little bit more.

When a guy needs a little cabbage, you know, there's no telling what, and I think he would have developed his piano thing. Then, of course, if he'd been around in the last 15 years or so, some of the -- when records started to come back, oh, those things, the way he played, you know, with the nice string background or even with some band, but with a nice string background and him playing it. After Harry James, you know; there's one thing about James. He took and played the whole tune for you. He played it, and then he played maybe another half chorus, and the tempos got slower and slower, so that you could put a chorus and a half on the side for about three minutes and do the whole business.

Now, I think Bix -- that would have been Duck soup for Bix, and besides a guy with his talent where, when he went down, you ran over the arrangement the first time for a take. He would play something, and it would be exciting. You ran over for the next take, he would play something, and it would be different.

And then maybe another one, and it would still be different. Now, all these things have been -- have been piled up, got together, collected, and they've been published as different takes of what he had done, and they're all

acceptable. With a guy -- a guy with talent like that would have -- oh, he would have been quite a ways ahead, and I don't think he ever would have gone in for anything high note, or -- maybe he wouldn't have got very far, but also recently you heard -- there's -- what's his name, Kaempfert? He has a nice band, and, gees, he plays a whole chorus with his trumpet, and it's just nice -- a little off the melody here and there. And it's pleasant.
You may not like that. I don't think you would. But there are any number of people, because his records sell. And he keeps making more -- it's commercial.
Oh, yeah, it's the melody, you know.
Right. It's the melody. You get a nice tune, and like we used to say in the band, all you need is a piano, banjo and shotgun, and it sounds good.
(Laughter.)

To finish up with your career, I wanted to touch on the fact you said you had done teaching in recent years, and you mentioned that you studied the Schillinger method, and the way you put it was that you went backwards.
Well, I did. I would say I went backwards. When I got into this business and went with -- with those bands I told you about, the local bands -- and went

out playing my horn, and then I went away to college, and I had a band. Now, I sort of backed into writing. And then when I -- with the band the first year I'm out of college, I'm writing a little bit more, and I didn't know what it was all about to score. And then I got with the Goldkette band, and they taught me an awful lot.

And I rubbed elbows with I think, at the time, the greatest. And then from there on to the Whiteman band, although at this time, from the Goldkette band on, I learned how to score. Now then, after the Whiteman band, I got into the radio business, and there you have to know how -- by that time I had built up a certain amount of musical techniques that -- which you usually learn when you first start to go to school. You learn all these things, and you spend your first few days being a tyro, you know. So you -- you work hard at something like that.
And then by the time you get along out of a band like the Whiteman band or out of radio, you're ready for -- for Hollywood. You know, you go into something further.
study with Schillinger?
So when did you stay in the show?

So, when I got out, and with doing radio work, I found out that the music, the type of music they were playing were backgrounds. Everything was a background. If you wanted to work, there were any number of guys that could sit down and write a background to a story. Bernie Green was
expert at it, any number of those guys, and I wished all the time I could do it.

On the Kate Smith show I couldn't do the backgrounds to the dramas. They would have about 20 minutes of Tallulah Bankhead or somebody like that from the show that she had, Alan Ladd. A bunch of them would come over and do 20 minutes on the hour show, and it would have to have background music. I didn't --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
