Well, I didn't know particularly how to get started on this. I'd never done this type of music. My bag was working with a dance orchestra. And the dance orchestras were going out of existence. We're coming now into radio.

So I remember to getting one job after another, and some of these little jobs, you could get a whole -- you could get a whole detective story job to do, and, you know, make yourself an income at least for 13, 26 or 39 weeks, as long as it was on, and all you had to do was make noises, naturally, behind what was going on, instrumental noises or whatever.

I used to look at, I didn't think much of it in the first place, and I -- if I were going to do something like that, I'd want to do it intelligently. Now, I'd never had any musical training for that. As Schillinger -- Schillinger calls it connotative type of music. And this is music that enhances the field story, and this is being done in movies, and this is a thing that to me is strange.

Yet the radio business is going into it. There are very few, if any, dance bands around, and at least the type that are not too much interested in me. So I find out that most of the arrangers who were working around the studios have at some time or other had a good portion of Schillinger, who was -- well, he had a very popular (inaudible) the whole of, let's say, Columbia.

All of those arrangers went to Schillinger and several of the ones at NBC, they were still doing -- what do they call them -- not only standby shows, but they still do house -- they're using the house orchestra, and this is what they would do.

So I thought, Jesus, I'd like to get started on something like that. So now, this is somewhere around in the middle '30s or early '30s or middle '30s, right around in there. And I went up to Schillinger, called up to see if he would take me on.

And, "Sure," he said. You come along. All he cared about was if you pay your ten bucks, you get an hour. So -- but a lot of guys that I knew were studying with him, had studied with him, and we're doing all this type of work, and it wasn't bothering him.

So as far as I was concerned, what -- I wanted to get started in this, because it would have helped me further my career. I'd have to put the dance bands behind me. Now, this was before some of these bands started to come up again and use the television as their showcases. But that was quite a while.
So you were studying with Schillinger.
[That opened] up, and he had a long, drawn out course which is mostly mathematical, but it's wonderful, really. And you -- for six months to a year you had to stick on just rhythm.
Once a week?

And it wasn't the easiest thing in the world to understand. So I went up -- you sit down and he writes the whole thing out for you for an hour, explains it as he's going along. Then it's up to you to take it home and either rewrite it or understand what he's doing. So I did that for quite a while.

Besides, it takes quite a bit of your time. Now, I go along about 2 1/2 years of this, and it doesn't seem to be helping me any, except I'm still thinking dance music. I'm still thinking rhythm music, and it's not helping me to go along making what he calls -- lay down in his book -- later on connotative music.

So he ups and gets a cancer of some sort and dies. Now then, I have to spend a little time. I'd had -- I'd had a good bit of it, and it helped me an awful lot in figuring things out of what I knew, but to go on further and do, to progress along what I didn't know or didn't have any experience with, I had to find somewhere else to go. So I decided to -- well, I saw it advertised where New York University was giving it.
The Schillinger method.
The Schillinger method, given by a guy by the name of Rudy Schrann. And Paul Start, of all people, was one of his cohorts.

Did you -- you didn't know Paul Start? Remember "Polly and Her Pals"? Cliff Start that used to write Polyano-Cars? His son -- now, he was working over at Columbia, good friend of mine, and he was one of the instructors there.
So I went down there once a week again. It was hard to take more than once a week. And -- but it was in the evening. And it was being given as a -- for the GIs as one of those --
Yes, this was in the '40s?
Now, this gets up into the '40s. Some time has passed where I can't get it. And there was the GI bill, and we had a lot of guys in there. And who was in one of my classes? Eubie Blake.
(Laughter.)
Absolutely.
That's wonderful.
Yeah. We used to gad around together.
Well, he wasn't doing anything then except this. He was trying to -- he was doing the same thing. All those guys pretty much -- and Eddy Barefield, I ran into -- he was doing this too.

Now, there's one thing you could do. You had to take the whole course, which took about four, 4 1/2 years. And then you had to pass an examination, and then they gave you a certificate to teach. But that didn't mean a thing in the
public schools. They didn't even know what the name Schillinger was all about.

So I stuck with it, stuck it out, and then it was a matter of you have to take what you have there and practice it. And Bernie Benny Green gave me a chance to practice some of it, and he, you know, he had that kind of talent that I didn't, and I got very disgusted, discouraged, and I was expecting that this would do the job.

And that why I say I was equipped, and I could understand what the other guys were doing, but you do have to have a certain amount of talent to -- talent in that respect in order to put these things down or to have an idea what to do, and this will just merely give you the technique.
And it seems more like an aptitude than a talent, in a way. I don't know if I'm splitting hairs semantically, you know.
Yeah.
So what eventually happened with it? That was --

Well, I'd pass it. But then all I could tell is -- I knew what I was -- I knew the course. I knew the techniques of it, and I was qualified, according to what they said, to passing the course. I got a certificate that I was qualified to teach it.
So teaching something like that, I mean, I try to

get pupils, but trying to get pupils is -- it's ridiculous. However, some guys knew that I was giving it, and I had one pupil who was -- he came over and he studied. I say that we talked it over, you know. I tried to try and give him my -- what I got out of it. But I said, 'You'll probably have to do the work,' and that's Nat Shilkret, Bubsie.
(Of all people.)
So he wasn't doing much, and he lives out near me. He used to come over once a week.
This was in the '50s?
Well, it could have been. Yes, I guess it was, the '50s. And then I had a couple of kids, and they -- they had the money. They could pay. But they didn't have the stick-to-it-iveness.
(Recording interruption.)
You have to know how much two times two is, two times three. Kids today rather rely on the computer or the calculator.
Yeah, right, calculator.

So it wasn't going so well, so I didn't bother. But some guys would come around and stick it out and then come back awhile, very few, though, not enough to make a living, and I would get all interested in telling them a few of these things, because I could see where it could help them.

But, you see, here I'm they aren't getting this stuff at the end. If I'd had it at the beginning, at the time where I could just sit down and do anything I wanted, I could have used an awful lot of it. I can see that now. However, as a guy in the Whiteman band told me, "Your arrangements may not have been -- would possibly not have been the same, what you had to give."
You would have used it for movie scoring (Unaudible) and things like that, wouldn't you?

Well, I would have hoped to -- to get into that. Like you say, it's an aptitude possibly. That would have been something that I would have aimed for. You see, all the bands, where did they go? They got out -- they took their bands. They took them around the cold regions, New England and all that. They broke their bands in. They got them to the point where they were a finished product, and then the idea for them was to -- "Let's make some money. We'll go out to Hollywood."

And they go out. And there's nothing they ever did there that -- that could compare to any of those records that they would make. So with the arrangers it was the same thing. There were a lot of arrangers cropping up -- talented guys. And they could go out -- they could go right off -- "What do I want making a dance band arrangement? I could make three, five, four times as much if I can write something for some
detective story" or something like that.
So for me it was the -- it was the -- wasn't the horse and the cart; it was the cart and the horse. At least that's what I think. That's my reaction at this point.

But now that they're looking back on some of the early bands because they don't have too much recall for them; they don't have too many records. Swing -- from the swing period on, yeah, they got everything. But back in the 1920s you have to pick out a record here and pick out a record there, and you might find it in somebody's cellar, and it's a 78. Nobody wants anything to do with it, and it has to be reprocessed.
(Side B.)

And -- but that sort of thing gives us a little bit of Americana, a little bit of mystery in the early jazz period. And it was the Jazz Age. I always tie in the swing age up to Benny Goodman when he made his famous trip across the country, when he got out to California, and besides I've divided almost, although this isn't quite accurate, but generally speaking, we delved into two beat music. We didn't have the influence of the Latins, of the Latin people coming up here and giving this eight / eight in and a bar. I had to go to Schillinger to get eight / eight in and a bar. We had mostly oom-pah, oom-pah, and he had -- even a lot of it was built on that. There were a lot of things that were
even more so, like Benny Pollock and our Goldkette band, and even you know the Whiteman band was like that for a time in the early '30s or late 1920s, when we were developing a lot.

But then you have to have -- the people have to buy it, and they stopped buying that. They were ready for something else, and they got it out of radio. So I'm not -- I can't deny that eight in and a bar -- did a lot of it with Shaw, did a lot of it with the Glen Gray band, that is, not to get mixed up with the early Casa Loma. That was when all these guys used percussive sounds, particularly in the bass. Everything had to be four beats.

And that's one of the things about that concert that I did. With all that Goldkette stuff, I still have it, but I'm not going to -- I wouldn't go up there and let a guy play four beats on the bass. And I was afraid of that, one of the things I was afraid of, although there were guys like Chauncy Morehouse plays fine two beat music. Ray Bauduc, guys like that, even Davey who went with he can play the Tough when Artie Shaw, was playing four. He was a These are real old timer in two-beat music. But they could give you can get the good rhythms in that. It wasn't just an afterstick. Oo-cha, -- cha, -- cha, it wasn't just a clap like that, you know. It was -- it went along with the arrangement --
Now, even Steve Brown in "My Pretty Girl," he thumps his bass and slaps his bass, but he did it a whole lot
differently than that slapping, wooden type noise that came out of all the guys who figured, 'Well, Steve Brown slaps the bass; I can do that.' And all they were doing was making wooden noises.

And then when I got to the Glen Gray band, for instance, notes didn't mean a thing. It was all percussive boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom - boom, -- din, din, din, din, din, duh-duh, you know. And this is a percussive sound. Guys were taking it way up on the bass fiddle. This takes the bottom out of the band because there's no bass note, no nice bass note; however, the transcriptions, never many got away from that. You listen to the transcriptions, and you hear a nice bit of harmony.
For instance, like the bands behind Sinatra -- beautiful. He's a fine talent --
: And Axel Stordahl?
Well, Axel was very good too. No, the guy that does it now.
: Oh, I know who you mean, but I just can't think of it.
(Nelson Riddle -- ed.)
Yeah. Well --
: Well, anyway, his orchestrations are beautiful.
And you take a guy like Sinatra, he don't have anything else. Even Andy Williams -- they're singers. But they can afford to go along with big bands,
beautiful instrumental sound, and they don't have more than one, two arrangers. But not everybody can work for those guys.
I would like to have been able to do that, because singers -- we got away from orchestral dance music.
And the singers took over.

And the singers took over. Everything was a vocal. You had to do a vocal. And by the time you're working here with an orchestral dance band, somebody else a lot of times has got ahead of you, let's say, and he's working with like a Sinatra singer, one of the singers that's taken over, and he's doing very well -- Perry Como, all those guys. They always had nice, big bands, beautiful big orchestral sounds to work with. And you never got away from it.

They didn't come in with, you know, behind the Beatles' stuff. But that's -- I don't take anything away from that. The business as I see it was due for a rhythmic change, and although the early Latins brought the eight-to-the-bar and four-to-the-bar in, it wasn't four-to-the-bar; it was eight-to-the-bar, you know, their type of doing it, but the melding of the thing, it took a while to do.
So that's -- that's my story, Mr. Agony.
(Laughter)
Do you remember Mr. Agony?
Oh, sure. 'Please don't touch the
microphone. // (Recording interruption.)

Ira Gitler with an addendum to the Bill Challis interview. Bill told me that in recent years he worked with the vocal group, Manhattan Transfer, on one of their albums for Atlantic. I don't know which one it was. But the reason it came about was that they thought he had done the original arrangement of Sunny Disposition back in the '20s. He hadn't, but he did become involved with them in this recording project.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
Attilio J. Macero

I also have one commercial recording to my credit which features my quintet and four of my original compositions. This is on the Debut label and came out this year. I have also within the past year appeared on several radio shows presenting some of my compositions. These were on W.O.V. and the most recent on W.N.Y.C. on their Adventures In Music program August 1954. At this time I am also negotiating with one of the large record companies to record several of my new compositions. All of this I believe has helped in this thing I believe in concerning the progress of music, since it gives me the opportunity to present my ideas to the listening public in both words and music. Through my efforts and those of others, will come, I hope, an acceptance by the public of a type of music that is unfamiliar to them.

I have not found a teacher of this particular type of hybrid music, but have certainly found sympathetic people in music who are making efforts along these same lines; such people as Peggy Glanville-Hicks, David Broekman, Henry Brant, William Schuman, and many more.
Attilio J. Macero

For several years I have been interested in composition but really did not start any serious writing until around 1948. At this time I minored in composition at the Juilliard School of Music until I completed my studies there in 1952. Following my graduation in 1952, I began studying composition privately with Henry Brant.

I have always been interested in jazz, since I have continually played with dance bands for about the last ten years. Then, at Juilliard, I had an opportunity to strengthen my classical, musical background. Sometime during this period I began to be dissatisfied with what was happening to our present day music and the direction, or rather, non-direction, it was taking. This is where I first began to experiment with the idea of combining the elements which I felt were the strongest of classical and jazz composition together to give us a more meaningful and progressive, if you will, type of expression. I surely do not feel that I have been entirely successful in this yet, but, like others, feel very strongly that it is something that needs to be done and that many worthwhile advances in music could come from such conscientious effort to improve our standard of composition.

To date I have written thirteen major works which have all been performed publically; most of them within the past year in New York City. Among these works are several collections of quartets, duets, and some short pieces for piano which have been performed in various music classes at the Juilliard School of Music.

I believe I should mention here also that while a student at Juilliard I organized and let a dance band that played for Juilliard functions such as dances, etc. This was done with the consent of the administration. We also played several times for the Bandstand U.S.A. show over radio W.O.R. and gave several benefit performances at local veterans and mental hospitals. This, of course, does not bear on my project, but does, I believe, add to my knowledge of the current danceband, music field.

segments.title: Opening and birthplace in Wilkes-Barre coal country
segments.summary: Interview opens with Challis's birth in Wilkes-Barre on July 8, 1904, and talk of the anthracite coal region, Scranton and the Scranton Sirens.

segments.title: Musical family: sister, uncle, grandfather
segments.summary: Nobody in the family was seriously musical; his sister played piano and he thumped out harmony by ear.

segments.title: Violin traded for a C-melody saxophone and lessons
segments.summary: He gave up the violin for a Wurlitzer C-melody saxophone, took lessons from a Bohemian clarinetist and was soon invited to play paid jobs.

segments.title: Listening to the Original Dixieland Jazz Band and the All Star Trio
segments.summary: He played along with ODJB records, copying saxophonist Benny Krueger, and copied Wheeler Wadsworth's C-melody solo on Just Blue.

segments.title: Non-union bands, failing the union test and getting in
segments.summary: Early local bands had no bottom; he flunked his union reading test, then got in when pianist Freddie Small vouched for him.

segments.title: High school orchestra and playing five nights a week
segments.summary: He joined the high school orchestra, played dances five nights a week and summers at Harvey's Lake.

segments.title: Learning tunes from records and working out the harmony
segments.summary: He picked up tunes and chords from records, supplying harmony to the band while improvising the ODJB way.

segments.title: Race records, Johnny Dunn, Miff Mole and slow blues
segments.summary: He rarely heard black records, then called race records, and describes Johnny Dunn, the growl, and blues at slow tempo; Ethel Waters came later.

segments.title: Saxophone styles of the day, slap-tonguing and slow dances
segments.summary: He disliked slap-tongue noises, preferred tone and a straight melody, and recalls playing slow blues for black dances.

segments.title: Arriving at Bucknell and playing in Diffy's orchestra
segments.summary: At Bucknell he joined Diffendaffer's dance band for the fraternity dance circuit, playing fox trots, waltzes and light classics.

segments.title: Leading his own Bucknell orchestra and the Whiteman model
segments.summary: He took over the band for his remaining years, enlarged it, and used the Whiteman orchestra and its players as his model.

segments.title: Liberal arts studies and writing arrangements by ear
segments.summary: He studied liberal arts, never formally arranging, and worked out parts by ear and chord names.

segments.title: Growing the band and a trip to record at Edison
segments.summary: With more saxophones in the band, he describes a Lafayette College group making an acoustic Edison record.

segments.title: Hearing Whiteman live and the fuller orchestral sound
segments.summary: He heard Whiteman at Wilkes-Barre, praised Ross Gorman on Rhapsody in Blue, and relates fuller bands to better phonographs.

segments.title: Waring's band and roommate Hack Gibson
segments.summary: Traveling bands like Mason-Dixon and Fred Waring's played the college, with his roommate Hack Gibson booking for them.

segments.title: The Scranton Sirens offers and the Dorseys
segments.summary: He turned down the Scranton Sirens twice, after sitting in with Freddie Small and leader Billy Lustig, and recalls hearing the Dorseys there.

segments.title: Summer jobs, sitting in with traveling bands, and plans for law school
segments.summary: He played summers with local bands, sat in with Waring and Dave Harman, and intended to go to law school.

segments.title: Syracuse restaurant job and Vincent Lopez's offer
segments.summary: His band played a Chinese-American restaurant in Syracuse where Vincent Lopez offered them a hotel job they turned down.

segments.title: Back in Wilkes-Barre: his father and bandleader Guy Hall
segments.summary: After graduating he was undecided; his father was street superintendent, and Guy Hall, composer of Johnson Rag, led a local band.

segments.title: Joining Dave Harman's band in Williamsport
segments.summary: He replaced saxophonist Joe Venuti in Harman's band and began writing arrangements for them.

segments.title: Toledo, Detroit and the Sirens men now with Goldkette
segments.summary: On a Toledo job he visited his brother in Detroit and found former Sirens men in the Goldkette band.

segments.title: Russ Morgan, Charlie Horvath and a first arrangement for Goldkette
segments.summary: Russ Morgan took him to meet manager Charlie Horvath, who asked for a trial arrangement; Challis explains the Goldkette bands around Detroit.

segments.title: Writing for Guy Hall, the Book-Cadillac band and law school doubts
segments.summary: He left Harman, arranged for local bands, sent a semiclassical arrangement to Detroit, and debated law school.

segments.title: The Goldkette band plays his arrangement at the Cinderella Ballroom
segments.summary: Goldkette's band, with Trumbauer and Bix, came through Wilkes-Barre and played his Baby Face arrangement.

segments.title: Earlier encounters with Bix and the Goldkette band split
segments.summary: He had earlier heard Bix with the Wolverines and describes how the Goldkette band was reorganized that summer.

segments.title: Ray Ludwig, the Blue Room arrangement and the invitation to join
segments.summary: Ludwig asked for more arrangements; after Blue Room came a phone call inviting him to join the band.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Joining the band, first rehearsal and heading to New York
segments.summary: He travelled to Massachusetts with his instruments, heard his arrangements played and was told of the Roseland engagement.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Hearing Bix's piece that became In a Mist
segments.summary: Trumbauer and Bix played the unfinished piece, and Challis felt the musicians were far above him.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Hired as arranger: the band's few arrangements and Trumbauer's book
segments.summary: Horvath said saxophonists were plentiful but arrangers were not; Trumbauer's St. Louis arrangements and Don Murray's work are discussed, with Jack Pettis.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Waiting for tunes, learning to score and the Roseland debut
segments.summary: Challis admits he did not know what scoring was, while the band waited for hit tunes and then impressed Roseland audiences.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Jean Goldkette, Horvath and who fronted the band
segments.summary: Goldkette never appeared with the band, Horvath had been a fine drummer, and nobody led it except Ray Ludwig starting tempos.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Trumbauer's ambitions and the Red Nichols example
segments.summary: Trumbauer wanted to lead and record in New York as Red Nichols did and wanted Challis as arranger.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Reconstructing Bix and Trumbauer arrangements for students and the band's sound
segments.summary: He wrote out the flag-waver arrangements for an NEA-funded concert and describes the band's rich sound.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's band at Roseland
segments.summary: The Goldkette and Henderson bands alternated at Roseland, with Redman, Buster Bailey and Hawkins, and musicians filled the hall.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Poor tunes, Eddie King and the push to sound like Whiteman
segments.summary: Management assigned weak pop tunes and singers and wanted a Whiteman-style band, suppressing Bix; Sunday and My Pretty Girl were the exceptions.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Lang and Venuti on the records and why they failed commercially
segments.summary: Eddie Lang and Joe Venuti were brought in for recordings, and Challis explains how the band's records made no hits.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Trumbauer fronting, Ludwig and arrangement swaps with Fletcher
segments.summary: Trumbauer stood in front while Ludwig still counted off; Blue Room and possibly Stampede went to Henderson, and he later arranged for Fletcher.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: First stay in New York, Roger Wolfe Kahn's club and Redman
segments.summary: During a month in New York they heard Kahn's band at his society club, and Challis comments on Redman's influence.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Big bands, recorded sound and Jack Kapp at Decca
segments.summary: He compares black and white big bands and how better recording and phonographs let arrangers use fuller sounds, contrasting Decca's demand for vocals.

segments.chapter: With the Goldkette band: Bix and Trumbauer
segments.title: Audiences: college crowds versus ballroom dancers
segments.summary: College students listened closely while ballroom dancers just danced fox trots.

segments.title: Back in Detroit 1927: no direction from the Goldkette organization
segments.summary: He wrote constantly in Detroit, but the organization gave no requests and no feedback.

segments.title: Ostrich Walk with Bix and the Oldsmobile arrangement
segments.summary: He and Bix worked up Ostrich Walk at Goldkette's school, and he wrote In My Merry Oldsmobile for a car company party.

segments.title: Bix's classical listening at the hotel suite
segments.summary: Bix visited Challis's hotel suite to listen to Debussy and other impressionist works.

segments.title: Eastwood Lane and Bix's harmony
segments.summary: Challis explains Eastwood Lane's harmonies and how they resembled Bix's use of sixths, ninths and augmented chords.

segments.title: Bix at the piano and notating his compositions
segments.summary: Challis notated Bix's five piano pieces exactly and describes them as pianistic yet orchestral with a cornet-like melody.

segments.title: Bix dictating saxophone choruses and trumpet voicings
segments.summary: Bix dictated saxophone choruses such as Ostrich Walk and Challis harmonized three-part trumpet passages under his lead.

segments.title: Hoagy Carmichael, Stardust and Trumbauer's influence
segments.summary: Challis agrees Hoagy absorbed Bix and Trumbauer in Stardust, praises his early tunes, and Gitler mentions Lester Young.

segments.chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
segments.title: Opening of Cassette 2: Back in Detroit and the Pollack admiration
segments.summary: The second cassette begins with the easy Detroit pace and the band's admiration for Ben Pollack.

segments.chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
segments.title: Trip to Chicago to hear Ben Pollack and Benny Goodman
segments.summary: The Goldkette men drove to Chicago to hear Pollack's band, especially the drum and clarinet feature with Goodman.

segments.chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
segments.title: The Pollack band visits the Greystone
segments.summary: Pollack's musicians came to Detroit to hear the Greystone band; Challis recalls Teagarden and Glenn Miller.

segments.chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
segments.title: Spring 1927 road trip, Cork O'Keefe and decline of the dance business
segments.summary: O'Keefe booked a road trip finishing in Atlantic City while radio began to hurt dance business and tunes lasted longer.

segments.chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
segments.title: Bob-Lo boats and the band that became Casa Loma
segments.summary: While Goldkette was away, Challis wrote for a Detroit band playing the Bob-Lo boats that later became the Casa Loma orchestra.

segments.chapter: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
segments.title: Atlantic City: still no direction from management
segments.summary: At Atlantic City he did few arrangements because no one directed the band's writing.

segments.title: Whiteman visits Atlantic City and conducts the Goldkette band
segments.summary: Whiteman, Busse, the Rhythm Boys and Malneck drove down; Whiteman led the band in St. Louis Blues to huge applause as Goldkette arrived.

segments.title: The Goldkette band breaks up and Whiteman's offer
segments.summary: Goldkette's men could not get bookings; Whiteman told them to join him, and Challis was told to come to the Paramount on September 20.

segments.title: Why the Whiteman band looked like an advancement
segments.summary: The large Whiteman orchestra, with Grofe, Jimmy Dorsey, Chester Hazlett and a film planned, appealed to the young arranger.

segments.title: Adrian Rollini's New Yorkers offer and the choice to join Whiteman
segments.summary: Rollini tried to take the Goldkette men to the New Yorker Hotel; Challis chose Whiteman and could not persuade Bix and Trumbauer to follow.

segments.title: Clementine: the last Goldkette head arrangement
segments.summary: Doc Ryker pushed the band to work up Clementine at the final Victor date, with a strong Bix chorus.

segments.title: Joining Whiteman on the road and enlarging old Goldkette arrangements
segments.summary: Challis joined in Boston, roomed with Jimmy Dorsey and rewrote his Goldkette arrangements for the large Whiteman instrumentation.

segments.title: Writing on tour with a pump organ
segments.summary: He worked in hotel rooms with a small pump organ, still learning arranging by hearing the chords.

segments.title: Hoagy Carmichael plays Washboard Blues in Indianapolis
segments.summary: In the early hours Whiteman and Jimmy Dorsey brought Hoagy to Challis's room; he arranged Washboard Blues around Hoagy's singing.

segments.title: Steve Brown joins and the Whiteman stage repertoire
segments.summary: He recommended Steve Brown for the band and describes Whiteman's stage show of Rhapsody in Blue, Chloe and the 1812 Overture.

segments.title: Bix and Trumbauer join Whiteman; the Washboard Blues record and Changes
segments.summary: Bix and Trumbauer joined in Indianapolis; Challis added a small jazz group to the Hoagy record and used all the singers on Changes.

segments.title: Tommy Dorsey quits and Bill Rank replaces him
segments.summary: Tommy decided to leave in Chicago; Challis recruited Bill Rank, and Tommy impressed the band playing Louis Armstrong choruses on a small trumpet.

segments.title: The jazz band Whiteman never used
segments.summary: Challis regrets he never suggested using Bix, Trumbauer and the Dorseys as a jazz band within the orchestra.

segments.title: Working with Ferde Grofe, who picked good tunes for him
segments.summary: Grofe was kind to him and passed him good tunes, unlike the competitive arranging staffs he knew elsewhere.

segments.title: Notating In a Mist with Bix and Jack Robbins's added theme
segments.summary: Publisher Jack Robbins asked him to get Bix's piano piece on paper, which took about six months and ended with Bix improvising an ending and a slow theme.

segments.title: Victor recordings, Lonely Melody and Whiteman's arrangers
segments.summary: He discusses Victor and later Columbia sessions in this period and who arranged what, including Satterfield and Lenny Hayden.

segments.title: Venuti and Lang and the California movie trip
segments.summary: Challis stayed in New York while Whiteman went west; Venuti and Lang were in the band by then.

segments.title: Ravel at a Victor rehearsal and Bix's part in Grofe's suite
segments.summary: Ravel visited a rehearsal and noticed Hazlett's subtone; Bix rehearsed his part in a Grofe suite, though not a strong reader.

segments.title: Arranging Vincent Youmans's music for Fletcher Henderson
segments.summary: Henderson asked him to arrange Great Day music for Youmans, who played songs and had Marian Harris sing them; Youmans loved the results.

segments.title: Great Day recording, Andy Secrist and Mildred Bailey
segments.summary: He arranged Youmans songs for Whiteman on the coast; Bix was absent, Mildred Bailey sang, and Whiteman wanted the Great Day record recalled.

segments.title: Declining to go west and staying in New York to find tunes
segments.summary: The band returned from California raving about the trip; Challis stayed in New York to deal with publishers while they filmed.

segments.title: The Depression, King of Jazz and its Roxy flop
segments.summary: The picture was a bust and the Roxy show with Gershwin drew nobody, ending the band's good run.

segments.title: Fired when Whiteman cut the band to sixteen pieces
segments.summary: Whiteman told him he was fired as he downsized, and eight men left together.

segments.title: Bix after Whiteman and studio reading skills
segments.summary: Challis doubts the story that Whiteman offered Bix a job later, explaining Bix could read but lacked studio expertise.

segments.title: The radio show and the shrinking band
segments.summary: The Whiteman band was now on radio with Roy Bargy in front, records weren't selling, and the band shrank for the summer.

segments.title: Radio arranging pace: Bargy and Hayden versus Grofe and Challis
segments.summary: Bargy and Hayden turned out many fast arrangements for extra pay while Challis and Grofe plodded along at two a week.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Freelancing after Whiteman and working for Nat Shilkret
segments.summary: He wrote for Willard Robinson and Don Voorhees but mostly for Nat Shilkret's radio work for about three years.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Arranging for Casa Loma and Fletcher Henderson at Connie's Inn
segments.summary: He wrote and rehearsed arrangements for Casa Loma and Henderson, including My Gal Sal and Stardust, and recalls Henderson's sidemen.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Swing Era neglect and Glenn Miller's remark about Bix
segments.summary: In the studios during the swing years, Miller asked for arrangements, never used them, and remarked that they were Bix-like.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Casa Loma at the Paramount and standby pay
segments.summary: He wrote for Casa Loma at 75 dollars each and was offered union standby pay instead.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Dick Himber's Studebaker Champions with Artie Shaw
segments.summary: He arranged for Himber's group, which featured Shaw's subtone clarinet and a string section.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Tommy Dorsey and Artie Shaw start their own bands
segments.summary: Dorsey and Shaw formed bands and Challis stayed contentedly in the studios, not seeking work with them.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Artie Shaw's new band: Lena Horne record and Lips Page arrangements
segments.summary: Shaw's lawyer called him to write for the new band; they made a Lena Horne record and he arranged Blues in the Night before Shaw joined the Navy.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Bonnie Lake and Ray Conniff in the Shaw band
segments.summary: He names Jack Jenney's wife Bonnie Lake, who sang with Shaw and wrote the Dorsey Brothers theme, and recalls Ray Conniff.

segments.chapter: Freelance and studio work in New York
segments.title: Rejoining Casa Loma as the Glen Gray orchestra and the Kate Smith show
segments.summary: O'Keefe asked him to work for Glen Gray's band, which he did for nearly five years, including a Florida stint, alongside the Kate Smith show.

segments.title: After the war: scaling down in the 1950s and 60s
segments.summary: He moved to Forestville in 1944, did few jobs in the 50s and 60s, and did not revive until the 1970s.

segments.title: Bill Borden and recording Bix's piano pieces
segments.summary: Bill Borden asked at the Hot Platter Club for something to record, leading him to work out Bix's piano pieces for a 1974 album.

segments.title: Goldkette arrangements, the NEA grant and the Disney World offer
segments.summary: He reconstructed the Goldkette arrangements from records, applied for an NEA grant, and refused to perform them with little rehearsal at Disney World.

segments.title: Venuti, Sudhalter and the Williams College Whiteman library
segments.summary: Others copied his Whiteman arrangements from Williams College and performed them in England without paying him.

segments.title: Time-Life Beiderbecke project and the lack of payment
segments.summary: Sudhalter, working for Time-Life, asked for information without pay, which irked him.

segments.title: Office job in the 1960s and television work for Bernie Green
segments.summary: He spent over a year as a cement company dispatcher while still doing some TV orchestrations for Bernie Green.

segments.title: Joe Venuti and Eddie Lang as colleagues
segments.summary: Challis never found Venuti difficult, used him and Lang on Goldkette sessions, and worked with Lang later.

segments.title: Glen Gray's nickname Spike and the Venuti connection
segments.summary: Glen Gray was called Spike, and Venuti had played in the Goldkette band before Challis.

segments.title: Visiting Venuti's wartime band in Miami
segments.summary: During wartime shortages Venuti hired two girl saxophonists from the union and laughed through their poor playing; Challis explains his hiring problems with 4-F musicians.

segments.title: Bing Crosby with the Whiteman band
segments.summary: He remembers Bing as ambitious, musical and funny, recalls the Rhythm Boys' start, and says Crosby drew on Jolson, Bix and Louis.

segments.title: Frank Trumbauer: ambition, Indian ancestry and flying
segments.summary: He describes Trumbauer as a nice man who wanted big money and a band, and was a keen pilot, like Roger Wolfe Kahn.

segments.title: Why the C-melody saxophone faded
segments.summary: The C-melody lacked printed parts, since orchestrations were written for alto and tenor.

segments.title: Start of Cassette 3
segments.summary: Cassette 2 ends and Cassette 3 begins with the transcription headers.

segments.title: Arranger versus orchestrator: radio cuts and commercial breaks
segments.summary: By the 1930s radio dictated brief orchestrations that were cut for announcements, unlike his freer 1920s arranging.

segments.title: Bernie Green and television orchestration
segments.summary: He praises Bernie Green's method of handing him sketches for TV specials, including the Martin and Merman show.

segments.title: Mark Warnow and the Lucky Strike formula
segments.summary: His arrangement for Lucky Strike worked without brass in the first chorus, and the director rejected the experiment.

segments.title: A Detroit beer program and Phil Wall's quick arrangements
segments.summary: A sponsor told him not to educate listeners with divided strings, and he would not copy Phil Wall's fast formula arrangements.

segments.title: The Kate Smith show: every section must be heard
segments.summary: The show demanded sixteen bars featuring every brass and sax player, and he admits he was an unsuccessful radio orchestrator.

segments.title: Working for Nat Shilkret on radio
segments.summary: Shilkret was more of a musician, never cut him down, and the Saturday evening show had good sidemen but lasted one season.

segments.title: Arranging for Duke Ellington and Irving Mills
segments.summary: He wrote Stardust and one other arrangement for Ellington, and Irving Mills had expected something more spectacular.

segments.title: Meeting Ellington at the Cotton Club and the Bobby Hackett Decca album
segments.summary: He recalls meeting Ellington and recording a Decca album with Bobby Hackett in the Glen Gray band.

segments.title: Red Nichols in the Glen Gray band and O'Keefe
segments.summary: Red Nichols joined Gray's band after leaving factory work during the war, with manager O'Keefe a neighbor from the 1920s.

segments.chapter: Glen Gray band: Red Nichols and Bobby Hackett
segments.title: Red Nichols asks to join the Glen Gray band
segments.summary: Challis, who did the hiring of 4-F wartime musicians, doubted Nichols's temperament but O'Keefe overruled him.

segments.chapter: Glen Gray band: Red Nichols and Bobby Hackett
segments.title: Nichols works his way up the trumpet section
segments.summary: Nichols started on fourth trumpet to rebuild his lip while younger wartime trumpeters guarded their parts.

segments.chapter: Glen Gray band: Red Nichols and Bobby Hackett
segments.title: Nichols's solo on Don't Take Your Love from Me and his departure
segments.summary: Challis wrote Nichols a chorus, which was one of his best, then Nichols fronted the band when Gray was ill and left claiming he was held down.

segments.chapter: Glen Gray band: Red Nichols and Bobby Hackett
segments.title: Finding Bobby Hackett and bringing him into the band
segments.summary: Challis met a drunken Hackett on 52nd Street and got him hired after getting his horn out of hock.

segments.chapter: Glen Gray band: Red Nichols and Bobby Hackett
segments.title: Hackett stops drinking and later career
segments.summary: Hackett swore off drinking after attending AA meetings, improved in the band, made the Decca album and later worked in radio and with small groups.

segments.title: Willard Robison's Deep River Orchestra and William Grant Still
segments.summary: He describes Robison's spiritual-based music and recalls William Grant Still as one of Whiteman's staff arrangers.

segments.title: Shilkret's package shows and Robison arrangements credited to Eddie Sauter
segments.summary: At Robison's Tuckahoe house Challis arranged Mildred Bailey numbers that were credited to Eddie Sauter.

segments.title: Robison's rehearsals and business troubles
segments.summary: Robison had fine studio musicians but was a poor businessman who lost his home.

segments.chapter: Bix after Whiteman and his piano pieces
segments.title: Bix on a big NBC radio band and the director who interfered
segments.summary: When Bix, back from Davenport, joined a Shilkret radio show, a director hovered over his solo and he was soon off the show.

segments.chapter: Bix after Whiteman and his piano pieces
segments.title: Bix's last years, where he lived and his death
segments.summary: Challis lost touch with Bix, heard of his death from a Whiteman man, and reflects on his lack of studio skills.

segments.chapter: Bix after Whiteman and his piano pieces
segments.title: Bix's piano pieces sound alike; transcribing Davenport Blues
segments.summary: He explains the family resemblance of Bix's pieces and how he wrote Davenport Blues from a record after Bix's death.

segments.chapter: Bix after Whiteman and his piano pieces
segments.title: For No Reason at All in C and why he refused to notate it
segments.summary: He declined to transcribe it because it was improvisation on I'd Climb the Highest Mountain with little thematic material.

segments.chapter: Bix after Whiteman and his piano pieces
segments.title: Notating In a Mist and Candlelights for Jack Robbins
segments.summary: He recounts getting In a Mist down on paper, adding the broad theme, then Candlelights, flashes and In the Dark in the same formula.

segments.chapter: Bix after Whiteman and his piano pieces
segments.title: What Bix might have become
segments.summary: Challis imagines Bix developing his piano works and recording like Harry James or Kaempfert if he had lived.

segments.title: Going backwards: how he learned scoring
segments.summary: He describes backing into arranging, learning scoring from Goldkette and Whiteman, then technique in radio.

segments.title: Radio background music and the Kate Smith dramas
segments.summary: Radio increasingly wanted dramatic background music, which he could not do for Kate Smith's dramas.

segments.title: Start of Cassette 4
segments.summary: Cassette 4 begins with transcription headers.

segments.title: Deciding to study Schillinger for radio background writing
segments.summary: Dance orchestras were dying and he joined other arrangers in studying with Schillinger for connotative music.

segments.title: Schillinger lessons and his death
segments.summary: Lessons were mathematical, rhythm first, and after about two and a half years Schillinger died.

segments.title: Schillinger course at NYU with Eubie Blake as a classmate
segments.summary: He finished the NYU course under the GI bill, with Eubie Blake and Eddie Barefield in his class, and found he lacked the talent for background writing.

segments.title: Teaching Schillinger: Nat Shilkret and few pupils
segments.summary: He got a teaching certificate, but had few pupils, among them Nat Shilkret.

segments.title: Hindsight: arrangers who went to Hollywood
segments.summary: He wishes he had had Schillinger earlier, and notes that bands and arrangers moved to Hollywood for money.

segments.title: The Jazz Age, swing and the shift from two-beat to eight-to-the-bar rhythm
segments.summary: He contrasts two-beat 1920s music and the later influence of Latin rhythms, and notes the shortage of early records.

segments.title: Reviving the Goldkette book and the sound of the bass
segments.summary: He refused to let a modern bassist play four beats in the Goldkette concert, and compares Steve Brown's slap to percussive wooden noises.

segments.title: Singers take over and the end of orchestral dance music
segments.summary: He admires Sinatra's arrangers, says singers took over after dance bands faded, and ends his story.

segments.title: Brief interruption
segments.summary: A recording interruption follows the end of the interview.

segments.title: Addendum: Challis and Manhattan Transfer
segments.summary: Gitler adds that Challis worked on a Manhattan Transfer Atlantic album because they thought he arranged Sunny Disposition.

segments.summary: An unrelated statement by Attilio Macero about his compositions and combining jazz and classical elements is appended.
